A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia and information obtained from the White County Emergency Management Director confirmed that flash flooding had occurred at several locations in White County as a result of heavy rain associated with the remnants of tropical storm Fay.  Cumulative rainfall of six to eight inches fell across much of White county during the 5-day period that Fay affected the area.  However, in excess of three inches of this rainfall occurred on the 26th.  Flash flooding was observed along the Chattahoochee River at Helen when the river reached the flood stage of six feet at 230 pm EDT.  Minor flooding of parks and tubing businesses along the river was observed.  In addition, Brucken Strasse near the Ramada Inn was temporarily closed because of flooding and a sidewalk along Troll Tavern was also closed.  Approximately five miles west-northwest of Cleveland, a culvert pipe and asphalt road were washed out at 277 Mill Lane from flash flooding.  Finally, approximately four miles northwest of Cleveland, Towns Creek rose out of its banks and flooded several yards in portions of the Paradise Valley Campground.  Towns Creek went into flood at Adair Mill Road overflowing the culvert with at least one foot of water flowing over the road.  Finally, there was a mudslide on Kellum Valley Road approximately five miles northwest of Cleveland causing temporary closure of the road.  The mudslide was 15 feet wide by 20 feet tall.  With the exception to damage to Mill Lane, damage from these incidents was minor and mainly in the form of debris cleanup.

The Lumpkin County Emergency Management Director confirmed that flash flooding had occurred at several locations in eastern Lumpkin county as a result of very heavy rainfall caused by the remnants of tropical storm Fay.  Five-day total rainfall for the eastern portion of the county was in the six to eight inch range, but three to four inches of this fell on this day alone, resulting in flash flooding.  A mudslide was observed on Corporate Road upstream from the Chestatee River Bridge approximately 5.4 miles east-northeast of Dahlonega.  This resulted in the temporary closure of Corporate Road in this area.  The mudslide was 20 feet by 60 feet tall.  A culvert pipe on Wahoo Creek Road, a gravel road was washed out by flood waters.  This was located approximately 7.9 miles east of Dahlonega.  Finally, a stream crossing under Mount Olive Church Road, approximately 6.4 miles southeast of Dahlonega, overflowed its banks by at least a foot resulting in minor flooding of upstream agricultural fields.  Approximately six miles east of Dahlonega, a stream overflowed onto Georgia Highway 115 near Grindale Brothers Road by at least one foot.  Finally, Pecks Mill Creek overflowed its banks at the Pecks Mill Creek Road Bridge with at least two feet of water over the road.  Significant erosion occurred and the culvert pipe was damaged.  With the exception of this later incident, overall damage was minor and mostly in the form of debris cleanup.

The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down across the county from two miles southwest of Canton, to seven miles southeast of Canton to Ballground in the northern part of the county.  Power lines were brought down with the trees in several instances and several roads were blocked as a result.  Wind gusts of 49 mph were measured at the Canton Emergency Operations Center at 845 am EDT.  All together at least six trees and at least four power lines were downed.  A home was damaged two miles southwest of Canton when a large tree fell onto the structure.  A large tree was down on power lines in downtown Ballground blocking the road.  A large tree was also down on power lines seven miles southeast of Canton blocking a road.  Trees were also down on power lines five miles southeast of Canton.  Two large trees were down on a power line five miles north of Canton, also blocking the road.  Finally, a large tree was down four miles northwest of Canton.

The Towns County Emergency Management Director reported that flash flooding was observed along the Hiawassee River just west of Georgia Highway 75 south of Hiawassee in the Enchanted Valley Resort trailer park.  The river reached a stage of 10.0 feet approximately one mile downstream from the USGS stream gage on Riverside Drive.  The primary impact of the flooding was the wash up of debris into the backyards of several trailer homes.  Minor flood damage occurred to the lower portions of some storage sheds.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia and the Hall County Emergency Management Agency confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down approximately six miles north-northeast of Gainesville, or about 3 miles east-southeast of Murrayville near Mount Vernon Road and tracked on the ground for approximately one mile before lifting.  Nearly 200 trees were uprooted or blown down.  The downed trees and wind caused damage to approximately 20 homes in the area.  The maximum path width of the tornado was about 200 yards.  Maximum wind speed in the tornado was estimated to be 90 mph.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia and the Hall County Emergency Management Agency confirmed that a second tornado had touched down in Hall county.  This was an EF1 tornado and occurred in the southwest part of the county.  The tornado was broken into two segments, the first 3/4 mile long and the second 2.25 miles long.  The tornado first touched down about one mile southwest of Oakwood and traveled on the ground for approximately 3/4 mile before lifting.  Within this segment of the tornado 20 to 30 trees were knocked down in the area.  Up to 10 homes in the area sustained minor roof damage.  Oakwood Elementary School also suffered minor damage.  Maximum path width for this segment of the tornado was 100 yards.  About five minutes later the tornado touched down again, this time approximately 4 3/4 mile southwest of Gainesville.  This time the tornado was on the ground for 2.25 miles with a maximum path width of 200 yards.  Within this segment of the tornado, dozens of trees were uprooted or blown over.  Up to 15 homes in the El Rancho Estates Subdivision suffered at least minor roof damage from the downed trees and wind.  Lyman Elementary School also sustained minor damage.  Maximum wind for this tornado was estimated to be 90 mph.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City and the Hall County Emergency Management Agency confirmed that yet a third tornado associated with the remnants of tropical storm Fay touched down in Hall county.  This brief tornado touched down just southwest of Gillsville in the extreme northeast part of Hall county and lifted just before reaching the Banks county line.  The majority of the damage along this 3/4 mile-long path was done near the city of Gillsville.  At least 20 trees were uprooted or blown over along the path of tornado.  In addition, the roof was blown off one home at the intersection of Timber Ridge and Hewell Road.  Three other homes sustained minor to moderate damage from the wind and downed trees.  The maximum path width was determined to be 100 yards.  Maximum wind within the tornado was estimated to be 90 mph.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City and the Jackson County Emergency Management Agency confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down and caused considerable damage in northeast Jackson county.  The tornado initially touched down very briefly about three miles east-northeast of Arcade near the Brockton Loop before lifting.  Only minor damage to tree limbs was noted in this area.  The tornado then touched down again within the city of Commerce and tracked approximately 1.25 miles through the city before lifting before reaching the Banks county line.  Approximately 40 trees were uprooted or blown over by the tornado, which caused extensive damage to homes in the area.  A total of three mobile homes were destroyed, one by wind, and two others from downed trees, while up to 15 site-built homes sustained minor roof damage.  Three residents of the destroyed mobile homes were treated for injuries.  The maximum path width of the tornado, within the city of Commerce, was determined to be 100 yards.  Maximum wind within the tornado was estimated to be 100 mph.

The Taliaferro County Sheriff's Department observed a flash flood along a stream that flows into Lick Creek, approximately 1.7 miles northeast of Crawfordville.  The stream washed out a portion of Old Sandy Road, a dirt and rock road.  Severe erosion occurred around the drainage culvert pipe.

The Macon Telegraph reported that 12 people, nine adults and three teenagers, were injured when lightning struck a goal post on the football field at Bonaire Middle School during a Thursday evening football game.  The athletic director from the opposing school, Warner Robins, was left in critical condition and transferred to a burn center along with three of the other adults.

The Pickens County Progress reported that lightning struck two homes west of Jasper.  A home on Hobson Drive was struck and set on fire causing considerable electrical and smoke damage to the home.  However, the house was apparently not destroyed.  Another home in the 3600 block of Georgia Highway 53 was also struck and set on fire by lightning.  The home was completely destroyed.
The Daily Tribune of Cartersville reported that lightning struck homes on homes on Vigilant Street and Harris street in Atco.  Damage was minimal in both incidents.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a very brief EF0 tornado had touched down in the northeast part of the Fayette Pavilion Shopping center, just north of downtown Fayetteville located between Georgia Highways 314 and 85.  The tornado caused the back wall of the two-story Christian Bookstore to buckle outward.  An air conditioning unit was also blown off the roof pad of the adjacent Marshalls Department store.  A few trees behind these buildings were also blown down.  Minor damage was also observed to the facade and utility lines of adjacent buildings.  The tornado path length was 150 yards long with a maximum path width of 50 yards.

A deputy with the Wilcox County Sheriff's Department observed baseball-sized hail in the Rochelle area.  The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the far northern part of the county in the Pineview area.  Several car windshields were observed to have been damaged in the area.

The Wilcox County Emergency Management Director reported that thunderstorm winds resulted in damage to several chicken houses.  The roof was blown off nine chicken homes and five others were left leaning slightly.

The Pulaski County Emergency Management Director reported quarter-sized hail north of Pineview and nickel-sized hail was reported in Finleyson.  Golf ball-sized hail was also reported in Wilcox county near the Pulaski county line.  Radar data supports hail of quarter or larger size from the Wilcox county line just south of Finleyson to just north of Wallace.

A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia and information from the the Fayette county Emergency Management Director confirmed that thunderstorm winds had blown down over a dozen trees in the northwest part of the county between Tyrone and the Fulton county line.  Up to a dozen trees were blown down along Arrowhead Road and superficial damage was observed to office buildings along Palmetto road.  Along Meadowbrook Road, off Senoia Road, a couple of power lines were also down.

The Macon Telegraph reported that very strong winds blew down numerous trees and dozens of power lines throughout the county.  At least 10,000 people in the Bloomfield and north Macon area left without power for several hours following the incident.  In addition, a large window was shattered at the Acapulco Mexican Restaurant in downtown Macon was shattered by the high winds.  At least seven other buildings in the downtown area sustained window damage from the high winds.  There were also several reports of garage doors being blown in by the strong winds.  Doppler radar base velocity data showed 50-60 knot winds affecting much of Bibb county on the back side of a rain area moving eastward through the county during this time frame.
The Twiggs County 911 Center reported that two trees and one power line were blown down in the southern portion of the county.
The Wilkinson County 911 Center reported that six trees were blown down, scattered about the county.
The Laurens County 911 Center reported that at least six trees were blown down, scattered about the county.

The Baldwin County 911 Center reported that from six to nine trees were blown down, scattered about the county.  Trees were down along Carr Station Road, Highway 243, J.F. Hall Road, and Highway 212 near Meriwether.  The Union Recorder of Milledgeville reported that several of these trees fell on power lines, resulting in power outages to about 6000 customers in the area.
The Toombs County 911 Center reported that at least three trees were blown down near the Toombs and Montgomery county lines.
The Toombs Count 911 Center reported that at least three trees were blown down across Toombs and Montgomery counties.
The Johnson County 911 Center reported that less than 10 trees were blown down, scattered about the county.

The Rockmark Journal reported that strong winds and rain resulted in power outages to approximately 300 residents in the area when tree limbs fell on power lines.  Most of the outages were in the Goodyear Village neighborhood along Third Avenue.

The Laurens County Emergency Management Director and the Courier Herald of Dublin reported thunderstorm wind damage in the far northeast part of the county in the Buckeye area.  A couple of homes suffered minor damage.  A carport roof was blown off, underpinnings from a home were damaged, and an adjacent home had minor roof and porch damage.  A pump house also suffered minor damage.  A window was also broken out of a van parked in the area.  From 15-20 trees were either uprooted or snapped in the area.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, GA concluded that a brief EF0 tornado touched down at the Haralson County High School, approximately three miles east-northeast of Tallapoosa.  The tornado traveled on the ground between 100 and 150 yards with a maximum path width of 50 yards.  The main classroom building suffered the majority of the damage, where a heating and air conditioning unit was blown off the roof and into the adjacent parking lot, causing minor damage to a few cars.  A few windows were also broken and an outdoor scoreboard was destroyed.  Several small trees on the campus were snapped, including one which fell onto the visitor's bleachers.
The Dade County Emergency Management Director reported that thunderstorm winds blew siding off a home, a trestle off a barn, and at least 14 trees down across the county.
WMAZ Television of Macon reported that about three large trees were blown down in northern Dodge county.
The Jones County Emergency Management Director reported that three trees were blown down in and around the Gray area.
The Pulaski County Emergency Management Director reported that three trees were blown down northeast of Hawkinsville.
The Morgan County Emergency Management Director reported that a few trees were blown down in southern Morgan county near the Putnam county line.  U.S. Highway 411 was blocked at the county line.

The Chattooga County 911 Center reported stream and creek flash flooding in at least four different locations.  At least a foot of water was flowing over Ragland Road from a stream two miles southwest of Lyerly.  At least six inches of water was flowing over Spring Creek Road from Spring Creek three miles southeast of Trion.  At least six inches of water was flowing over Hair Lake Road from Raccoon Creek three miles northwest of Summerville.  Finally, six inches of water was flowing over Fish Hatchery Creek Road from a stream four miles west-southwest of Summerville.  Although several roads in the area were closed because of the high water, damage was limited to debris removal.
The Walker County 911 Center reported that up to 10 trees were blown down across the county from thunderstorm winds.

The Forsyth County Emergency Management Director reported that minor flooding occurred along portions of Yellow Creek and Settingdown Creek between Wallace-Tatum and Hurt Bridge Roads.  Damage was confined to minor debris cleanup.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported that several creeks and streams across the county exceeded bank full and resulted in minor flooding.  Six to seven inches of rain fell across this area in less than 24 hours.  Some urban areas also experienced street flooding as well.  At least two roads, including a portion of Georgia Highway 257, had to be closed because of water flowing over the roads.  Damage was limited to minor debris cleanup.

The river gage on Turkey Creek at Byromville rose above flood stage at 215 pm EST on December 11th and remained above bank full stage until 910 am EST on December 12th.  Minor flooding of low lands and agricultural low lands occurred along the creek in this area.  Damage was confined to minor debris cleanup.

The river gage on the Coahulla Creek at Keith's Mill near Dalton recorded that the river rose over 2.5 feet above flood stage during this period.  One road was affected by the flooded creek and was closed for some period.  Otherwise, damage was confined to minor debris cleanup.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of street and highway flooding at Morris Mill Road and Howell Road.  All lanes of Interstate-75 were blocked in this area because of high water, except the HOV lane.  Heavy rain of 1.0 to 1.5 inches fell in about one hour across much of Cobb county as a line of heavy thunderstorms traversed the area during this time frame.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of street and highway flooding on Interstate 85 at Shallowford Road.  Water was reported to be eight to twelve inches deep on the interstate.  Rainfall of 1.0 to 1.5 inches fell across much of western DeKalb county in about one hour as a line of heavy thunderstorms traversed the area during this time frame.
The Wilcox County 911 Center reported that some water was flowing over a road in one spot.  The western part of the county received three to four inches of rain in less than 24 hours.

The gage on the Oconee river at Oconee along the Washington/Wilkinson county line crested around 18.0 feet at 2 am EST December 14th.  The river remained above the flood stage of 17.0 feet from mid-morning on December 13th until late afternoon on December 15th.  Minor flooding of low land agricultural areas near the river occurs.  Damage was limited to minor debris cleanup.

The Zebulon Newspaper reported that a few trees and several tree limbs were blown down across the county when a line of thunderstorms moved through the county from southwest to northeast.  A couple of roads were blocked by downed trees.

The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that two areas in the county suffered from flash flooding.  At least six inches of water from a local stream was flowing over Yukon Road just north of Scarlett Drive.  Approximatly $1000 of erosion damage was observed to the asphalt road.  Further east, another flash flood was observed when flood waters from Holden Creek tore out a 10 by 12 foot section of Big Creek Road just west of Pisgah Road.  Damage to the road was estimated to be $5000.

The gage on the Oconee river at Oconee along the Washington/Wilkinson county line crested around 18.0 feet at 2 am EST December 14th.  The river remained above the flood stage of 17.0 feet from mid-morning on December 13th until late afternoon on December 15th.  At this stage, minor flooding of low land agricultural areas near the river occurs, as well as along the boat ramp near Georgia Highway 57.  Damage was limited to minor debris cleanup.
The U.S. Forest Service reported that a wildfire occurred in the Three Forks area of the Chattahoochee National Forecast.  The wildfire took four days to contain.
The U.S. Forest Service reported that there was a wildfire in the Woody Creek area of the Chattahoochee National Forecast.  The wildfire took three days to contain.

The U.S. Forest Service reported that there was yet another wildfire in Fannin county in the Dry Branch area of the Chattahoochee National Forest.  The fire was contained within about five hours of breaking out.

The ASOS at the Columbus airport recorded a wind gust of 59 mph.  The high winds were associated with a line of showers and a strong low-level jet accompanying a deep upper-level trough sweeping through the region.  Columbus television stations and the Columbus Ledger Inquirer reported that dozens of trees and a number of power lines throughout the county, as well as the city of Columbus, were knocked down by the high winds.  Approximately 12,000 homes in the Columbus area were left without power for several hours following the wind storm.  In addition, the Allstate Insurance Agency on Buena Vista Road lost 20 feet of its metal roof from the high winds.

The Harris County Emergency Management Director reported that high winds knocked down several trees and power lines throughout the county.  The high winds were associated with a line of heavy rain showers moving through the area from southwest to northeast and a strong low-level jet traversing the region ahead of a deep upper-level trough.

WSB TV of Atlanta reported that a police chief was killed during the afternoon in an automobile accident on Georgia Highway 515 in Blue Ridge.  Up to one inch of snow and sleet was observed on the road at the time.  CocoRahs observers and the public reported that up to 1.6 inch of snow had fallen across extreme northwest Fannin county, with up to 1.0 inch in the southern part of the county.
The CoCoRaHS observer in north Dawson county observed 0.3 inch of snow.
The CoCoRaHS observer in east Gilmer county reported 0.7 inch of snow, while the CoCoRaHS observer in northwest Gilmer county observed 0.5 inch of snow.
The CoCoRaHS observers in east and southeast Union county observed 0.3 inch of snow.
The Dade County 911 Center reported some sleet and ice accumulation on Georgia Highway 136 and in the Lookout Mountain area.  A couple of accidents occurred.
The Walker County 911 Center reported that some sleet was observed in the northern and western parts of the county.
The Whitfield County 911 Center reported that sleet fell off and on during the mid and late morning hours.  Brief heavy sleet showers were observed.

The Forsyth County Emergency Management Director reported that the Etowah River had risen out of it banks at Old Federal Road and Nicholson Road in the northwest part of the county.  Nicholson Road was inundated with at least a foot of water near Bannister Creek.  In addition, Setting Down Creek was flooding at Concord and Oak Grove Roads.  Six roads were closed as a result of these flooding incidents.  Windermere Park in the southeast part of the county was also closed as a consequence of flooding from the Etowah River.  Damage was limited to debris removal.

The USGS gage on the Etowah River, 1.5 miles northeast of Canton near Interstate-575, reached flood stage of 17 feet at 1220 pm EST on January 6th and continued at or above flood stage until 702 pm EST.  In addition, the Little River at Georgia Highway 5, two miles northeast of Woodstock, reached flood stage of 11.0 feet briefly at 230 pm EST on January 6th.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The USGS river gage on the Armuchee Creek, three miles southeast of Armuchee at Old Dalton Road, reached flood stage of 19 feet at 615 pm EST on January 6th.  The creek remained in flood stage at this point until January 11th at 1015 am EST.  Then, five miles west-southwest of Armuchee, Health Creek reached flood stage of eight feet for approximately 15 minutes at 1100 pm EST.  Finally, the Coosa River six miles southwest of Rome at the Mayo Lock and Dam reached flood stage of 24 feet and remained in a minor flood state until January 10th at 725 am EST.  Several roads in the county were at least temporarily closed because of high water and flooding.  The Rome News Tribune reported that 62 roads across the county that were closed during the height of the flooding.  In addition, Heritage Park and Ridge Ferry Park were also flooded.  Damage from the flooding resulted in debris removal in portions of the county.

The Banks County Emergency Management Director reported that Webb Creek, approximately four miles southeast of Homer, overflowed its banks at Marshburn Drive.  At least six inches of water was flowing over the road at this location for about two hours.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a brief EF0 tornado touched down four miles east-southeast of Chattoogaville and moved north-northeast paralleling Georgia Highway 100 for just a little over a 2-mile long track.  Spotty tree damage was observed along Old Holland Road and Georgia Highway 100 along the tornado track.  Light to moderate damage was observed to the roofs of three buildings and several outbuildings, some of which may have been a product of straight-line winds.

A CocoRaHS observer on the southeast side of Rome reported that several trees and at least one power line were down in the area.  A wind gust of 61 mph was measured at the Floyd Medical Center in Rome at 530 pm EST.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia determined that flooding occurred on the West Chickamauga Creek, the South Chickamauga Creek, and Peavine Creek.  All of these creeks overflowed their banks and caused minor flooding of adjacent low-lying areas, woodlands, and fields.  The Catoosa County News reported that the Battlewood Apartments off Fant Drive were threatended by flood waters.  Residents of the apartment complex were evacuated as a precaution, but no damage to property occurred.  Overall, damage was limited to debris removal.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia determined that flooding occurred on Racoon Creek at Hair Lake Road, and Spring Creek at Spring Creek Road.  Small streams also overflowed their banks at Fish Hatchery Road and Ragland Road.  In addition, the Chattooga River went into minor flood until the January 8th at 232 AM EST.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.
The Gordon County 911 Center reported that four trees and one power line were down across the northern part of the county.

The Chattahoochee County 911 Center reported that numerous trees were down on Fire Tower Road east of Cusseta and about six trees were down on Georgia Highway 26 east of Cusseta near mile marker number eight.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down near 412 Reedy Creek Road, approximately five miles southeast of Forsyth, then tracked eastward for approximately three miles across southeast Monroe county.  The maximum path width was estimated to be 100 yards.  Maximum winds were estimated at 85 mph.  The tornado moved east across U.S. Highway 41 near the Smarr water tower, then dissipated as it crossed Interstate-75 southeast of the Rumble Road Industrial Park.  One home sustained moderate damage to its roof and siding.  Three other structures sustained minor shingle damage along the path of the tornado.  Trees were sporadically either snapped or uprooted along the path of the tornado.

The USGS stream gage on Oothkalooga Creek at Georgia Highway 53 Spur, one mile south of Calhoun, reached its flood stage of 18 feet at 0300 AM EST on January 7th, and remained at or above flood stage until 1345 on January 7th.  In addition, the Coosawattee River at Pine Chapel Road, five miles east of Resaca, reached flood stage of 22 feet at 0712 AM EST on January 7th and remained above flood stage until 0512 AM EST on January 8th.  The Calhoun Times reported that 36 roads across the county were closed because of flooding.  Two drivers that disregarded barricades had to be rescued from flood waters.  Finally, parts of the Calhoun Recreational Department were flooded for the first time in 10 years.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Whitfield county Emergency Management Director reported that a person sustained minor injuries when a falling tree limb struck them in the head as they were walking along LaFayette Road just southwest of Rocky Face.  One tree fell on an unoccupied home in Dalton, destroying the home.  At least five other trees were blown down within the county.
The Banks County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees and several power lines were blown down on roads across the county.
The Henry County Emergency Management Director reported that four trees were blown down north of McDonough.
The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that a few trees and power lines were blown down.

The Clarke County Emergency Management Director reported that a number of trees, several power lines, and some traffic signals were down, especially within the city of Athens.  Two homes were damaged from downed trees.
The Jackson County Fire and Rescue Department reported that a power pole was blown over onto a mobile home in Jefferson.  The home was set on fire by the downed power line.

The White County Emergency Management Director reported that strong winds associated with a line of showers blew down several trees across the county.  Two homes sustained minor to moderate damage when trees fell on the structures.

The Oglethorpe Echo of Lexington reported that the canopy over the gas pumps at a convenience store located at the intersection of Arnoldsville Road and U.S. Highway 78 collapsed.  The gas pumps were destroyed.

The Atlanta-Journal Constitution reported that a live power line was blown down onto a school bus carrying 30 children.  Georgia Power removed the line from atop the bus and there were no injuries.  At least 5000 people in the area were left without power after the strong winds blew through.
A large 40-inch diameter tree was blown over onto West Avenue at Bartow Street.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported that a human caused wildfire had to be contained at Dockery Gap.  Approximately 0.16 acres of forest were burned.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported that approximately 1/10 of a forest area was burned by a human caused wildfire.  The fire was named 630F.

The Daily Tribune News of Cartersville reported that four roads in the county were closed because of flooding.   These included Parr Wade Bishop and Old Grassdale Roads in Cartersville, Puckett Road in Emerson, and Euharlee Road in the Mission Ridge Subdivision.  The later of which was a result of a collapsed retaining wall.  Damage was limited to minor debris removal.
The Chattooga County 911 Center reported that a power line was blown down in the northwest part of the county and a tree was blown down onto a house in Summerville.

The Dade County Emergency Management Director reported that two power lines and three trees were blown down.  Two of the trees were down in Trenton, while the other was northwest of Trenton in the Dogwood community.  One of the power lines was down northwest of Trenton and the other in Trenton.

The Walker County 911 Center reported that a few trees were blown down in the far southwest part of the county in the 23,000 block of Georgia Highway 157, also known as Lula Lake Road.  A few trees were also down in LaFayette on Cordele Avenue, Chamberlin Road, and Foster Mill Drive.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that six to ten trees were blown down across the county.  A few power lines were also down in the county as well.  The Rome News Tribune indicated that more than 12 trees were down...especially in the Rome, Lindale, and Silver Creek areas.

The Gilmer County 911 Center reported that a few trees were down on Georgia Highway 5 in the northeast part of the county and a few trees were down on Georgia Highway 52 in the southeast part of the county.

The Rockmart Journal and the Cedartown Standard documented two flooding events in Polk county.  Euharlee Creek overflowed its banks in downtown Rockmart submerging a portion of Silver Comet Trail.  A portion of Seaborn James Park was also flooded.  Cedar Creek also overflowed its banks causing temporary flooding of some city streets in Cedartown.  A portion of West Avenue was briefly submerged under several inches of water at the height of the flooding.  Damage was limited to debris removal.

The Pickens County Progress of Jasper reported that heavy rain pushed many creeks in the county out of their banks.  Talking Rock Creek rose from one foot to eight feet.  Part of Talking Rock Highway had to be closed because of a mudslide.  Several other roads were closed because of localized flooding, including Petit, Jordan, Mineral Springs, Fortner, and Thompson Lane.  Damage was limited to debris removal, mostly as a result of the mudslide.

The Daily Citizen of Dalton reported that heavy rain caused flooding on many roads throughout the county.  Some specific roads impacted by high water included Cohutta-Varnell Road, Old Mill Road, Old Cleveland Highway, along with several others.  Damage was confined to debris removal.

The Dalton Citizen of Dalton reported that heavy rain caused several creeks and streams across the county to overflow their banks.  High water forced the closure of several roads.  Approximately 4000 acres of the Perry Farm were flooded by the Conasauga River and Sumach Creek when they came out of their banks.  Mill Creek rose out of its banks and flooded a trailer park on Third Avenue.  Norton Bridge on the north end of the county was flooded and had to be closed as well as parts of Georgia Highway 225 North above Red Cut Road and Patricia Avenue in Spring Place.  Also on Georgia Highway 255, saturated soil from the heavy rain caused a tree to fall on the road blocking the highway in both directions between Spring Place and Central for more than an hour.  In addition, several pastures on Maddox Mill Road were flooded by Cohulla Creek.  Two men stranded in high water near Old Georgia Highway 2 in Cisco had to be rescued and two other men had to be rescued from rising waters while boating down Jacks River.  All were rescued without injury or incident.

The News and Farmer Jefferson Reporter of neighboring Jefferson county reported that strong winds blew a tree over onto a mobile home on Railroad Avenue in Gibson.  The tree fell through the roof of the home trapping a woman and her 3-year old boy in a recliner where they had been watching television.  Although rescue personnel were able to remove them from under the tree, the woman suffered a broken hip.

The Madison County Journal of Danielsville reported that strong winds ripped off part of the tin roof of a home on Georgia Highway 191 in Danielsville.  Parts of the tin roof were found in a nearby oak tree, some drive into the side of the tree like stakes.
The Times Herald of Newnan reported that lightning struck the Coweta County 911 Center.  Damage to the center was minor and service was only briefly disrupted.
The public reported that a tree was blown down onto a power line on Grandview Road.
The Bartow County Emergency Management Director reported that two large trees were uprooted near Pleasant Valley and Clear Creek Roads.
The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director and the public reported that about 10 trees were down north through east of Canton.  One tree was down on a house in Ball Ground.
The Dawson County 911 Center reported that a few trees were blown down on Georgia Highway 53 west of Dawsonville.
The Forsyth County 911 Center reported that a number of trees were blown down across the county.  Radar data supported that most of this likely occurred across the northern half of the county.
The White County 911 Center reported that a few trees were blown down in town.
The White County 911 Center reported that around 30 trees were blown down from Flowery Branch through the Gainesville area.

The Banks County 911 Center reported that eight trees and two power lines were blown down between Wilson Shoals and Pinefield Crossroads.  A storm spotter reported that 12 trees and a couple of power poles were down near U.S. Highway 441 and Line Creek Road.
An amateur radio operator reported that four to five trees were blown down in the far northern part of the county about two miles east-southeast of Ellenwood.

The Macon Telegraph reported that strong winds associated with a line of showers blew down several trees and trees down onto power lines across the county.  One tree fell down on a vehicle.  Scattered power outages were reported in Bibb and surrounding counties of Baldwin, Crawford, Houston, and Taylor as well.
The public observed penny-sized hail in Chattoogaville and Lyerly.
Several reports of large hail, ranging in size from quarters to golf balls were received from the public across northern Floyd county.
The public spotted a funnel cloud about halfway between Rome and Shannon.  Doppler radar indicated a supercell thunderstorm in the area at the this time.
The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that a number of trees were blown down in the far northern portion of the county near the Forsyth county line.

The Forsyth County Emergency Management Director reported that a few trees were blown down in the Buford Dam area at the southern end of Lake Lanier in the far southeast part of the county.  The Forsyth County News reported that the Spondivits restaurant in Cumming had a door ripped off and suffered significant roof damage.
The Forsyth County Emergency Management Director relayed a report of a funnel cloud in the Buford Dam area of the far southeast part of the county on the south end of Lake Lanier.

Several reports of large hail were received from the southern half of the county.  The public observed golf ball-sized hail in Clem.  The Fire Department observed nickel-sized hail in Bowden. The county emergency manager observed penny-sized hail in Carrollton.  Finally, a National Weather Service employee observed quarter-sized hail in Whitesburg in the far southeast corner of the county.  The Target store at McIntosh Plaza suffered considerable roof damage from the hail, causing leaks and damaging merchandise.  The public reported that windshields of vehicles in the area were damaged.

The Carroll County 911 Center relayed reports of funnel clouds and a possible tornado just north of Bowdon near Georgia Highway 100 and Indian Creek Road.  Doppler radar indicated a strong circulation in this area and a tornado warning was in effect at the time.  However, no damage was observed or reported in this area.
The Weather Channel reported quarter-sized hail southeast of Marietta near Vinings and the Fulton county line.  The public reported nickel-sized hail at the Windy Hill Apartments.

Very large hail was observed in far northeast Coweta county.  Numerous reports of large hail were also received from northeast Coweta county.  The hail fell from a supercell that tracked across the northeast part of the county from just south of Palmetto, along the Fulton-Coweta county line to just east of Cannongate along the Fayette county line.  The large hail storm continued into northern Fayette county as well.  The Coweta County Emergency Management County Director reported 4.25 inch diameter hail approximately four miles northeast of Madras near the Fulton county line.  Several reports of golf ball-sized hail were received from the public in the Cannongate area.  Extensive damage to roofs and windows of homes was reported from the area.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director relayed reports of large hail from extreme southern Fulton county near the Coweta and Fayette county lines.  Penny-sized hail was reported in the Chattahoochee Hills area in the far southwest part of the county near the Carroll county line and golf ball-sized hail between Palmetto and Union City near the Fayette county line.  The public observed penny-sized hail in the College Park area.

The Taylor County Emergency Management Director reported that an EF0 tornado touched down near the intersection of Tommy Purvis Junior Road and Eubanks Drive in Reynolds and traveled eastward along a three to four mile long path.  One home was damaged and a mobile home was moved off its foundation.  At least 10 trees were down in the area, including several across one road.  A tractor barn was damaged, the roof was blown off an old store, and a double-wide mobile home was damaged.  The maximum path width was estimated to be 33 yards (100 feet) with maximum winds estimated to be 70 mph.

A storm spotter observed reported golf ball-sized hail in the eastern part of the county.  Location and time were estimated since report and radar data did not match.  The public observed nickel-sized hail in western Peach county.
The public reported nickel to golf-ball sized hail across northern DeKalb county from Chamblee to Tucker.

A deputy with the Gwinnett County Sheriff's office observed larger than golf ball-sized hail in the Lilburn area.  The Gwinnett County 911 Center relayed reports of quarter-sized hail near Lilburn.  Approximately three miles southwest of Snellville, a trained spotter observed quarter-sized hail.  Hail up to three inches in diameter was reported just across the border in Loganville in Walton county as the storm continued moving east-southeast.

Numerous reports of very large hail were received from the Fayette County Emergency Management Director, the public, and off-duty National Weather Service employees across the northern part of the county from Tyronne, across the Sandy Creek and Lees Mill area, east-southeast toward Fayetteville, and to just east-southeast of Fayetteville.  Most of the hail ranged in size from 2.75 to 3.0 inches throughout this area.  Extensive damage was observed to the roofs and windows of homes and automobiles along the path of the supercell thunderstorm.  The Fayette County Emergency Management Director reported that at least $250,000 in damages along was observed to county school skylights and windows.  The public reported extensive damage to the roofs and windows of homes across the northern portion of the county.

The public and an off-duty National Weather Service employee reported very large hail across Clayton county.  This was from the same parent thunderstorm that produced the 3.0 to 4.0 inch diameter hail in northeast Coweta and northern Fayette counties.  Three-inch diameter hail was observed just southwest of Jonesboro in the Irongate subdivision and golf ball-sized hail fell elsewhere from just south of Jonesboro to Lovejoy.

Several reports of large hail were received from the Henry County Emergency Management Director and the public in a swath across southern Henry county extending from just northwest of Hampton to southeast of Ola.  Hail was reported to be the size of quarters near Hampton and quarters to golf balls from southwest of McDonough to southeast of Ola.  Nickel sized-hail was reported when the storm first entered the northwest part of the county near Interstate-75 and Jodoco Road.

Large to very large hail was observed by the public and storm spotters across Walton county from Loganville, to Monroe, to Good Hope.  Three inch-diameter hail was reported from Loganville to Bold Spring along the Gwinnett county line, while quarter to golf ball-sized hail was observed from Monroe to east of Good Hope.  Golf ball-sized hail was also observed around Between.

The official on duty weather observer at Warner Robins Air Force Base reported that a very brief EF0 tornado touched down just off the end of one of the end of the runway and quickly moved into the adjacent woods.  No damage was reported or observed.
A storm spotter observed golf ball-sized hail in the eastern part of Peach county.  Location was estimated by radar data since reported time and radar reflectivity data did not match.

A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia, confirmed that an EF3 tornado touched down in extreme western Oconee county, just east of the Apalachee River near the intersection of U.S. Highway 441 and Tappin Spur Road.  The tornado crossed U.S. 441 between county mile marker two and three, then continued on an almost due eastward track across the southern part of the county.  The tornado lifted near the intersection of Hale Road and Colham Road, about two miles east-southeast of Salem, just shy of the Greene county line.  The tornado path length was approximately five miles long, the maximum path width was estimated to be 1/2 mile, and maximum winds gusts were estimated to be 90 mph.  Extensive damage to trees was observed along the path of the tornado.  U.S. Highway 441 was completely closed for several hours as it was blocked from downed trees.  The most extensive damage to trees occurred within the Georgia Nature Center, where several hundred trees were either blown down, uprooted, or topped along the path of the tornado.  A vehicle was overturned on U.S. 441 as the tornado crossed the highway.  Several homes along the path of the tornado sustained minor room damage and a mobile home was moved off its foundation.  Also, at the Georgia Nature Center, two tent areas were destroyed and several solar panels were damaged.

The Oconee County Emergency Management Director relayed numerous reports of quarter-sized hail across the southern half of Oconee county, generally along and south of a line from North High Shoals, to Bishop, to Farmington, to Salem.

A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia concluded that the same thunderstorm cell that spawned an EF1 tornado across southern Oconee county produced strong damaging straight-line winds in far northeast Greene county, approximately two miles northeast of Woodville.  Twenty-three trees were either uprooted or snapped within an approximately 50-acre wide area of woods.
A Haralson County Sheriff's Deputy observed half-dollar-sized-hail in southern Haralson county.

The Butts County Emergency Management Director reported nickel to golf ball-sized hail across northern and northeastern Butts county.  Nickel-sized hail was observed near Worthville and golf ball-sized hail further southeast toward the Jasper county line.  Half-dollar-sized hail was observed near Lake Jackson.

The public observed half-dollar and slightly larger-sized-hail in the Monticello area.  Radar data supported that hail of this size or larger likely fell in a large swath from the northwest to the east central part of the county.

The Putnam County Emergency Management Director reported golf ball-sized hail in the Eatonton area.  Several reports of golf ball-sized hail were received from the southwest to the northeast part of the county.  Radar supported that hail of this size likely fell across in a swath from west to east near and just north of Georgia Highway 16.

An aerial and ground survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in cooperation with the Putnam County Emergency Management Director confirmed that an EF1 tornado carved an approximate 8-9 mile track across Putnam county very near Georgia Highway 16.  The tornado first touched down near Williard, west of Eatonton and continued on an east-southeastward track toward, lifting very near the Hancock county line.  Much of the resulting damage occurred near Glenwood Springs Road.  A restaurant and two other commercial buildings were completely destroyed on the southwest side of Eatonton.  At least one person was injured from debris in this area.  A number of trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path of the tornado, along with many downed power lines.  U.S. Highway 129, south of Eatonton, was closed for several hours as it was blocked from numerous downed trees and power lines.  Several individuals were trapped in their vehicles in this area.  The tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 3/4 mile.  Maximum winds gusts within the tornado were estimated to have been 110 mph.

An aerial and ground survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia in cooperation with the Jasper county Emergency Management Director confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down in far eastern Jasper county, approximately one mile west of Smithboro.  The tornado continued on a 3-mile long eastward path parallel to and just south of Georgia Highway 16, lifting just before reaching the Putnam county line.  This was one of two EF1 tornadoes to touch down in Jasper county on this date.  The same thunderstorm that spawned this tornado continued on to produce yet another EF1 tornado near Eatonton and later an EF3 tornado in Hancock county.  Several homes near Georgia Highway 16 were damaged, one in Smithboro sustaining major damage.  A saw mill warehouse was destroyed.  Many trees and power lines were down along the path of the tornado.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast office in Columbia, South Carolina, confirmed that an EF3 tornado had tracked across far southern Wilkes county causing considerable damage along its path.  The tornado continued its east-southeastward track into extreme northeastern McDuffie county.  The total tornado path length was 18.6 miles.  The tornado initially touched down in the Tyrone community in southwest Washington county.  Here a cinder block home was completely destroyed with the cinder block debris blown downstream nearly 1/2 mile.  Fifteen other homes along the path of the tornado sustained moderate to major damage from the tornado.  Nineteen outbuildings and a commercial chicken house was destroyed.  In addition, a steeple was blown off a church and a 2-ton truck was moved 60 feet.  The maximum path width was approximately 1/2 mile with maximum winds estimated to be 160 mph.
A police officer reported damage to his vehicle from hail.  Hail size and location were estimated based on radar data since specific information was not provided.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado had touched down in southern Newton county causing extensive damage to some 30 homes in a heavily wooded subdivision just south of High Point.  The tornado touched down near the intersection of King Bostwick Road and Channing Cope Road and travelled approximately three miles almost due east to a point approximately 1/2 mile southeast of the intersection of Henderson Mill Road and Taylor Road.  Damage to the homes was nearly 100 percent the result of downed trees.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that the EF2 tornado that touched down at 923 Bradberry Road, just inside the Meriwether county line, quickly crossed into Coweta county and continued on an east-northeastward track across far southern Coweta county, crossing into Spalding county approximately four miles east-northeast of Haralson.  Within Coweta county the tornado caused minor to moderate damage to several homes.  One home completely lost its roof.  A horse was killed from flying debris near U.S. Highway 27A.  Hundreds of trees were also blown down along the path of the tornado.  The tornado tracked almost 16 miles within Coweta county.  The maximum path width was estimated to be one mile with maximum winds of 120 mph.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that the EF2 tornado that caused extensive damage across southern Coweta county and into Spalding county initially touched down just inside the Meriwether county line at 923 Bradberry Road.  The property at this address straddles the Meriwether/Coweta county line.  Damage within Meriwether county was primarily confined to a fence.  The tornado was likely less intense within its short distance in Meriwether county than its maximum EF2 rating in Coweta and Spalding counties.  The tornado tracked less than 50 feet within Meriwether county.  Maximum path width within Meriwether county was less than 100 feet.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that the tornado that initially touched down in Meriwether county, then tracked across southern Coweta county, crossed into Spalding county approximately four miles east-northeast of Haralson or 7 miles west of Zetella.  The tornado remain an EF2 as it tracked across southwest and into south central Spalding county, lifting just shy of the Pike county line about five miles west of Rover.  Extensive damage was observed along the track of the tornado  Four homes were completely destroyed and 40 others sustained minor to moderate damage.  Dozens of trees were also down along the path of the tornado.  The tornado tracked roughly five miles with southern Spalding county with a maximum path width of one mile and maximum winds of 120 mph.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the Newnan area and nickel-sized hail south of Sharpsburg.  Nickel-sized hail was observed around Turin.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City confirmed that yet a second EF1 tornado touched down in Jasper county, just a little less than an hour before the first one.  This tornado tracked across northern Jasper county, touching down approximately nine miles west-northwest of Shady Dale and ending about two miles northwest of Shady Dale.  The tornado was estimated to have a maximum path width of 1/4 mile with estimated winds of 100 mph.  Damage began along Shepard Road in northwest Jasper county and continued to near Tucker Town Road, two miles northwest of Shady Dale.  Major damage was observed to a small cottage in the northeast part of the county, with minor damage observed to five other homes along the path of the tornado.  More than 100 trees were down along the path of the tornado.  This tornado developed from the same thunderstorm that just prior had spawned a tornado in southern Newton county.
The Oconee County Emergency Management Director reported penny-sized hail.
The Spalding County Emergency Management Director reported that a person was struck and injured by lightning.
The Taylor County 911 Center reported that several trees were down near Reynolds.  One home was damaged from a downed tree.
The Troup County 911 Center reported penny-sized hail.
The Butts County Emergency Management Director reported that nickel-sized hail was observed across the southern half of the county.

A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF3 tornado touched down approximately five miles east-southeast of Sparta, or about three miles east of the intersection of Georgia Highway 15 and 16.  The tornado then moved along a nearly eight-mile long path across far southeast Hancock county and continued into extreme southern Warren county and then into extreme northwest Glascock county.  The total tornado path length was nearly 11 miles long.  The maximum path width was estimated to be 500 yards with maximum winds of 140 mph.  A church, two site-built homes, and four mobile homes were completely destroyed in the Hickory Grove Community.  One fatality and three injuries occurred where the mobile homes were destroyed.  Hundreds of trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path of the tornado.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that the EF3 tornado which originated in Hancock county, continued across extreme southern Warren county and then into extreme northwest Glascock county.  The tornado weakened to an EF1 as it crossed into Warren county with a maximum path width of 100 yards.  While the total path length of the tornado was nearly 11 miles, just a little over one mile of this path was within Warren county.  Since the tornado traveled through an extremely rural part of Warren county, damage was confined to around 100 downed trees.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that the EF3 tornado that first touched down in Hancock county, causing extensive damage in the Hickory Grove Community as well as killing one and injuring three, continued across extreme southern Warren and into extreme northwest Glascock counties before lifting.  The tornado remained a weaker EF1 with a maximum path width of 100 yards as it crossed from Warren into Glascock county.  The tornado traveled a total distance of nearly 11 miles, but less than two miles within Glascock county.  Within Glascock county, the tornado tracked across a very rural area.  Thus, damage was confined to around a hundred downed trees.

The Marion County Emergency Management Director reported that an EF0 tornado touched down in eastern Marion county, approximately two miles northwest of Putnam, and traveled east-northeast into extreme western Schley county before lifting.  The total path length of the tornado was around two miles.  The maximum path width was 100 yards.  Within Marion county, one tin outbuilding was destroyed and patio furniture was overturned.  Some trees were also down in the area.

The Marion County Emergency Management Director reported that the tornado, which began in eastern Marion county approximately two miles northwest of Putnam, continued on a two-mile east-northeastward track into extreme western Schley county.  The tornado lifted approximately 2.1 miles northwest of Walls Crossing.  The tornado continued to have a maximum path width in Schley county of 100 yards.  Within Schley county, nearly 500 trees were either snapped or uprooted along the brief 1/2 mile long path.  No structural damage was reported within Schley county.
The Stewart County Emergency Management Director reported that a few trees were down south of Lumpkin along with minor structural damage to a building in the far southern part of the county.
The Marion County Emergency Management Director reported that a few trees were down along Georgia Highway 30 in the far southeast part of the county between Draneville and Friendship.

The Sumter County Emergency Management Director considerable damage near the Americus Wal Mart at the corner of U.S. Highway 280 and Feldar Street.  In addition to many trees and power lines down in the area, considerable damage was noted to several buildings and property in the general area.  A Goodwill drop off box was turned over as well as several truck bed covers which were blown over and about.  To the southeast of Americus, several trees and power lines were down along Brady Road.  Part of the roof was blown of the Textron building and a wall of the same building collapsed.  Another building at Caravel Boats also sustained roof damage.  The liners of three trucks at a nearby Ford Dealership were blown near 1500 feet to the east and landed on Sherwood Road.  The emergency manager indicated that the wind was caused by strong straight line winds and not a tornado.

Wind gusts of 62 mph were measured by a University of Georgia (UGA) Mesonet site located near Cordele.  The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported that some power lines were down on 15th Street in Cordele, five to six trees and some power lines were down near Lake Blackshear and Georgia Veterans State Park along U.S. Highway 280 in the western part of the county, and at least four trees were down north of Cordele near the Dooly county line.

The Dooly County Emergency Management Director confirmed that a brief EF0 tornado touched down along Pleasant Valley Road, between Steele Road and Truman Road, approximately four miles northwest of Vienna, and tracked northeast for about 1/4 mile or 500 yards.  The maximum path width was determined to be 50 yards.  At least 50 trees were uprooted or snapped in half along the path of the tornado.  Several homes were damaged from the downed trees.  Six homes sustained minor roof damage when shingles or guttering was blown off.  Some metal carports were damaged and a few outbuildings were destroyed.

The Houston County Emergency Management Director reported that a home was struck by lightning of Arena Road between Georgia Highway 129 and U.S. Highway 341.  The home minor damage from the resulting fire.  Lightning was also likely the culprit of a downed power line southwest of Perry near Henderson, but may also have been the result of thunderstorm winds.

The Pulaski County Emergency Management Director reported that two trees were down in the area just southeast of Browndale.  One of the trees was down on a home causing considerable damage to the roof of the structure.
The Wilcox County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were blown down across the county.
The Harris County 911 Center reported penny-sized hail.  The Harris county Emergency Management Director observed less than penny-sized hail just south of Pine Mountain Valley.

The USGS gage located on Falling Creek four miles east of Juliette in far northwest Jones county, reached the flood stage of 13.0 feet at 221 pm EDT on March 28, 2009.  The creek crested at 1045 pm EDT more than five feet above flood stage later at 18.79 feet.  The creek fell below flood stage at 1219 pm EDT on March 29, 2009, but flash flooding ended at 815 pm EDT on March 28th.  Given that the flooding was confined to very rural areas immediately along the creek, damage was confined to minor debris removal.

A Harris County Sheriff's Deputy observed penny-sized hail west of Hamilton. This is a separate thunderstorm from the storm which also produced penny-sized hail earlier between Hamilton and Pine Mountain Valley.

Penny to golf ball-sized hail was reported near Locust Grove with quarter-sized hail near Ola as the storm moved further northeast.
The Telfair County Emergency Management Director reported that three trees were blown down in the far southern part of the county near between Jacksonville and Lumber City.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of golf ball-sized hail on the east side of Griffin.  Nickel-sized hail was observed in Griffin.  Radar data suggests that hail of nickel or larger size likely continued to the far east central portion of the county as the storm produced hail just across the line in Henry county.

Numerous reports of quarter to half-dollar-sized hail were received from Henry county as a second thunderstorm tracked from the southwest corner of the county to the northeast corner of the county. Amateur radio operators relayed reports of nickel to quarter-sized hail in the Conyers area.  Radar data and reports from Henry county suggest that hail of similar size fell from the southwest to the northeast part of the county.

Flooding continued until 300 am EDT on March 30, 2009.  Flooding was confined to low lands immediately adjacent to the river with no reported damage to structures or property.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The river gage on the Alcovy river near Lawrenceville exceeded the flood stage of 9.0 feet at 404 pm EDT on March 27, 2009.  It remained above flood stage until 812 pm EDT.  The river crested at 9.5 feet at 630 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Flint River at Lovejoy just above Spalding county exceeded the flood stage of 12.0 feet at 915 am EST on March 1st.  Flooding continued until 252 am EST on March 3rd.  The river crested in this area at 12.9 feet on March 2, 2009.  Damage was limited to minor debris removal.

Flooding was observed in western Washington county along the Little River, which forms the border between Washington and Taliaferro counties. Flooding was observed along the Oconee River at Oconee for several days. The river crested at 21.3 feet on March 4th at 400 am EST.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

Several roads were blocked from the downed trees and power lines.
The Houston County Emergency Management Director reported that lightning struck a home on Blue Ridge Lane resulting in minor electrical damage.
The public observed penny-sized hail southwest of Zebulon.  At one location, the hail lasted for approximately two minutes.

Although flash flooding had ended along Falling Creek in northwestern Jones county, the stream gage on Falling Creek near Juliette remained above bankful through the morning.  No additional damage was observed.

The Daily Tribune News of Cartersville reported that gusty northwest winds caused several trees and power lines to fall across the county.  Two homes in Cartersville, one at the corner of Courrant and Porter Street and the other on Parmenter Street were damaged when trees fell on the structures.

The Manchester Star Mercury reported that heavy rain, upwards of two inches during the afternoon on already saturated ground, caused a 27-foot long gas tank at the Quick Stop Food Mart on Georgia Highway 85 to rise out of the ground.  This occurred despite the fact that there were eight inches of concrete on top of the tank.  The tank had been empty for some time.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in the Conyers area.

The Polk County Fire and Rescue Department reported that penny-sized hail fell for up to 20 minutes in the Antioch area.  Radar data suggests that penny-sized hail likely fell from Antioch to northeast of Aragon.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in the Duluth area.  Exact time and location obtained from radar data.
The Monroe County Sheriff's Department observed nickel-sized hail in the Forsyth area.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the Mableton, Floyd, and Dunn Hills area.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director and the Rome News Tribune reported that a narrow, 5 to 10-mile wide line of thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts of at least 60 mph from the southwest to the northeast part of the county.  Several large trees were blown down in the Cave Spring, Rome, and Shannon areas.  Extensive damage was reported to about seven homes in Rome on Fernwood Drive, Shoreline Drive, Brookwood Avenue, East Fourth Street, East Glover Street, and Flannery Street.  Six homes were damaged in Cave Spring from downed trees.
The Dade County Emergency Mangement Director reported that four trees were blown down from strong gradient, non-thunderstorm winds.
The public reported that a portion of the siding and part of the roof was blown off an apartment building.

The public reported a lightning strike to a tree at a private residence on Bridge Point Drive.  The tree was destroyed with tree debris scattered all about the immediate adjacent area.  In addition, a light fixture near the tree was blown.

An amateur radio operator reported that lightning struck a home in Planfield.  The lightning entered the home through the satellite dish mounted the roof.  Heavy rain extinguished the resulting fire.  Damage was minor.

The Gordon County Emergency Management Director reported that strong straight line winds associated with a line of thunderstorms blew down several trees and power lines from Calhoun to Redbud.  A haybarn near Calhoun was destroyed with the debris scattered all about the adjacent field.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of nickel-sized hail in the northeast part of the county near the Spalding county line.

A deputy with the Monroe County Sheriff's Office observed penny, possibly larger-sized hail around Forsyth.  Radar data suggests that penny-sized was probably the largest hail size with this thunderstorm, although nickel-sized hail was reported.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in the Trion area.
The Floyd County 911 Center reported that a tree was blown down onto a house in Rome causing damage to the structure.  The exact address was not provided.
The public reported quarter-sized hail approximately three miles south of Dalton on Old Dixie Highway.
A storm spotter for the National Weather Service observed quarter-sized hail between Dahlonega and Porter Springs.
The Banks County 911 Center relayed a report of nickel-sized hail southeast of Lula.

The Dade County Emergency Management Director and 911 Center reported that many trees were blown down across the county, the majority of which occurred in the New Home community.  One home in this community was damaged when the tree fell on the structure.

The Walker County 911 Center reported that at least two dozen trees were down across the county.  The majority of the damage appeared to be in the Chickamauga area.  Several power lines were down across the county as well.  No structural damage was reported.
The public observed half-dollar-sized hail in the Chickamauga area.

The Chattooga County Emergency Management Director reported penny-sized hail in the northwest part of the county.  The public observed quarter-sized hail in the northeast part of the county, east of Trion.  Radar data suggests that hail of penny or larger sized likely fell across much of northern Chattooga county.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a brief EF2 tornado had touched down approximately one mile southeast of Summerville and tracked less than one mile almost due east.  The tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 200 yards with maximum winds estimated to be 120 mph.  Considerable damage was noted in the Summerville area.  Over 30 homes were damaged along with 10 businesses.  Most of the damage to these structures was determined to be minor.  The majority of the damage occurred on Commerce Street.  The brick wall of a car care center collapsed, the roof was shifted and lifted from a lumber warehouse, and windows were blown out of a barbecue restaurant.  All of these events occurred on Commerce Street.  At the intersection of Cleghorn and Scoggin Streets nearby, a single-wide mobile home was completely destroyed.  Although the mobile home was anchored, the metal frame was ripped from the foundation and the home was tossed on its side.

A CoCoRAHS spotter observed 2.0 inch diameter hail near Lyerly.  The Chattooga County Emergency Management Director reported golf ball-sized hail in the far southern part of the county around Chattoogaville.  This hail occurred from a separate thunderstorm from the one that spawned a tornado just southeast of Summerville and also dropped penny to quarter-sized hail across the northern part of the county.
Several reports of quarter-sized hail were received from the public across northern Catoosa county.

The Catoosa County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down across the northern part of the county.  Some trees were down on homes causing damage to the structures.  The public reported that trees were also down on a storage bulding on Mohawk Trail causing significant damage to the structure.

Many reports of large hail, ranging in size from golf balls to baseballs were received from the public across northern Floyd county, including the northern side of Rome and Shannon, as a supercell thunderstorm tracked from west of Armuchee to Pinson.  At least one report of shattered windshields was received from the public in the Armuchee area.
The public reported golf ball-sized hail with a second thunderstorm that tracked across northern Floyd county.  Golf ball-sized hail was reported from the north side of Rome to Shannon.

Several reports of hail, ranging in size from pennies to baseballs were received from the northern part of Floyd county as yet a third supercell thunderstorm tracked across the region from Coosa to just south of Shannon.  Hail in Rome ranged in size from less than pennies to baseballs.  Golf ball-sized hail was observed near Shannon.

The Murray County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were blown down scattered about the county.  The roof was blown off the porch of a mobile home and a portion of the siding was also off the home south of Chatsworth near the intersection of Smyrna Church Road and Blackwell Drive.

The public observed nickel-sized hail in the far northeast part of the county near Oakman and the Murray county line.  Penny-sized hail was observed by the public southeast of Calhoun as the storm first became severe.

The Gordon County Emergency Management Director reported that strong thunderstorm straight-line winds blew down a number of trees across the county.  The majority of the damage appeared to be concentrated in the Fairmount area, where some minor structural damage was observed.

The Gordon County Emergency Management Director reported golf ball-sized hail in the far northeast part of the county along the Gilmer county line.  Radar data suggests that hail of at least penny size likely fell from west of Calhoun to northeast of Ranger.

Amateur radio operators relayed reports of funnel clouds near Calhoun.  Radar data suggests that the thunderstorm in this area was very close to producing a tornado at this point.  As this circulation continued into neighboring Pickens county to the east, an EF1 tornado touched down at 604 pm EDT just northeast of Jasper.

The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down across the county.  Radar data suggest that the majority of the downed trees were in the southern half of the county.  A roof was blown off a home northwest of Ellijay.

The Gordon County Emergency Management Director reported that golf ball-sized hail was observed near the Gordon/Gilmer county line to near the intersection of Georgia Highways 136 and 382.  The public reported nickel-sized hail in the southeast part of the county, near Cartecay.  Radar data supports nickel or larger sized-hail likely fell across much of southern Gilmer county.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City confirmed than an EF1 tornado touched down in Pickens county, approximately one mile northeast of Jasper, near the intersection of Georgia Highay 136 and Old Grandview Road and continued on an eastward approximately 3.5 mile-long path before lifting.  The maximum path width was determied to be 440 yards with maximum winds estimated at 90 mph.  Damage was greatest along Old Grandview Road near the Grandview community.  In this area, at least forty 18-inch and less diameter hardwood trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path of the tornado.  A number of power lines were down in the area and several utility poles were snapped.  While no direct fatalities or injuries were reported, one person was said to have suffered a heart attack because of anxiety during the event.  Only minor structural damage was reported.

The Murray County Emergency Management Director relayed a report of penny-sized hail.  While the exact location was not provided, radar data suggests that this occurred in the far southern portion of the county near Carters Lake.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the extreme east central portion of the county near the White county line.

The public observed half-dollar-sized hail east and north of Cleveland.  The White County 911 Center reported quarter-sized hail in Cleveland.  The public observed quarter-sized hail southeast of Helen.  Hail was earlier reported along the White/Lumpkin county line west of Cleveland.  Radar data supports hail of penny or larger size likely fell from west of Cleveland along the Lumpkin county line to southeast of Helen near the Habersham county line.  The public reported that hail the size of quarters fell for up to 15 minutes in the Sautee area.

Several reports of large hail were received from the public across northern Bartow county from west of Adairsville along the Floyd county line to east of Funkhouser along the Cherokee county line.  Baseball-sized hail was observed in the Adairsville area, with 2.0 inch diameter sized-hail west of Adairsville and half-dollar-sized hail near Funkhouser.  Windshields of vehicles were broken by the large hail in the Adairsville area.
The public observed 2.0 inch diameter hail in the Adairsville area from a second severe thunderstorm that tracked across the northern part of Bartow county.

A number of reports were received from the public of quarter to golf ball-sized hail across the southern half of Bartow county.  This was the result of two severe thunderstorms that moved east across the county.  The first storm tracked from west of Kingston to near Red Mountain State Park, while the second storm tracked from the Floyd county line west of Euharlee, to the south side of Cartersville, to Lake Allatoona.  Although these storms were separate and distinct, they tracked across the same areas within a 10-mile/15-minute period.  Golf ball-sized hail was reported near Euharlee decreasing to quarter-sized hail on the south side of Cartersville.
Amateur radio operators relayed a report of golf ball-sized hail in the extreme southeast part of the county near the Gwinnett and Hall county line.

The public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail near the Gwinnett county line south of Flowery Branch and golf ball-sized hail in the Gainesville area.  Radar data suggests that large hail, likely near golf ball-sized hail continued northeast from Gainesville toward Lula.

The public observed golf ball-sized hail near Jasper and quarter-sized hail northeast of Nelson in the far southeast part of the county.  Nickel-sized hail was observed by the public in Marble Hill.  Radar data and previous reports from Gordon county support quarter or larger sized-hail beginning west of Blaine near the Gordon county line.  The public reported that hail fell for up to 20 minutes in the Marble Hill area.

The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director observed quarter-sized hail north of Waleska.  Radar data and reports from bordering Bartow county to the west support large hail beginning near the Cherokee/Bartow county line northwest of Waleska.  The storm weakened as it moved east of Waleska.  This was the first of three severe thunderstorms to track across Cherokee county, each producing large hail.

The Hall County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were blown down scattered about the county.  Most of the damage appeared to be in the Flowery Branch and Gainesville areas.  An outbuilding was destroyed in Flowery Branch.
The Hall County Emergency Management Director relayed reports of penny-sized hail.
The Heard County Emergency Management Director reported penny to nickel-sized hail across the northern portion of the county.
The Heard County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees and power lines were down across the northern portion of the county.
The Carroll County Emergency Management Director reported penny-sized hail across the far southern portion of the county along the Heard and Coweta county lines.

The public observed quarter-sized hail in the Dawonsville area.
