Radar data, and reports from neighboring counties to the west and east, supports that hail this size or larger likely fell in a west to east swath across the county from west of Dawonsville along the Pickens county line to the Hall county line east of Dawsonville.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail west of Dahlonega and penny to quarter-sized hail west of Georgia Highway 9 in the Mill Creek Station Subdivision near the Dawson county line.

The public observed quarter-sized hail across west central Cherokee county, south of Waleska.  This was the second of three severe thunderstorms producing large hail to track across Cherokee county.  This storm tracked across the central portion of the county and weakened as it moved east-southeast.

The public observed penny to quarter-sized hail across the far southern portion of Cherokee county, especially in the Woodstock area.  This was the third severe thunderstorm to track across Cherokee county.  Hail was observed to be at least one inch deep on the ground in the Woodstock area after the storm had passed.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia, confirmed that an EF1 tornado had touched down just west of a home at the end of Bay Circle off an inlet of Lake Lanier.  The tornado tracked across this home and across a small inlet of Lake Lanier to another home at the end of Bay Court on the other side of the lake inlet.  At least 50 large trees were uprooted or snapped around the home off Bay Circle, several of which fell on and caused considerable damage to the structure.  Two vehicles in the driveway of this home were crushed when large trees fell on them.  Three boats and two boat docks were destroyed.  The boat docks, and one of the boats, were blown inland some 200 yards, overturned, and portions wrapped around or underneath fallen trees.  The home on Bay Court on the other side of the Lake Lanier inlet suffered minor roof and structural damage from downed trees.  However, at least another 50 large trees were uprooted or snapped on the adjacent land between the home and the lake inlet.  The tornado lifted as it approached a steep hill behind the home on Bay Court.  A couple of adjacent homes also suffered minor roof and window damage.
A storm spotter observed quarter-sized hail near and west of Cumming.

The public observed penny-sized hail near Homer.  The thunderstorm producing this hail tracked east from Hall county, crossing into Banks county near Lula.  The main part of the storm moved east between Homer and Hollingsworth, then continued east to the Franklin county border east of Hollingsworth.  Hail of at least penny-size likely fell along the path of the thunderstorm according to radar data and reports from Hall county immediately adjacent to the west.
The Union County Emergency Management Director relayed a report of nickel-sized hail in the far southern portion of the county around Suches.
The public reported quarter-sized hail in far northern Carroll county near Villa Rica.  This was from a second and separate thunderstorm that  earlier produced hail near Whitesburg.

Several reports of hail, ranging in size from pennies to quarters, were received from the public across central and eastern Coweta county.  Quarter-sized hail was observed near Newnan and north of Newnan, while penny-sized hail was observed near Sharpsburg.
The Bartow County Emergency Management Director reported that lightning struck and set a home on fire.  The structure suffered minor damage before the fire was extinguished.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that penny to golf ball-sized hail fell across far northern Fulton county around Alpharetta.  The public observed penny-sized hail near Crabapple.  Most of the hail reports were penny to nickel-sized.
The Banks County 911 Center reported that many trees were blown down across the northern portion of the county.  No structural damage was indicated.
Several National Weather Service employees and the public observed penny-sized hail in the Peachtree City area.
Several reports of golf ball-sized hail were received from the Polk County Emergency Management Director from east of Cedartown to Rockmart, including Aragon.
The Polk County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down around Cedartown.
The public observed quarter-sized hail near Commerce.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in the far southwest part of the county near the Jackson county border.

A storm spotter observed penny-sized hail in the far southern part of Forsyth county near the Fulton and Gwinnett county borders in the Big Creek area.  This hail fell from a separate thunderstorm from the one that earlier produced an EF1 tornado southeast of Cumming on the west side of Lake Lanier.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that at least a dozen trees were down in the far northern portion of the county between Crabapple and Alpharetta in the Milton community.  One home suffered structural damage from downed trees.

Several reports of nickel to half-dollar-sized hail were received from amateur radio operators and the public across north and western Paulding county, especially in the Dallas area.  Radar data and reports from Polk county immediately adjacent to the west indicate that large hail likely fell from Braswell to just east of Dallas before the storm weakened.
The Henry County 911 Center reported nickel-sized hail in the McDonough area.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the extreme northern portion of Cobb county, near the Cherokee county line, northeast of Acworth.

The public observed quarter-sized hail in Winder on Georgia Highway 211, Rockwell Church Road, and near the Barrow-Winder High School.  The public observed penny-sized hail between Thompson's Mill and Auburn.  Winds were estimated at 60-70 mph with this thunderstorm, but no tree or structural damage was reported.

A storm spotter observed half-dollar-sized hail southwest of Arcade while another storm spotter observed penny-sized hail in southern Jackson county, south of Jackson.  This was the second severe thunderstorm to track across the county, this time across the far southern portion of the county.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail in the Johns Creek area of north Fulton county.  This was one of several severe thunderstorms to track across Fulton county during the evening, each one progressing a little further southward within the county.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of nickel-sized hail north of Sharpsburg in the Thomas Crossroads area.  Penny-sized hail was observed along the Coweta-Fayette county line near Peachtree City.
The Butts County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees were down across the county.  A tree was down on a home on Georgia Highway 16 causing damage to the structure.
Amateur radio operators and the public observed penny-sized hail from Peachtree City to Brooks.
Several reports of quarter-sized hail were received from the northwest side of Griffin into the Griffin area.
Amateur radio operators reported that several trees were down on the northwest side of Griffin.  The trees were at least eight inches in diameter.
A storm spotter observed nickel-sized hail on the east side of Atlanta in the Grant Park area.
The Putnam County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees were blown down throughout the county.  No structural damage was reported.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the southwest part of the county from a second severe thunderstorm that moved east out of southern Jackson county.
An off duty National Weather Service employee observed penny-sized hail in the Hampton area.
The Rockdale County Emergency Management Director reported that a few small trees were blown down across the northern portion of the county.  Pea-sized hail was also observed.

The Haralson County 911 Center reported that hail fell across much of the county.  Radar data and reports from neighboring counties from the same thunderstorms support at least penny-sized hail.  Exact times were estimated using radar data.
The Barrow County 911 Center reported golf ball-sized hail in the Winder area.
The Walton County 911 Center received several reports of penny to nickel-sized hail were received from the public.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia, confirmed that an EF1 tornado had touched down approximately 2.5 miles south of Ochille and continued on an east-southeastward track across central Chattahoochee county, lifting about 4.0 miles east-southeast of its touchdown point.  The path width was determined to be 440 yards with maximum winds estimated at 80 mph.  The damage appeared to have begun as a downburst, within which the brief EF1 tornado spin up occurred.  Combined damage from the downburst and EF1 tornado consisted of destruction of several out buildings and sheds.  Hundreds of trees were flattened along the path of the tornado.  Another EF1 tornado was spawned from the same supercell thunderstorm, also within Chattahoochee county, just eight minutes later and four miles further east.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a second EF1 tornado touched down within Chattahoochee county from the same parent supercell thunderstorm that spawned an earlier EF1 tornado 2.5 miles south of Ochille.  This EF1 tornado touched down approximately 2.5 miles east-northeast of Cusseta and also traveled on the ground about 4.0 miles to the east-southeast just north of and paralleling Georgia Highway 26.  The maximum path width was determined to be 100 yards with maximum winds estimated at 80 mph.  Minor damage was observed to at least two homes and one church.  A 20 by 24 foot metal storage building on Georgia Highway 26 was destroyed.  Several other storage sheds or outbuildings along the path of the tornado suffered minor to moderate damage.
The public observed penny-sized hail in extreme southern Cobb county near Six Flags.
The public observed penny-sized hail in western Fulton county near Six Flags and the Cobb county line.
The Warren County 911 Center reported that a few trees were blown down in the far western portion of the county near the Hancock county line.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail in extreme southern Newton county near Stewart.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a brief EF1 tornado touched down approximately two miles northwest of Sparta and traveled only 1.5 miles before lifting.  This was the first of three tornadoes to touch down in Hancock county between 1019 pm EDT and 1028 pm EDT, each near Sparta.  This tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 100 feet with maximum winds estimated at 80 mph.  This first tornado tracked through a quite rural area.  However, one mobile home suffered moderate damage to its roof, siding, and windows.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that yet a second tornado touched down in Hancock county.  This was also a brief EF0 tornado and touched down just north-northeast of downtown Sparta.  The path width of this tornado was determined to also be 100 feet with maximum winds estimated to also be 80 mph.  Numerous large trees were down along the path of the tornado in a primarily rural area.  No structural damage was noted in association with this tornado.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that yet a third tornado touched down in Hancock county within a 15 minute period of time.  However, this tornado was determined to be an EF3 tornado.  This tornado touched down about halfway between Sparta and Culverton in east central Hancock county.  The tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 1/2 mile with maximum winds of 160 mph.  Much of the damage occurred along Dunn and Hickory Grove Roads.  Along the path of the tornado, one 4000 square foot site-built home was completely destroyed.  The debris from the home was scattered across an area up to 400 feet downstream.  A resident of this home suffered serious injuries.  Another nearby double-wide mobile home was also completely destroyed.  Two other nearby homes on Dunn suffered minor damage and two additional homes on Youngblood Road toward Jewell suffered extensive roof damage.  A swath of 116 mature pecan trees at a pecan orchard on Hickory Grove road were flattened.  These were owned by a resident adjacent to one of the damaged homes on Hickory Grove Road.  One of the homeowners also lost a Shetland pony during the tornado.
The Hancock County Emergency Management Director relayed a report from a weather spotter of golf ball-sized hail in the Shoulderbone area.

The Monroe County Emergency Management Director and local newspapers reported that up to five inches of rain fell during a 24-hour period on top of already saturated soils resulting in flooding of area creeks and streams.  This caused several roads to be washed out and closed.  In all, eights roads were closed as a result of flooding.  Most of the damage was the result of washed out culvert or drainage pipes.  Chambers Road at the intersection of Juliette Road was washed out by Chambliss Creek and left closed for an extended period of time.  Montpelier Springs Road was flooded at the Tobosofkee Creek bridge near Georgia Highway 42 and left closed for several days.  Zellner Road at Smith/Goodwyn Road was washed out and left impassible for an extended period of time.  Ebenezer Road at Lake Juliette was flooded for several days until the water receded.  Byars Road, a dirt road near the intersection of Georgia Highway 83 and Juliette Road, was covered with over a foot of water for over 24 hours, and washed out.
A wildfire, labeled Town Mountain, burned 1.5 acres.  The fire was human caused.
A wildfire, labeled Rocky Flats, burned 2.0 acres.  The fire was human caused.
A wildfire, labeled Rabbit, burned 0.25 acres.  The fire was human caused.
Yet a third wild fire was reportd in Murray county.  This fire was labeled Old Highway 2 and burned 3.0 acres resulting in $5000 in damages.  The fire was human caused.
A second fire was reported in Murray county.  This fire, Labeled Old Highway 2 No. 2, burned 0.50 acres.  The fire was human caused.
A wildfire, labeled Narrows, burned 0.50 acres.  The fire was human caused.
A wildfire, labeled Bowater Road, burned 6.4 acres in Walker county.  This was the most significant wildfire observed during the month resulting in $10,000 in damages.  The fire was human caused.
A second wildfire, labeled Gore, was observed in Chattooga county.  This fire burned 3.9 acres.  As with the others, this fire was human caused.

The Putnam County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees and power lines were down around Eatonton.  Trees were down on at least three mobile homes causing damage to the structures.  Radar data suggests that this storm traveled from just west of Eatonton to the southeast corner of the county near Flat Rock.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down in extreme northeast Sumter county, approximately three miles east-southeast of Methvins and continued on an east-southeastward track for approximately 25 miles across extreme southern Dooly county and into extreme northwest Wilcox county before lifting approximately five miles north of Seville in Wilcox county.  This was the first of three tornadoes to touch down in Sumter county the evening of April 10th.  Within Sumter county, this tornado had a path length of about 2.5 miles.  It was also apparent that this tornado was spawned from the same supercell thunderstorm that spawned two earlier tornadoes in Chattahoochee county.  The maximum path width of this tornado was determined to be 250 yards with maximum winds estimated at 110 mph.  Damage in Sumter county was mostly confined to hundreds of downed trees.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City confirmed that the EF1 tornado, that originally touched down in far northeastern Sumter county three miles east-southeast of Methvins, continued on an east-southeastward track across far southern Dooly county and into extreme northwest Wilcox county, lifting approximately five miles north of Seville in Wilcox county.  The tornado tracked around 21 miles within Dooly county.  The maximum path width was determined to be 250 yards and the maximum winds were estimated at 110 mph.  The tornado passed just north of Drayton and just south of Vienna in Dooly county.  Several hundred trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path of the tornado.  A number of pecan trees in an orchard south of Vienna were destroyed.  Two site built homes suffered significant roof damage from downed trees on the structures.  Two mobiles homes were also damaged by the high winds of the tornado.  Several barns and outbuildings were destroyed along the path of the tornado.  Several irrigation systems were rolled over.  A small radio tower in the eastern part of Dooly county was also blown over.  No deaths or injuries were reported.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City confirmed that the EF1 tornado, that initially touched down in far northeast Sumter county, continued across far southern Dooly county, before ending just inside Wilcox county, approximately five miles north of Seville.  The tornado tracked a little over one mile within Wilcox county with a maximum path width of 250 yards and maximum winds estimated at 110 mph.  Within Wilcox county, only around 100 downed trees were noted along the path of the tornado.
The public observed quarter-sized hail around Ellaville.
The Glascock County Emergency Management Director reported that the roof was blown off the carport of a home.  No other damage was noted in the area at this time.
The Newton County Emergency Management Director reported several trees and large tree limbs were down in the far southern part of the county near Georgia Highways 36, 162, and 212.
The Butts County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 10 trees were down in the far southern portion of the county, south of Indian Springs near the Monroe county line.

A damage survey conducted by the Dooly County Emergency Management Director confirmed that yet another, weaker EF0 tornado was tracking across Dooly county, just north of Vienna, as the longer-lived EF1 tornado was tracking across all of southern Dooly county south of Vienna.  This EF0 tornado touched down approximately two miles north of Vienna and traveled east-northeast approximately six miles before lifting.  This tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 100 yards with maximum winds estimated at 85 mph.  Spotty damage was observed along the path of the tornado.  A chicken house was destroyed, one home suffered minor roof damage, and a tin roof was peeled off a barn.  From 15 to 20 trees were uprooted or snapped along the path of the tornado.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a brief EF0 tornado had touched down just southeast of the city of Gibson and traveled approximately 1000 yards or about 0.6 mile on an east-southeastward track.  This tornado was spawned by the same supercell thunderstorm that spawned the earlier EF3 tornado in eastern Hancock county.  The tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 150 yards with maximum winds of 100 mph.  A number of large pine trees were uprooted or snapped along the path of the tornado.  However, no structural damage was noted as a result of this tornado.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a brief EF0 tornado touched down in western Sumter county near the Experimental Station on U.S. Highway 280, approximately one mile northeast of Plains, and tracked about one mile to the east-southeast before lifting.  The tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 200 yards with maximum winds estimated at 100 mph.  Wind equipment at the Plains Research Center measured a wind gust of 110 mph as the tornado passed nearby.  This was the second of three tornadoes to affect Sumter county during the late evening of April 10th and the early morning hours of April 11th.   Damage along the tornado path was spotty with many downed trees.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the Sugar Hill and Lake Lanier/Buford Dam areas and penny to nickel-sized hail in the far northeast part of the county in the Chateau Elan area.
The public observed penny to quarter-sized hail near Duluth and southward.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in the Eatonton area.  Radar data suggests that penny to nickel-sized hail likely fell across much of the central portion of the county from west to east.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that yet a third EF1 tornado touched down in Sumter county.  This was a long-lived tornado and tracked across three counties, Sumter, Crisp, and Wilcox, for an approximate path length of 33 miles.  This tornado touched down in far southeast Sumter county in the Cobb community and crossed Lake Blackshear into Crisp county about three miles east-southeast of Cobb.  The tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 200 yards with maximum winds estimated at 100 mph.  Within Sumter county, one home was destroyed and 45 suffered minor to moderate damage.  The damage was largely the result of downed trees on the structures.  Two to three dozen trees and several power lines were down along the path of the tornado.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that the third EF1 tornado to touch down in Sumter county the evening of April 10th, continued on a sporadic, but long path, across Crisp and into Wilcox county before lifting.  The tornado crossed into Crisp county at Lake Blackshear, just south of the Georgia Veterans State Park.  The tornado entered the county as an EF1 with a maximum path width of 200 yards.  However, as the tornado crossed the lake into western Crisp county, it weakened to an EF0 with a maximum path width of 100 yards.  Maximum winds were estimated at 100 mph as the tornado entered the county, but quickly weakened to 80 mph as it progressed across the lake.  The path length within Crisp county was approximately 14 miles.  Within Crisp county, 20 homes sustained minor to moderate damage.  This damage was primarily the result of large downed trees on the structures.  At least two to three dozen trees were down along the path of the tornado within Crisp county.

Data gathered from the Wilcox County Emergency Management Director and from a damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia concluded that the EF1 tornado that began in the Cobb community of far southeast Sumter county and tracked east-southeast across Crisp county, continued into far southwest and south central Wilcox county before lifting.  The total path length of the tornado was around 33 miles.  Damage was sporadic along the path of the tornado.  The tornado tracked approximately 12 miles within Wilcox county and remained as a weaker EF0 tornado with a maximum path width of 100 yards and maximum winds of 80 mph.  Within Wilcox county, most of the damage was concentrated in the Owensboro area, with just isolated tree damage from Hatley, along the Crisp/Wilcox county line to the west side of Ownesboro.  One home at the intersection of County Roads 60 and 61, just southwest of Owensboro, suffered considerable damage.  A mobile home was destroyed just east of the intersection of Georgia Highways 233 and 238.  Finally, considerable damage was noted to a pecan orchard east of County Road 63 or about one mile east-southeast of Owensboro, near the point where the tornado lifted.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the far northern part of the county in the Hamburg State Park area.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City confirmed that yet a second tornado touched down in Glascock county during the evening of April 10th.  This tornado was determined to be an EF1 and touched down in the far eastern part of the county, approximately 4.5 miles east-northeast of Gibson.  The tornado continued on an almost due eastward path for five miles into northern Jefferson county, lifting approximately three miles northeast of Stapleton.  The maximum path width was determined to be 200 yards with maximum winds estimated at 110 mph.  Damage within Glascock county from this tornado was confined to several downed trees.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that the EF1 tornado that initially touched down in extreme eastern Glascock county continued into far northern Jefferson county along a five mile-long path before lifting approximately three miles northeast of Stapleton.  The tornado was determined to have a maximum path width of 200 yards with maximum winds estimated at 110 mph.  The majority of the damage associated with this tornado occurred in Jefferson county.  Significant damage was observed to the Heartsgrove Baptist Church at the intersection of Georgia Highways 80 and 296, just across from the Glascock county line.  Part of the roof, brick siding, and the chimney were removed from the structure.  Several granite headstones in the adjacent cemetery were tipped over.  Many trees were down along the path of the tornado, especially along a 3/4 mile-long path east of the damaged church.
The public observed penny-sized hail across southern Baldwin county.  Time and location estimated from radar data.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the far northern part of the county near Ivey.

Two reports of golf ball-sized hail were received from the public in the Weston area.  Radar data indicates that golf ball-sized hail likely fell from Weston east-southeastward to the southeast corner of the county.
The Sumter County Emergency Management Director reported that more than a dozen trees were blown down in the Andersonville area of far northern Sumter county.

The Washington County Emergency Management Director reported that more than 50 hardwood and pine trees were down along a sporadic path from just west-southwest of Harrison at the intersection of Adams Circle and Georgia Highway 15 eastward to Red Hill Drive just west of Wrightsville-Riddleville Road, east-southeast of Harrison.  Five large pine trees were down on Adams Circle, one causing considerable damage to a barn.  On South Railroad Avenue, some minor structural damage was noted, also from downed trees.  From 40-50 trees were down along Red Hill Drive.  It was concluded that because nearly all of the trees were blown down in one direction that this was caused by a downburst or straight-line winds and not a tornado.
The Sumter Electric Management Cooperative (EMC) reported that several trees and tree limbs were down across the county.  This brought some power lines down as well.

The Dooly County 911 Center reported that a few trees were down on Georgia Highway 230 near Drayton in the western part of the county and a few more trees were down on a local road in the eastern part of the county just west of Tippettville.

The Houston County 911 Center reported that a few trees were down near Henderson in the western part of the county and a few trees were down near Elko in the south central part of the county.  The tin roof of a church at County Line Road and Georgia Highway 26 two miles east of Elko was damaged.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that more than 80 trees were down across the county along with many power lines and utility poles.  Horse Leg Creek Road was blocked from utility lines.  Several homes also sustained minor to moderate damaged from downed trees, especially on East Third and Wright Streets in Rome.  At least 10,000 residents of the county were left without power following the event.

The RAWS station at Cohutta recorded a wind gust of 48 mph, almost high wind criteria.  A wind gust of 50 mph was reported from the Murray county mesonet site five miles east-southeast of Cisco.  Up to 10 trees were blown down in the northern part of the county.
The public reported that several trees and power lines were blown down in the eastern part of the county at elevations above 2000 feet.

The Paulding County Emergency Management Director reported extensive damage across Paulding county.  There were more than 50 incidents of downed trees and power lines.  There were 37 trees down on roads.  Four vehicles were either heavily damaged or destroyed from downed trees.  Eight structures were damaged, two from downed trees.  The roof was blown off a dry cleaners store and shingles were blown off the roof of two fire stations.  Vinyl siding was blown off a home on Crestworth Crossing Road in the far southeastern part of the county near Powder Springs.  The only weather observing station in Paulding county is a RAWS station in Dallas, which recorded 39 knot wind gusts.  However, the extent of the damage indicated that wind gusts of 58 mph were likely observed in some areas.

A trained spotter estimated wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph near Trenton.  Several trees were down across the county.  Electric transformers were observed to be exploding from downed trees and power lines.
The public observed that many trees were down from Talking Rock to Jasper.

The Union County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees and power lines were down across the county.  A number of trees were down on power lines and widespread power outages were observed across the county.  The Brasstown Bald RAWS station recorded a wind gusts of 44 mph.  Damage suggested that higher wind gusts were likely observed in some areas.

The Forsyth County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees and power lines were blown down across the county.  At least four homes in the Cumming area sustained major damage was several large trees fell on the structures.  One of these homes was rendered uninhabitable until it could be repaired.  Blown electrical transformers started fires on some utility poles.  A vehicle was destroyed and a home suffered minor damage on Buford Drive when a large oak tree fell on the property.  Extensive damage was also reported at a marina at Port Royale on Lake Lanier.  The strong winds caused two docks to collide.  This action caused two boats to collide, one subsequently sunk, and a third was pushed over a walkway.

The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director reported that more than 100 trees were down across the county.  At least 40 roads were blocked from downed trees.  Several homes sustained structural damage, at least 12 of which suffered moderate damage.  At least 10,000 residents of the county were left without power following the event.
The public reported that several trees were blown down near South Cobb Drive.

The Hall County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees were down across the county, especially the south part of the county.  Several homes suffered extensive damage from downed trees.  Several boats were overturned on Lake Lanier at the Lan-Mar Marina.  A man was injured on Joe Chandler Road when a tree fell on him causing cuts and bruises to his head.  The Gainesville Times reported that nearly 300 trees had to be removed from roadways across the county.  Nearly 9000 residents of the county were left without power during the event as well.

The public reported that several trees and power lines were blown down in the northern part of the county, especially around Decatur.  Power lines were knocked down by fallen trees on Ashford-Dunwoody Road, near Cross Street, and on Stratfield Drive N.E.  Two trees were also down on Windsor Parkway and near Oglethorpe University.

The public reported significant damage to structures in the northwestern part of the county.  A roof was blown off a barn causing the walls to collapse.  At least six homes between Summers McKoy Road and Tom Witcher Road sustained roof and siding damage from strong to high winds.  Several power outages were reported in the area from downed trees and power lines.

The Dawson County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees were down in the Big Canoe area of northern Dawson county.  Seven homes were damaged during the wind storm, including one on Bearden Road that suffered significant damage.  A female was initially trapped in the home, but was able to escape on her own.  In addition, an individual was injured when they were struck by a tree limb.  Thirty-five roads were blocked and closed from widespread downed trees.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down in the northern portion of the county.  A tree had fallen on a home at 125 West Spalding Drive in Sandy Springs causing extensive damage to the home.  An individual was killed on Nacoochee Drive near the Peachtree Battle Shopping Center in Buckhead, approximately five miles north of Atlanta, when a tree fell across the cab of his truck.  The Atlanta ASOS, 10-15 miles south of the area with the heaviest damage, recorded a wind gust of 45 knots at 953 am EDT.  Higher winds may well have been observed in the northern part of the county.

The Bleckley County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 30 medium size pine trees were either blown down or snapped in half in the Cochran area.  Several center pivot irrigation units were turned over.  A witness in Cochran noted the strong straight-line winds when his full-size Ford pickup truck was blown around.  Several other trees and power lines were also down on Magnolia Road in northwest Bleckley county and in northeast Bleckley county on Cary Road.

WMAZ Television from Macon, Georgia reported that the metal roof of a home on U.S. Highway 341 near Brownwood was damaged from strong straight-line winds.  Several outdoor objects were blown around.  A tree was also down in the area and a window was blown out of a barn.
The Dodge County 911 Center reported that a few trees were blown down on Venison Power Road in the far northern portion of the county.
The Telfair County 911 Center reported that several trees were down near Jacksonville along U.S. Highway 441.

The Telfair County 911 Center relayed a report of a funnel cloud about halfway between Lumber City and Jacksonville near Georgia Highway 17.  This coincided with a distinct mesoscale circulation detected on the Doppler radar in this area at the time.
Employees at the United States Post Office in Lumber City observed quarter-sized hail.
The public observed penny-sized hail just east of Lexsy or about 10 miles southwest of Twin City.
A storm spotter observed quarter-sized hail in the Dublin area, while the Emergency Management Director observed penny-sized hail in the Dublin area.
The Johnson County Emergency Management Director observed penny-sized hail about four miles north of Kite.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Athens.
The public reported that three trees were blown down around Athens.
The Walker County Emergency Management Director reported that a few trees were blown down in the southern part of the county.

The Georgia Emergency Management Agency relayed reports of funnel clouds from northeast Cobb county near the Interstate 75 and Interstate 575 split.  A mesoscale circulation was clearly evident on Doppler radar in this area.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down in far southeast Cherokee county near the Cobb county line in the Woodstock area.  The tornado touched down near the intersection of Georgia Highway 92 and Dial Drive, then continued north-northeast along Dial Drive crossing a large section of Coleman's Bluff.  The tornado lifted just south of the intersection of Windcrest Court and River Chase Drive.  The total path length of the tornado was 1.5 miles with a maximum path width of 1/2 mile or 880 yards.  Maximum winds were estimated to be 90 mph.  EF1 tornado damage to trees and structures was observed along a 3/4 mile-long path paralleling Dial Drive beginning just north of its intersection with Georgia Highway 92.  Damage was observed to 120 homes along the path of the tornado, 12 of which were completely destroyed.  The majority of the damage took place in the Coleman's Bluff area.  Most of the damage was the result of large trees falling on the structures.  Two residents of the affected homes were injured by debris.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado, which initially touched down in Phenix City - Russell County, Alabama as an EF2 tornado at the intersection of Dillingham and Broad Streets, continued into Muscogee county, Georgia and the city of Columbus.  The total tornado path was determined to be approximately four miles in length, two of which fell within Muscogee county, Georgia.  The maximum path width was determined to be 250 yards with maximum winds estimated at 105 mph.  Damage within Georgia was first observed at Columbus State University.  Significant damage was observed to buildings and trees on the campus.  The Old Rankin Building, an older building which had been converted to dormitories, suffered substantial damage.  From this point, spotty tree, roof, and window damage was observed along the path of the tornado and it continued moving eastward.  At the intersection of 13th Street and 13th Avenue, a small utility truck used at a nursery had been picked up and moved at least 25 feet and through a neighboring fence.  Minor damage to displays, trees, and plants was also observed in the adjacent nursery.  From here to where the tornado lifted near the intersection of Macon Road and Preston Drive in Columbus, hundreds of large mature oak trees were either snapped or uprooted through Lake Bottom Park and Hilton Avenue and Harding Drive.  Extensive damage was observed to homes throughout this area, largely a result of the downed trees.  Many power lines were down along the path of the tornado as well.  Over 100 structures, including homes and businesses, suffered minor to moderate damage.

The public observed half-dollar-sized hail in the far southeast corner of Paulding county near the intersection of Georgia Highway 92 and Brownsville Road.  The hail fell in the area for up to seven minutes.  Earlier, the public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail further west near New Georgia in south central Paulding county.  In addition, a wind gust of 51 mph was measured on personal wind equipment on a private vehicle on Georgia Highway 92 at Brownsville Road.

The public observed at least one funnel cloud in the Cobbleston subdivision, about one mile east-southeast of Kingston or about nine miles south of Adairsville.  Additional funnel clouds may have been observed with other thunderstorms that passed through the area during the evening.  No tornado touch downs were reported or confirmed in this area, but Doppler radar clearly showed several mesoscale circulations passing through the county during the evening.
The public observed a funnel cloud near Ellaville.  Doppler radar data clearly indicated a strong mesoscale circulation passing just south of Ellaville at the time.
The public observed penny to quarter-sized hail south of Buena Vista in the Draneville community.
The public observed penny to nickel to quarter-sized hail in the Decatur area.

A storm spotter/firefighter for Lumpkin county reported that more than 100 trees were blown down in the Mill Creek Station Subdivision in western Lumpkin county near the Dawson county border, west of Georgia Highway 9.  One house suffered significant damage from a downed tree and a vehicle was smashed from a fallen tree.  Many of the trees were uprooted or twisted off approximately 20 feet above ground level.
A report was received via e-spotter of a large oak tree down on University Drive along with several large tree limbs down on Millege Avenue.

The Carroll County 911 Center reported that many trees and power lines, at least 35, were blown down throughout the county.  Widespread power outages were observed.  A spotter observed wind gusts in excess of 45 mph, but higher winds may have occurred in some areas.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in the Kirkwood and Clifton area in the southwestern part of DeKalb county.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in the eastern part of Cobb county in the Indian Hills, Crossgate, and Ashebrook area.

A deputy with the Floyd County Sheriff's Office observed a funnel cloud in the North Rome and Shannon area.  Numerous reports of funnel clouds from Coosa, to north Rome, to Shannon and on towards northern Bartow county were received at the Floyd County 911 Center from 515 pm to 545 pm EDT.

The Houston County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were blown down across the county by high winds associated with a line of showers moving through the area which accompanied a strong cold front.
The Dodge County 911 Center reported that a tree was blown down across a utility pole causing a power outage along Chester Highway in northeast Dodge county.

The USGS stream gage on Turkey Creek at Byromville rose above the flood stage of 10.0 feet on April 3rd at 456 am EDT.  It remained above flood stage through 637 pm EDT the same day.  The creek crested at 10.46 feet at 930 am EDT on April 3rd.  Damage was confined to debris removal near the creek.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported extensive flooding across Crisp county as a result of rainfall of five inches or more that had fallen on saturated ground from several prior weeks of wet conditions and above normal rainfall.  Several roads within the county had to be closed as culverts were washed out and the roads were rendered impassable.  Many roads in the Cordele area were inundated with high water during the height of the flooding and had to be closed.  In addition, several homes in the Cordele area sustained significant flood damage.

The USGS gage on Turnpike Creek reached the flood stage of 10.0 feet on April 2nd at 650 pm EDT.  However, general flooding was observed in lowland areas near the creek as early as 230 pm EDT on April 2nd.  The creek crested at 10.69 feet at 200 am EDT on April 3rd and dropped below the flood stage at 130 pm EDT on April 3rd.  Minor flooding of lowlands and fields adjacent to the creek experienced flooding during this time frame.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Wheeler County Emergency Management Director reported that several dirt roads across the county were washed out from heavy rain.  Minor flooding was also observed to fields and woodlands near streams and creeks.  Over six inches of rain fell in parts of the county over a 3-day period.  This was on top of saturated soils from prior weeks of above normal rainfall.

The Toombs County Emergency Management Director reported that up to 30 roads across the county had to be closed as a result of flooding from several days of heavy rain.  Several dirt roads were washed out.  Minor flooding was also observed to fields and woodlands near creeks and rivers in the county.  More than six inches of rain fell in parts of the county.  This rain fell on saturated soil from several prior weeks of above normal rainfall.

The Baldwin County Emergency Management Director reported that some roads were closed as a result of ponding of water on the roads from several days of heavy rainfall.  Parts of the county received five to six inches of rain over a three day period, on top of prior saturated soils from several weeks of above normal rainfall.  Minor flooding of fields and woodlands near creeks was also observed.  Damage was confined to debris removal.

The Bibb County Emergency Management Director reported that around 100 homes in the Macon area experienced basement flooding as a result of several days of heavy rainfall.  Parts of the county had a three-day rainfall total of five to six inches.  This rain fell on saturated soils from prior weeks of above normal rainfall.  In addition, up to 20 roads had to be closed as a result of flooding or ponding of water.  Minor flooding was also observed in fields and woodlands adjacent to creeks, streams, and rivers across the county.  Flood damages were generally the result of basement flooding, with only minor road repair or debris removal required.

The Crawford County Emergency Management Director reported that heavy rainfall had flooded some dirt roads in the county and rendered them impassable.  Minor flooding was also observed in fields in woodlands adjacent to creeks and streams throughout the county.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Jones County Emergency Management Director reported that eight dirt roads in the county were flooded, rendered impassable, and closed.  Minor flooding of fields and woodlands adjacent to creeks and streams was also observed.  Parts of the county experienced up to six inches of rain during a 3-day period.

The Monroe County Emergency Management Director reported that 13 roads across the county were flooded and rendered impassable from heavy rain over a 3-day period.  Several dirt roads were washed out.  Minor flooding of fields and woodlands along creeks, streams, and rivers was also observed.  Up to five inches of rain fell in parts of the county during the event.

The Johnson County Emergency Management Director reported flooding to woodlands and adjacent fields and lowlands along Swain Creek in the eastern part of the county and the Little Ohopee River near Kite.  Power line road was washed out and closed.  Six other roads in the area had water flowing over the road.  In addition, three camp houses along the Oconee River on the western side of the county were threatened from high water.  The combination of saturated soil and windy conditions caused six trees to fall on homes near the Oconee River resulting in minor damage to the structures.

The USGS gage on William Swamp Creek at Davisboro reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet at 400 pm EDT on April 3rd.  The creek remained above flood stage until 330 pm EDT that day.  The creek crested at 10.24 feet at 930 am EDT on April 3rd.  Minor flooding of woodland and fields along the creek were observed.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The USGS stream gage on the Little River south of Washington on the Wilkes/Taliaferro county line briefly reached and exceeded its flood stage of 19.0 feet on April 3rd.  The river reached its flood stage of 825 am EDT on April 3rd, crested at 830 am EDT, and then dropped below flood stage at 835 am EDT.  Minor flooding was observed along the woodlands and fields near the river.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Upson County Emergency Management Director reported that several roads were closed as a result of flooding.  Minor flooding of fields and woodlands near creeks and streams within the county was observed.  Up to five inches of rain had fallen across parts of the county over a 3-day period.

Several reports of half-dollar to golf ball-sized hail were received from the public in the northern part of Walker county near Chickamauga.  Penny-sized hail was reported from the southern part of the county near LaFayette.  Radar data supports that hail of similar size likely fell in a large swath from northwest to southeast across the county from High Point to Villanow.
The Walker County 911 Center reported that several trees were blown down between Naomi and Villanow.

The public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail in the Powder Springs area in the southwest part of the county.  This was the second of four severe thunderstorms to impact Cobb county during the evening of April 23rd.

Several reports of penny, quarter, and golf ball-sized hail received from the Smyrna and Vinings area in eastern Cobb county.  This was the second of four severe thunderstorms to impact Cobb county during the evening of April 23rd.

The Paulding County Emergency Management Director and the public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail across the southeast part of the county from southeast of Dallas to along the Douglas-Paulding county line, south of Hiram.

The public observed quarter-sized hail in northern Douglas county, north of Douglasville near the Douglas/Paulding county line, penny-sized hail in Douglasville, and golf ball-sized hail in the southeast part of the county near and southeast of Chapel Hill.  The public reported that hail completely covered the ground in some areas.  Significant damage to vehicles was reported from this area.

The public observed quarter-sized hail in the northwest part of the county west of Resaca and in Resaca, half-dollar-sized hail just north of Calhoun, and penny-sized hail in and just east of Calhoun.  This was the first of two severe thunderstorms to track across Gordon county during the evening of April 23rd.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in east central Paulding county near New Hope southeast toward the Cobb county line.

The public observed golf ball-sized hail just south of Emerson and quarter-sized hail southeast of Cartersville.  Radar data suggests that similar-sized hail likely fell from Cartersville to the southeast corner of the county near Lake Allatoona.

Several reports of large hail were received from southern Cherokee county.  The public observed penny to quarter-sized hail from southwest Cherokee county approximately six miles west-northwest of Woodstock into the city of Woodstock.  Golf ball-sized hail was observed by the public in the southeast corner of the county, or about five miles east-southeast of Woodstock.  The Fulton County EMA Director was in the area at the time and estimated wind gusts of 60 mph.  However, no tree, power line, or structural damage was reported.
The public observed penny-sized hail near and southeast of Calhoun as yet a second severe thunderstorm tracked from northwest to southeast across the county.

The public observed quarter to 1.50 inch diameter-sized hail in the far southeast corner of the county from just north and west of Mableton to around Six Flags.  This thunderstorm was the same thunderstorm that earlier produced hail in southwest Cobb county near Powder Springs.
The public observed quarter-sized hail northwest of Atlanta near the Cobb county line.

The public observed quarter-sized hail in the College Park area.  Earlier reports from the public indicated that golf ball-sized hail fell along the Douglas/Fulton county line southeast of Chapel Hill.  This storm tracked with similar intensity from this point eastward across southern Fulton county to College Park.  This was a separate thunderstorm from the one that was simultaneously producing hail further north in the county, northwest of Atlanta.

The Banks County 911 Center reported that penny-sized hail was observed at the Fire Station on Damascus Road northwest of Hollingsworth.  Radar data suggests that similar hail likely fell with this thunderstorm further southwest to east of Lula.

Many reports of quarter sized-hail were received across northern Cobb county from Acworth to Kennesaw to Marietta and the northeast corner of the county.  The public reported golf ball-sized hail northeast of Acworth near the Cherokee county line.  The public estimated that wind gusts with the thunderstorm were near 50 mph, but no structural, tree, or power line damage was reported.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in the Roswell area.  This was the third severe thunderstorm to affect Fulton county during the evening of April 23rd.

Several reports of large hail were received from the public across Clayton county as a slow moving severe thunderstorm tracked from the northwest to the east central part of the county.  The ASOS observer at the Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport observed penny to quarter-sized hail off and on for a period of 46 minutes.  Golf ball-sized hail was reported from the public in Forest Park and Morrow, while penny to quarter-sized hail fell near Rex, east of Morrow, and northeast of Jonesboro as the storm began to weaken slightly as it approached the eastern border of the county.  In addition, the wind gusted to 42 knots at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport during the hailstorm.  Frequent to continuous cloud-to-ground lightning was also observed at the airport during the thunderstorm.

The 398-foot tall FAA control tower at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport sustained a lightning strike.  Intense cloud-to-ground lightning during a severe thunderstorm had already resulted in a loss of power to much of the airport.  Employees of the tower smelled smoke in the tower immediately following the strike, which required a brief evacuation of the tower.  Ground operations were ceased for several minutes during this thunderstorm as a result, compounding an already bad situation at the world's busiest airport.  In addition, penny to quarter-sized hail fell off-and-on from 806 pm EDT to 852 pm EDT, winds gusts to 42 knots, and nearly 1.5 inches of rain fall during the one-hour period from 8 pm to 9 pm EDT.  Much of the metro Atlanta area reported power outages following these thunderstorms.  Despite the lightning strike to the tower and its impact on airport operations, no significant damages were reported.

The public observed penny-sized hail in the Tucker area and penny to golf ball-sized hail in the Stone Mountain area.  Radar data suggests that large hail likely fell from Tucker to Stone Mountain and points just to the east.
The Gwinnett County 911 Center reported that lightning struck a home on Riverwalk Trail just off Annistown Road.  The roof collapsed as as a result of the fire and the home was destroyed.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail just west of Snellville and half-dollar-sized hail in the Snellville area.  Amateur radio operators reported quarter-sized hail in the Lilburn area.

The public observed 1.50 inch diameter sized-hail on the east side of Dacula, while the public observed penny-sized hail for a 20-minute period on the northwest side of and near Dacula.  This hail occurred from a separate thunderstorm that developed more than 11 miles north of the one tracking across southern Gwinnett county from Lilburn to Snellville, which produced quarter to half-dollar-sized hail.

The public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail in the far northern part of the county near Bold Springs, while the public and the Walton County 911 Center observed nickel-sized hail further south in Monroe and south-southeastward toward the east side of Social Circle.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the southwest part of Madison county.  They reported that it hail for up to 12 minutes in this area.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that golf ball-sized hail fell at Turner Field just southeast of Atlanta.  The public observed penny-sized hail on the north side of Atlanta.  This was the fourth severe thunderstorm to track across Fulton county during the evening of April 23rd.

The public observed quarter to golf ball-sized hail in the far western part of Barrow county, especially in the Auburn area.  They reported that it hailed for up to 10 minutes in the Auburn area.  The public also reported nickel-sized hail in the Bethlehem area.
The public observed penny-sized hail.  Radar data suggests that this occurred in the northwest part of the county near Rutledge, not near Madison, where little to no radar returns were indicated.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the Covington area.  Radar data suggests that most of the hail fell on the east and southeast side of Covington.

A storm spotter observed quarter-sized hail just west of Stockbridge, while the public observed quarter-sized hail for up to 10 minutes in the Stockbridge area.  Nickel-sized hail was observed on Interstate-75 near Flippen and penny-sized hail was observed by the public in the McDonough area.
The Putnam County 911 Center reported penny-sized hail near Eatonton.  Radar data suggests that similar sized-hail or larger likely fell across the northwest part of the county.
The public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail from the northwest corner of the county near High Falls and Blount to just northeast of Forsyth.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the southwest part of Jones county, not far from Gray and Clinton.  Time and location of data refined with radar data.
The Bibb County Sheriff's Office reported that lightning struck a small shed on Mealer Street and set it on fire.

The Pike County Journal and Reporter of Zebulon reported that lightning struck a group of 16 cows lying down near a tree at a dairy farm on Kings Road near Meansville.  All of the cows were dead at the scene.
The Herald Tribune of Cartersville reported that lightning struck a home on Fairfield Drive and set the structure on fire.  The blaze in the two-story home was confined to the attic.
The Walton Times reported that the steeple of a church in Gratis was struck by lightning.  While no fire resulted, the sound system and some computers in the church suffered electronic damage.
The Cartersville Tribune reported that at least 25 downed trees and a number of power lines were down throughout the county.  At least 4000 residents of the county were left without power.
The News Observer of Blue Ridge reported that lightning struck a home on Dean Road causing minor damage to the structure.

The Gwinnett Daily post reported that at least 30 trees were down across the county.  Wind gusts were estimated at 45 mph, but radar data suggest that stronger winds may have occurred in some areas.  A police officer in Suwanee was struck in the head by a falling tree and injured.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a human-caused wildfire in the Shoal Creek area of Jones county.  The fire consumed 4.2 acres of forest.
The Georgia Forestry commission reported a human caused wildfire in Union county, labeled number 195.  The fire consumed 10 acres.

The Georgia Forestry commission reported a significant human-caused wildfire fueled by strong winds and low relative humidities in the mountains of Towns county.  The fire, labeled Bear Meat, burned for over three days and consumed 18.0 acres.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire in Jasper county in east central Georgia.  This fire was started as a result of power lines arcing in the wind.  The fire only consumed 1/2 acre.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a human-caused wildfire.  The fire was labeled Sharp Top and consumed 3.5 acres.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a human-caused wildfire.  The fire was labeled Cooper Gap and consumed 3.5 acres.
The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were blown down by strong straight-line winds.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that funnel clouds had been observed near the Rome High School.  Radar data showed a mesocyclone in the northeast part of the county between Rome and Shannon during this time frame.

Atlanta metropolitan television stations reported that a large tree was blown down during a thunderstorm on Virginia Circle, about two miles north-northeast of downtown Atlanta.  The tree fell across a power line and onto two cars.

The Carroll County Emergency Management Director reported that at least a dozen trees were down across the county.  One home in Amindon Estates suffered structural damage when a tree fell through the structure.

The Heard County 911 Center and the Heard County Sheriff's Office reported that more than two dozen trees were down across the county, and a number of power lines as well.  Two homes in Franklin suffered extensive structural damage from downed trees.

The Heard County 911 Center reported that a home was set on fire.  It was not entirely clear whether this was from a lightning strike or a downed tree, but there was considerable cloud-to-ground lightning in the area at the time as a squall line of thunderstorms moved through the county.
The Troup County 911 Center and the Troup County Sheriff's Office reported that more than a dozen trees were blown down across the county.  No other structural damage was reported.

A deputy with the Polk County Sheriff's Office observed a funnel cloud on the north side of Cedartown near the intersection of the bypass, U.S. Highway 27, and the Super Wal-Mart.  No structural damage or tornado touchdown was observed or reported.  Radar data indicated a weak mesocyclone in the area at the time.
The Fannin County 911 Center reported that at least a dozen trees were blown down near Blue Ridge on Raccoon Drive.

Local Columbus television media reported that wind gusts of 54 mph were measured on the top of Saint Francis Hospital.  Three to four trees were also down across the county, including one at Woodruff Farms and Branton Woods Drive and on 15th Street.
The Meriwether County Sheriff's Office reported that three trees were blown down in the Greenville area.  One of the trees fell on a home causing damage to the structure.
The Bartow County 911 Center relayed reports from the public of funnel clouds.  A weak mesocyclone was evident on the radar storm relative velocity data at the time.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 50 trees were down across mainly the southern half of the county, especially in the Monroe Drive, Interstate-285, and Interstate-20 areas.  At least one structure sustained damage in this area from downed trees.  The public reported that another home in Palmetto suffered substantial damage when a large tree fell on structure.  Three adjacent vehicles were also damaged substantially.

The Coweta County Emergency Management Director reported that more than 100 trees were down across the county.  More than a dozen power lines were also down.  The majority of the damage was observed across the western and northern part of the county from Handy to north of Madras to near Palmetto, along the Fulton county line.  One resident reported that a downburst had occurred in the Handy area where several dozen trees were down at a private residence.  Trees down included large pine and oak trees.  Some trees were also down in the eastern and southern parts of the county near Newnan, Sharpsburg, and Senoia.  No structural damage was reported.  Approximately 3000 residents of the county were left without power for a few hours following the storms.

The DeKalb County 911 Center reported that at least 20 trees were blown down across the county.  While no specific locations were provided, radar data indicated that 50 knot or greater winds primarily affected areas from Druid Hills northeast to Tucker.

The Cobb County 911 Center reported that more than a dozen trees were down across the county, including one that fell on a home causing damage to the structure.  A tree was also down on Alabama Road in Mareitta.  Radar data indicated that there were two lines of thunderstorms causing strong to damaging winds across Cobb county.  One line moved from near Powder Springs at 610 pm EDT to the northeast corner of the county, northeast of Marietta, by 630 pm EDT.  Another smaller line moved from Powder Springs at 630 pm EDT to near Smyrna around 645 pm EDT.

The Fayette County 911 Center reported that at least 20 trees were down across the county.  The majority of the downed trees were in the western part of the county in the Peachtree City area.  An off duty National Weather Service employee observed that four large pine trees were snapped along Georgia Highway 74 near the Cooper Lighting Facility about three miles south of Peachtree City.  Amateur radio operators reported that a one foot-diameter tree was down in Fayetteville.
The Henry County 911 Center reported that at least seven trees were down within the county.  Three of these trees were down on structures causing damage, while the other four were down on roads.
The Lamar County 911 Center reported that from six to ten trees were blown down across the county.  No damage to structures was reported.

The Spalding County 911 Center reported that more than 20 trees were blown down across the county.  Most of the downed trees were within the city limits of Griffin.  Widespread power outages were observed within the county from downed power lines.  No structural damage was reported, however.
The Upson County 911 Center reported that three to four trees were blown down in the Yatesville area.
The Monroe County 911 Center reported that eight trees were blown down across the county.  No structural damage was reported.
The public reported that four trees were blown down in the far northwestern part of the county near the Monroe county line.  Some pea-sized hail may also have been observed in the same area.

The Hall County 911 Center reported that up to 10 trees were down from northwest of Gainesville, along Club and Riverside Drives, into the city of Gainesville itself.  No structural damage was reported.
The public reported that three trees were blown down within the city of Athens.  No structural damage was reported.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported that three trees were blown down near Cordelle.  One fell on a police vehicle while being driven, causing the car to hydroplane.  The car was totaled.

A southerly wind gust of 59 mph was measured at Lawson Air Field in the Fort Benning Military Reservation.  The wind was associated was likely the effect of a small wake low caused by outflow from a departing area of showers and thunderstorms to the east and south.  No tree, power line, or structural damage was observed in the generally highly wooded area of the military reservation.
The public observed penny-sized hail around Kite.
The public observed penny to nickel-sized hail along Deepstep Road, Fall Line Freeway, and Commerce Street in and northwest of Sandersville.
A storm spotter reported penny-sized hail just north of the intersection of Georgia Highway 127 and Moody Road, between Kathleen and Bonaire.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail between mile markers 48 and 49 on Interstate-185, near its intersection with Georgia Highway 109 or about 1.5 miles south of Interstate-85.
The public observed penny-sized hail in Thomaston and on the south side of Thomaston at the Raintree Golf Course.
The public observed penny-sized hail just southeast of Cusseta.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that at least a dozen trees were down on the southwest side of Atlanta in the Childress and Adams Drive areas.  A few homes in the area sustained minor to moderate damage from the downed trees.  A tree was also down on the northeast side of Atlanta at Glen Arden Way and North Highland Avenue.
The public observed penny-sized hail in extreme northeast Henry county, just north of Whitehouse near the intersection of Georgia Highway 138 and White Road.
A CoCoRaHS observer reported nickel-sized hail near Oasis in northwest Fannin county.

The USGS gage on the Ogeechee River at Midville rose to the 6.0 foot flood stage during the evening of May 6th.  This caused backup of water and minor flooding on William Swamp Creek, Rocky Creek, and Daniels Creek, upstream from Ogeechee River at Midville.  Minor flooding of low lands adjacent to these creeks and streams occurred.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The USGS gage on the Ogeechee River at Midville rose to the 6.0 foot flood stage during the evening of May 6th.  This caused backup of water and minor flooding on William Swamp Creek, Rocky Creek, and Daniels Creek, upstream from Ogeechee River at Midville.  Minor flooding of low lands adjacent to these creeks and streams occurred.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that heavy rain during the early morning hours caused ponding of water on some roads.  Two roads in the county were closed for several hours because of high water.

The Harris County 911 Center relayed reports of penny to nickel-sized hail from the southwest part of the county, between the Alabama border and Mulberry Grove.  One tree was also blown down on Bethlehem Church Road.

The public observed penny to quarter-sized hail in far eastern Harris county, just east of Waverly Hall at the intersection of Georgia Highway 208 and 36, eastward toward the Talbot county line, continuing into Talbot county.  This hail occurred from a re-intensification of the the same thunderstorm that earlier dumped nickel-sized hail west of Mulberry Grove.

The Talbot County Emergency Management Director reported golf ball-sized hail in Talbotton at the Timberline North Subdivision.  Two large pine trees were also snapped in half within this subdivision.  The public observed penny to quarter-sized hail along the Talbot/Harris county line, approximately eight miles west of Talbotton.  A report of penny-sized hail was also received from the Talbot County 911 Center.
A Crawford county sheriff's deputy observed quarter-sized hail in the southwest part of the county, southwest of Roberta.

The Taylor County Emergency Management Director reported that four trees were blown down in the area around Fickling Mill in the far northern part of the county.  This damage was caused by a small thunderstorm that tracked southeast along the Upson, Taylor, Crawford county line.  This thunderstorm produced quarter-sized hail just north of the Taylor/Crawford county line, southwest of Roberta.  Meanwhile, a stronger severe thunderstorm was almost simultaneously tracking across the southwestern part of Taylor county.

The Taylor County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were blown down in the southern part of the county, between Butler and Charing.  Doppler velocity base radar data strongly suggests that additional trees were likely blown down in very rural areas further eastward as well, between Rupert, Butler, and Potterville.  The 911 Center reported that some trees were down in many areas of the county.  A few trees were down on Georgia Highway 137 southwest of Roberta.
The Macon County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the northwest part of the county around Hicks.
The Schley County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the far northern part of the county between Murray's Crossroads and the Taylor/Crawford county borders.

The Houston County 911 Center reported that an apparent downburst had resulted in several dozen downed trees, power lines, and structural damage in the Centerville area.  Much of the damage was concentrated in the Sentry Oaks Neighborhood, where more than a dozen trees were down, some resulting in damage to homes.  A portion of Interstate-75 had to be closed until downed trees blocking the lanes could be cleared.  In addition, a business in Centerville, adjacent to the Galleria Mall, sustained moderate structural damage, including several blown out windows as well as damage to siding and awnings.  A number of trees were also blown down further east near and east of Warner Robins toward the Twiggs county line.
Several reports of hail, ranging in size from pennies to quarters, were received from the Houston County 911 Center and trained spotters across northern Houston county.

Several reports of penny to nickel-sized hail were received from Macon television stations, trained spotters, and the public.  The hail fell across southern Houston county from just southwest of Perry to southeast of Hayneville.  This hail was caused by a separate thunderstorm occurring almost simultaneously with the thunderstorm producing extensive wind damage and penny to quarter-sized hail in the northern portion of the county.

Macon television stations reported that from 20 to 30 trees were blown down or uprooted in the southern part of the county, especially within the Longleaf Subdivision near Elko.  This damage occurred from a separate thunderstorm from the one that was almost simultaneously causing extensive wind damage and penny to quarter-sized hail in the far northern portion of the county.

The Pulaski County Emergency Management Director reported extensive wind damage in the northern part of the county from Hawkinsville to just northwest of Mobley Crossing near the Bleckley county line.  More than two dozen trees were down in the area and a number of power lines.  At least one structure suffered substantial damage when a tree fell on the structure.  Several homes on the northwest side of Hawkinsville, especially along Jackson and Dooly streets, sustained minor to moderate roof damage when shingles or portions of the roofs were torn off the homes.
The Pulaski County 911 Center reported nickel-sized hail in the northeast part of the county between Hawkinsville and Mobley Crossing.

The Bleckley County Emergency Management Director and Macon television stations reported extensive wind damage in the southern part of Bleckley county.  Several dozen trees trees and many power lines were down, especially in the vicinity of Mac Thompson Road and Chicken Road.  Structural damage was also observed.  Some 20 to 25 homes sustained minor damage from downed trees.  One mobile home sustained significant damage when a tree fell on the structure.  A horse barn near the intersection of Mac Thomsron Road and Chicken Road collapsed during the strong winds.  A horse inside was initially rescued from the fallen structure, but later died from injuries.
Macon television stations relayed reports of quarter-sized hail from southern Bleckley county, near Frazier.
The Dodge County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the far northern part of the county near Roddy.
The Dodge County 911 Center reported penny-sized hail in the far northern part of the county between Gresston and Yonkers.

The Wheeler County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were down in the southern part of the county between Jordan and Lumber City along the Wheeler/Telfair county line.  Some trees and power lines were down on Georgia Highway 19.
The Telfair County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the Lumber City area near the Wheeler county line.
The public observed penny-sized hail.
The public observed nickel-sized hail near Sautee.  One tree was also blown down further south near Mossy Creek as this thunderstorm developed southward toward 845 pm EDT.
The public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail in far western Douglas county west of Winston and toward Villa Rica and the Carroll county border.

The public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail in the Villa Rica area of far northeast Carroll county from 825 to 835 pm EDT, and further west near Temple in the far northwestern part of the county from 855 pm to 858 pm EDT.
The public observed nickel-sized hail near Marietta.
A storm spotter reported penny-sized hail near Cisco.
The public reported that lightning struck a tree at a residence on Walker Circle, just east of Cassville, causing the tree to fall.
The public observed quarter-sized hail near Bremen and the Haralson County 911 Center reported hail of unknown, but likely penny-size, in Tallapoosa.

The Heard County 911 Center reported that six roads between Franklin and Centralhatchee were flooded and closed.  Water rose up to the bridge on Five Notch Road near Nut Road.  Water also rose up to the door a mobile home in the area.  Water was flowing out of the ditches on Victory Road.  While no homes were damaged, some debris removal was required in the areas of flooding.
The public reported that at least five trees were down just southwest of Workmore.  Fence damage was damaged from the downed trees as well.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail just southwest of Workmore.  Radar data suggests that large hail likely continued to the southeast side of Workmore.
A storm spotter observed nickel-sized hail west of Thomaston in the western and northwest part of Upson county.
The Troup County 911 Center reported penny to nickel-sized hail.

The Troup County 911 Center reported that at least seven trees were blown down in the La Grange area.  The La Grange Daily news reported that one of the downed trees fell on an adjacent porch and two vehicles in the 300 block of Park Avenue.  Another large oak tree split and fell on a home in the 1200 block of Third Avenue, damaging the roof and totaling a Honda Civic.  On Houston Street, a tree was blown down onto a power line and an adjacent vehicle.  A few other power lines were also down in the area.
A CocoRaHS observed reported nickel-sized hail in far southern Fannin county between Dial and Pisgah.

The Vidalia AWOS measured a wind gust of 52 mph at 300 pm EDT.  The Toombs County 911 Center reported that two trees and two power lines were down as a result of the strong winds in the area.  Pea-sized hail was observed in the far northern part of the county near Normantown.

The Rome News Tribune reported that lightning struck the pump house of the pool at the Callier Springs Country Club on the southeast side of Rome.  The pump house suffered minor damage from the resulting fire.
The Douglas County Sentinel reported that a church, located on Chapel Hill Road, suffered minor damage when a tree fell on the structure during thunderstorm wind gusts.

The Gwinnett Daily Post of Lawrenceville reported that lightning struck a home in the 900 block of Nature Trail.  The home was completely destroyed from the resulting fire.  Three residents of the home were displaced because of the loss.  No injuries or deaths were reported.

The Gwinnett Daily Post of Lawrenceville reported that lightning struck a home in the 1200 block of Preserve Park Drive on the Gwinnett county side of Loganville, between Snellville and Loganville.  The fire was quickly extinguished with only minor damage occurring.  Although a family of four was home at the time of the incident, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported that lightning struck a home northeast of Dalton in the Pleasant Grove community.  The structure suffered at least minor damage.
The Gordon County 911 Center reported nickel-sized hail near Calhoun.  Radar data suggests that the hail likely occurred closer to Resaca.
The Carroll County 911 Center reported that four trees were down in the southern part of the county.  One tree was down on Oak Grove Road and another was down on Oak Grove Church Road.
The public observed penny-sized hail just east-northeast of Stockbridge.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported that at least seven trees were blown down around Tunnel Hill.  One of the trees fell on a house on Tunnel-Hill Varnell Road causing significant damage to the structure.  Some power lines and power poles were also down in the area.

The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 40 trees were either uprooted or twisted across the county.  Several power lines were also down.
