The roof was also ripped off an old fire station near Ellijay that had been converted into a parks and recreational building.  Pea-sized hail was also observed during the thunderstorm.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Six Flags and the Fulton county line, or about eight miles west to west-northwest of Atlanta.

Amateur radio operators relayed reports of nickel-sized hail near the Downtown Connector, Interstate 75/85, and Freedom Parkway.  The public observed penny-sized hail in the western part of the county near Six Flags.  The public also observed pea-sized hail in downtown Atlanta.  Wind gusts near 40 mph also blew over traffic barrels and caused minor damage to hanging plastic banners.

The public observed quarter-sized hail around Eastman.  The Dodge County 911 Center observed pea-sized hail in Eastman.  Radar data suggests that penny to nickel-sized hail likely fell from Eastman to approximately six miles east-northeast of Eastman.

The Banks County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 25 trees were blown down across the county, several blocking roads, and one downed tree causing significant damage to the roof of a home.  Widespread power outages were observed and a number of traffic signals were rendered inoperative as a result.  Some railroad crossing arms were also torn off by the strong winds gusts.

The Washington County Emergency Management Director and the county 911 center reported that four trees were down in the western part of the county, one of which was down near the Wilkinson county line.
The Morgan County 911 Center reported that two trees were down on High Shoals Road and another was down on Apalachee Road in the far northern part of the county between Bostwick and High Shoals.
The public reported that several large oak trees were either uprooted or blown over near Smyrna along Derby Lane.  A possible microburst was suspected.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down in the central part of the county.  Radar data indicates that most of this likely occurred between Six Flags and just northwest of East Point.  A tree fell on a vehicle trapping two people inside.  No injuries were reported.
The public observed nickel-sized hail near Blairsville.
The Madison County 911 Center reported that many trees and and power lines were down across the county.

The Oglethorpe County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were down across the county, including the communities of Crawford, Lexington, Stephens, and Maxeys.  Radar data suggests that the most significant wind damage occurred in the eastern part of the county.
The Clarke County 911 Center reported that a few trees were down around Athens.

The public reported that the roof was ripped off a barn by downburst thunderstorm winds.  Part of the side of the barn was also torn off the structure by the strong winds.  The resultant debris was scattered for several hundred feet downstream.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in the vicinity of Lakeshore Mall.

The Jackson County 911 Center reported that a number of trees and several power lines were down across the county.  The Jackson Herald reported that numerous large old oak trees were down at the Shields-Ethridge Heritage Farm near Arcade.  Some of these trees fell on the farm's historic outbuildings.  The Athens Banner/Herald reported that 16 roads were blocked during the night from downed trees.
The Laurens County 911 Center reported that at least 10 trees were down, scattered about the county.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that heavy rain resulted in a small unnamed tributary, located just west of Interstate 85 and between Georgia Highway 166/Langford Parkway and Langston Drive, rising out of its banks and flooding an adjacent home.  The flooding to the home was confined to the yard, crawl space, garage, and a parked car.  Further examination determined that the flooding was the result of a collapsed culvert pipe casued  by heavy runoff and debris buildup in the area.

Columbus television stations reported that extensive street flooding was observed throughout the Columbus metropolitan area.  A number of cars stalled out when people attempted to drive them through areas of high water.
The Monroe County 911 Center reported that four trees were blown down in the far southern portion of the county.
The Bibb County Emergency Management Director reported that a number of trees were blown down across the western portion of the county.

Wind equipment at the University of Georgia mesonet site at Tennille recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.  Several power lines were down east of Sandersville.  In addition, the roof was blown off a barn east of Sandersville.
The Johnson County Emergency Management Director reported that a home was struck by lightning just north of Wrightsville causing damage to the structure.

The Peach County 911 Center reported that at least a dozen trees were down across the county, especially in the northern part of the county around Powersville.  Several trees were down on homes causing damage to the structures.
The ASOS at the Warner Robins Airport recorded a wind gust of 59 mph at 637 pm EDT.  However, no damage to trees, power lines, or structures was reported from the area.

The Johnson County Emergency Management Director reported that many trees and a number of power lines were down across the county from Wrightsville to Kite and southward toward Spann.  Several roads were blocked from downed trees, including parts of Georgia Highway 15 south of Wrightsville.  Two homes in the Kite area were completely destroyed from downed trees and strong winds.  Two others homes in the area sustained minor to moderate damage.  Several animal shelters and pole barns were damaged as well.

The Laurens County 911 Center reported that six trees were blown down.  The downed trees were scattered all the way from the northeast corner near Lovett to the southwest corner near Cadwell.  Radar data suggests that the strongest winds occurred across the eastern part of the county from Lovett to Minter.

The Pulaski County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees (at least a dozen, possibly more) were down across the county.  Some roads were blocked from downed trees.  Radar data suggests that the strongest winds tracked across the county from northeast of Browndale to just west of Finleyson.
Augusta television stations reported that several large trees were down on Georgia Highway 23 between Garfield and Twin City in the far eastern part of the county.

The Emanuel County 911 Center reported that several trees were down.  Radar data suggests that most of this occurred between Stillmore and Norristown as an area of thunderstorms moved southwest across the county, initiated by the earlier thunderstorms that caused damage in the far eastern part of the county between Garfield and Twin City.

The Wilcox County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were down, scattered about the county.  Radar data indicates that storms and strong winds, likely of 60 mph or possibly greater, affected the far western part of the county from the northwest corner of the county west of Pineview to just south of Pitts in the southwest part of the county.
The Toombs County Emergency Management Director reported that three trees were down around Lyons.
The public observed penny-sized hail.

The Dodge County Emergency Management Director reported that approximately six trees were down within the county.  Most of the trees were located in the far southern part of the county around Rhine, although one tree was down on Georgia Highway 87 at Isham Springs Road.

The Butts County Emergency Management Director reported that an apparent thunderstorm downburst or microburst caused extensive damage to trees, power lines, and property in the northeastern part of the county from the Henry county line, just northwest of Fincherville to the south side of Lake Jackson along the Butts/Jasper county line.  At least 40 trees were down along this path.  Some of the most significant damage occurred near the intersection of Georgia Highway 36 and Barnetts Bridge Road, where a number of trees and power lines were down and one home in the area suffered major damage.  A total of six homes sustained damage, two of which were severely damaged and four others sustained moderate damage.

The Bibb County 911 Center reported that at least eight trees were down across the county from just north of Macon near Cross Keys to approximately five miles south of Macon.  This included a 70 foot pine tree that was down on Park Drive at Wimbliss Road near Cross Keys.  Several power lines were also down as a result of the downed trees.

The Houston County 911 Center reported that four trees were down in the southern part of the county, generally around Hayneville.  Two additional trees were reported down in the west central part of the county near Perry, one of which caused damage to the roof of a home.
The public observed half-dollar-sized hail.

The Dodge County Fire and Rescue Department along with a trained spotter reported that at least four large trees were down in the western part of the county, along with several large limbs.  One of the trees were down on Daniels Church Road in Eastman.

The Laurens County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the western part of the county between Dexter and Cedar Grove.  A storm spotter personally observed at least three of these downed trees.

The Pulaski County 911 Center and the public reported that at least eight trees were down across the eastern part of the county.  At least three trees were down in the Hawkinsville area, including on Anderson and 5th Streets.  Five trees were down in the far southeastern corner of the county, well east of Wallace, on Midway Church Road near the Dodge county line.
The Cobb County 911 Center reported that at least 15 trees were down around Marietta.
The Telfair County 911 Center reported that at least 12 trees were down in the far eastern part of the county along the Wheeler county line from Scotland to Lumber City.

A trained spotter reported that at least eight trees were down in the far western portion of the county near the Wheeler county line from the Erick and Avants area near Little Ocmulgee State Park to just across the Telfair county line from Scotland.  Some county roads were blocked from the downed trees.
The Wilcox County 911 Center reported that a couple of trees were down on power lines in the far eastern portion of the county near the Dodge county line.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in the far southeast part of DeKalb county, south of Lithonia, near the Rockdale county line.

The Greene County 911 Center reported that over a dozen trees were down in the western part of the county from southwest of Greensboro to southwest of Veazey.  Some power lines were also down in the area as a result.  At least one tree was down on Georgia Highway 44 southwest of Greensboro.
The Butts County 911 Center reported that at least six trees were down scattered about the county from northwest to southeast.
The Baldwin County 911 Center reported that at least 10 trees were down in the far eastern part of the county, with some down on Georgia Highway 22 and 24.
An amateur radio operator reported quarter-sized hail in the far eastern part of the county near the Bibb county line.

An amateur radio operator reported that at least a dozen trees were down in the far western part of the county, especially around Perry.  Some structural damage was reported.  Trees were down on Georgia Avenue, Georgia Extension, Fourth Street, Georgia Highway 96, and U.S. Highway 41, near the high school, all in the Perry area.  A home and an adjacent vehicle on Fourth Street sustained damage from a downed tree.  Two business signs were also damaged on Georgia Highway 7, either side of Interstate-75 in Perry.  The west bound lane of Georgia Highway 96 was blocked by a large downed oak tree and a tree was also down on Valley Drive at Interstate-75.

Broadcast media, through the National Weather Service Charleston, South Carolina office relayed a report of several trees down across the county, especially in the Powersville area.  Trees were down on Georgia Highways 49, 97, and 247.

The Laurens County 911 Center reported that around 100 or more trees were down across the county.  Doppler radar data suggests that the strongest winds with these thunderstorms tracked from the northeast corner, north of Dublin, south-southwest to the southwest corner of the county, southwest of Cedar Grove.
The Laurens County Fire and Rescue Department reported that lightning set several hundred hay bales on fire in a field in the far northeastern part of the county, north of Dublin.
The Henry County Emergency Management Director reported that 10 Poplar Trees were down in the Pebble Brook Subdivision east of Stockbridge near the Rockdale county line.
A CoCoRaHS observer reported that several trees and power lines were down in the southeastern part of Crawford county.  Several power outages were observed in the area.
The Dade County Emergency Management Director reported that a couple of trees and one power line were down in the northern part of the county between Sand Mountain and Trenton.
The Heard County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the Texas area.

The Athens Banner/Herald reported several lightning incidents across eastern Jackson county as strong thunderstorms moved from northwest to southeast shortly after midnight EDT.  The roof of a unit at the Oak Hill Apartments on Old Hull Road in Commerce was set on fire by a lightning strike.  Also, near Commerce, a chicken house on Wilson Road was set on fire and completely destroyed.  Further southeast on Birch Street in Nicholson, a barn was set on fire and destroyed by a lightning strike.

The Madison County Journal reported that lightning struck and killed an 8-year old quarter horse at a private residence on Fred Goss Road, just southeast of Danielsville.  On Rogers Church Road, just northwest of Danielsville, a home was struck by lightning, which set an inside wire on fall.  Damage was minimal as the fire was quickly extinguished by firefighters.

The Daily Citizen of Dalton reported that lightning caused serious injuries to a horse located at a private residence on Charlotte Drive in Dalton.  The lightning struck a tree next to which the horse was huddled during the thunderstorm.

The Troup County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were blown down across the county.  AT least 1500 residents of the county were left without power for several hours following the event.

The Troup County 911 Center reported that lightning struck and set a storage building on fire.  The building was located on Teaver Street in the southwest part of La Grange.  While significant damage occurred to the structure, it was not totally destroyed.
The Harris County 911 Center reported that thunderstorm winds blew down a tree along Georgia Highway 85 onto an adjacent barn and power line.  The public observed pea-sized hail in the Cataula area.

The Dodge County Emergency Management Director and WMAZ Television of Macon reported that several trees and power lines were blown down around Eastman.  The roof was also blown off a barn under construction near Eastman.

The public reported that a downburst or microburst caused extensive damage to trees and power lines from the south side of Griffin, near the Spalding Regional Medical Center, to the southern border of the county east of Orchard Hill.  The most significant damage was noted along Maple Drive, East College Street, and Macon Road heading south toward Orchard Hill.  More than 200 trees and power lines were down along the roads blocking the roadways.  Trees were also down in several residential neighborhoods in these areas as well.  Some minor structural damage was reported from downed trees.  Power was out for several hours to as many as 4000 people in the area.

The Towns County Emergency Management Director reported that from four to six inches of rain fell in southern Towns county causing flash flooding just south of the community of Mountain Scene, or about eight miles south to southeast of Hiawassee.  The heavy rain forced High Shoals Creek, Soapstone Creek, and Corbin Creek, all headwaters of the Hiawassee River, to all exceed their banks and flood nearby areas.  A few private dirt roads were washed out by the flooded creeks.  No significant structural or property damage was reported.
A storm spotter observed penny-sized hail southwest of Bonaire.

The USGS stream gage at the South Fork of Peachtree Creek reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 2045 EDT. The Fayette County Emergency Management Director reported that a large home on Surrey Park Drive, just south of Fayetteville, was struck by lightning and set on fire. The John's Creek Herald reported that lightning struck a home on Quail Brook in the John's Creek community, just southeast of Alpharetta.  No specific damage information was provided.

The Gwinnett Daily Post of Lawrenceville reported that lightning struck a home in the 1800 block of Pine Road igniting two small fires.  The fires were quickly extinguished leaving only minor damage to the structure.

The Rome News Tribune reported that several trees were blown down on Coral Avenue and Cave Spring Road on the southwest side of Rome, between Rome and Cave Spring.

The Gwinnett Daily Post reported that a woman, at her residence on the Gwinnett county side of Loganville, was injured by a nearby lightning strike.  She was just stepping off the back porch of her home in the 4000 block of Beaverton Circle when lightning struck a nearby tree.  She was treated and released from the hospital with non-life threatening injuries.

The Rome News Tribune reported that lightning struck an old 1800's residential home in the Boozeville community resulting in a fire that completely destroyed the structure. The Monroe County Emergency Management Director reported that a large oak tree was blown down onto a home and vehicle on Indian Springs Drive.  The home suffered minor damage as a result. A female was inside at the time, but escaped without injury  Another tree was down across power lines at the intersection of North Lee Street and North Lee Street Extension. The public observed penny-sized hail east of Nickelsville.
The public reported that a field of corn was flattened by strong thunderstorm wind gusts.

A storm spotter observed quarter-sized hail just east and southeast of Loganville, between Loganville and the city of Between.  One tree was also blown down in the Loganville area.

Fox 5 TV of Atlanta relayed a report from the Gwinnett County Fire and Rescue Department of a lightning-related injury to a 15-year old female. The young female suffered numbness to her back and legs as a result of the lightning strike.  She was transported to a local medical facility, then treated and released.

Fox 5 Television of Atlanta relayed a report from the Gwinnett Fire and Rescue Department of a downed tree from thunderstorm wind gusts causing damage to a house in the 1700 block of Litchfield Road in Snellville.  The large tree fell on the house and caused significant damage to the roof, resulting in subsequent water damage.  In addition, several power lines were down in the Arcado Road area of Lilburn. The Sumter County 911 Center reported that a few power lines were blown down in the Americus area as a line of thunderstorms moved through.

The Emanuel County 911 Center reported that lightning struck a power pole and set it on fire.

The public measured a wind gust of 61 mph on home-based weather equipment.  Further to the northwest, the awning of a BP gas station was damaged at the intersection of U.S. Highway 211 and Rockwell Church Road.  Several trees and power lines were also down in the vicinity.

The Oconee County 911 Center reported that more than 15 trees and several power lines were down, especially across the eastern part of the county from just west of Bogart to near Barnett Shoals.  A large old oak tree fell on the roof of a home along North High Shoals Road resulting in moderate damage to the structure.  A mobile home on Dials Mill Spur was destroyed when a tree fell on it. An 18-wheel truck carrying gasoline wrecked when it ran into a tree that had fallen across Atlanta Highway near Pete Dickens Road.  The driver did not suffer any injuries.

The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 10 trees were down across mainly the western portion of the county from the southwest corner at the Pickens county line to just northeast of Ellijay.

The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that one road along the Pickens/Gilmer county line was flooded as rainfall of up to 2.5 inches fell in the area in approximately 30 minutes.  The road was temporarily closed.

The Whitfield County 911 Center reported that two trees were down, one near Cohutta and another near Dalton, as thunderstorms moved through the county.  The tree near Cohutta also brought down a power line when it fell.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that strong thunderstorm winds blew down over 50 trees from just south of Rome to Cave Spring and just southeast of Lindale.  Two homes suffered considerable damage from the downed trees.  One of these homes was on the west side of Rome on Mountain Chase Road.  Several power lines were also down throughout the same areas. The Paulding County Emergency Management Director reported that at least nine homes across the county were struck by lightning.  Two of these lightning strikes resulted in fires and damage to the structures.  In addition, one individual approximately three miles north-northeast of New Georgia was injured as a result of a lightning strike.  Lightning also struck a power line approximately three miles north-northeast of New Georgia in the southern part of the county, causing the power line to fall.

The Paulding County Emergency Management Director reported that four trees were down in the north part of the county and at least three trees were down in the south part of the county.  Doppler radar indicated a downburst traveled across much of the county from northwest to southeast.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Dallas.
The Cobb County 911 Center reported that lightning struck a tree and caused it to fall across a road.

The public reported that a poultry house collapsed from very localized thunderstorm downburst winds.  A very small thunderstorm was noted in the area at the time.  The damaged occurred approximately four miles southeast of the county courthouse in Knoxville.
The Cobb County 911 Center reported that two trees were blown down in the northeast part of the county.  One fell on and caused damage to a home.

The Clayton County 911 Center reported that lightning strikes resulted in two house fires in the Riverdale area.  Specific damages were not provided.  One tree was also blown down by thunderstorm winds.

The creek continued to rise, cresting at 12.9 feet at 1030 am EDT. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that lightning strikes resulted in three fires in the Johns Creek area of far north Fulton county.  No significant fire-related damage was reported.

The Lumpkin County Emergency Management Director, the county 911 center, and the public all observed flash flooding in several areas of the county. A person had to be evacuated from their home near the Chestatee River.  A mudslide occurred along Corinth Church Road.  Fortunately, no injuries were observed and damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Union County 911 Center reported flash flooding along Wolf Creek, approximately three miles of Vogel State Park.  The creek flooded portions of Wolf Pen Gap Road and Virginia Drive.  Only minor damage occurred, mainly in the form of debris removal.

The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that flash floods in Carroll county took the life of a 2-year old boy.  The mobile home of a family of four was swept away by flood waters from Snake Creek.  The childs's body was found almost a mile away from where the trailer home was originally anchored.  The mobile home was located in a trailer park near Snake Creek, which was observed to have been nearly 20 feet deep.  Local law enforcement officials note that the creek is normally only at a depth of two to three feet.  It took nearly four hours to rescue the three other residents of the home, a man, wife, and 1-year old boy, which were found clinging to trees several yards downstream.  This initial flash flood marked the beginning of a period of historical and record flash flooding across several west central Georgia counties.  Flood damage during this initial time frame was estimated to be in excess of $1.3 million.

Record and historical flooding began to expand into Cobb county during this time frame as repeated thunderstorms streamed from southwest to northeast across the region.  The USGS stream gage on Sweetwater Creek near Powder Springs and the Cobb/Paulding county line began to show flash flooding expanding eastward into southwest Cobb county.  The creek exceeded the flood stage of 13 feet at 1033 pm EST and continued to rise for sometime thereafter.  Flooding of some roads and culverts began during this time period.  Flood damage during this time frame was estimated to be near $12,000.

Numerous emergency management sources, as well as local law enforcement, newspapers, broadcast media, and National Weather Service surveys confirmed that record and catastrophic flash flooding began across Douglas county during this time frame.  Repeated rounds of thunderstorms with heavy rain tracked from southwest to northeast.  Flash flooding was observed in most parts of the county during this time frame.  Up to six inches of rain fell in this area on already saturated ground.  Rain continued overnight beyond this time frame, with some parts of the county receiving nearly 22 inches by the afternoon of the 21st.  Hundreds of homes and businesses were impacted before the flooding subsided, many totally destroyed.  Dozens of roads and bridges were were washed out as well, including some major roads such as Georgia Highway 166.  Some roads, including Georgia Highway 166 will be closed for up to a year while washed out bridges are repaired.  In addition, Douglas county suffered six flash flood deaths during this event, the most of any county from the historical floods in late September 2009.  Flash flood deaths are documented as follows.  The first flash flood death occurred at 1030 pm EDT when a 44-year old female was attempting to cross Mobley Creek at Banks Mill Road and was swept away in her Jeep Liberty.  The second flash flood death occurred at 1100 pm EDT when a 29-year old male was swept way in his sport utility vehicle while attempting to cross Pool Creek at Poole Mill Road.  The third flash flood death was that of a 26-year old female who also was attempting to cross Mobley Creek at Banks Mill Road.  The fourth flash flood death was that of a 27-year old male attempting to cross Town Branch Creek at Mann Road.  The fifth flash flood death in Douglas county occurred where Stewart's Mill Road crosses Anneewakee Creek when a 49-year old nurse was swept away in her vehicle while attempting to cross the creek.  She was on her way to work at the time.  The sixth flash flood death in Douglas county was that of a 55-year old male.  He was swept away in his Ford Ranger pickup truck while attempting to cross West Bully Creek on North Helton Road.  Numerous other high water rescues took place.  Many took place via boat to rescue people from flood homes, businesses, and vehicles.||During this time frame, damage was estimated to be close to $1 million.  Damages rose into the millions overnight and Monday as the flooding continued and worsened.

Paulding county Emergency Management personnel, local law enforcement, broadcast media, and newspapers reported that the historical and record flash flooding began to impact the southern portion of Paulding county during this time frame as repeated thunderstorms tracked across the area from the southwest.  The most significant flooding during this time period was associated with Sweetwater Creek, which began its climb to record flood stage.  By 1030 pm EDT, Sweetwater Creek near Brownsville and the Cobb/Paulding county line rose above flood stage.  Several roads, culverts, and some bridges were beginning to flood during this time frame.  Flood damage in southern Paulding county through 1100pm EST was estimated to be near $40,000.

The Taylor County Emergency Management reported that flooding continued for several hours after the flash flooding subsided.  Several roads remained under water throughout the night.  Additional road damage was observed.

The Peach County Emergency Management Director reported that eight roads were closed from flooding across the county.  Some of the roads closed included Rolling Hills Road, Woolfolk Road, Lilly Road, and the Georgia Highway 49 bypass.  Some of the roads could be closed for days to weeks as repairs are made.  This flooding was a result of repeated heavy rainfall for several hours during the late evening of the 17th and the early morning hours of the 18th.  The flooding in Peach county did not reach flash flood criteria, thus damage to roads was minimal.

The Taylor County Emergency Management Director reported that general flooding continued across eastern Taylor county for several hours after the flash flooding of the late evening hours of the 17th had subsided.  Several roads, including Georgia Highway 96, remained under water for several hours.  Additional damage was minimal compared to earlier flash flood-related damage.

The Crawford County Emergency Management Director reported that general flooding continued for several hours after flash flooding had subsided.  Several roads remained under water throughout the night and early morning hours.  Additional minor damage was observed from the flooding.

Fulton county Emergency Management personnel reported that general flooding continued for another hour or so after late morning and early afternoon flash flooding subsided. The homes of 42 people across the county were affected by the flooding.  Additional monetary damage was primarily in the form of flooded apartments.

Clayton county Emergency Management personnel reported that general flooding continued across a small portion of far northern Clayton county as late morning and early afternoon flash flooding subsided.  Additional minor property damage was observed.

The Lumpkin County Emergency Management Director reported that general flooding continued across the county following earlier flash flooding.  One home along the Chestatee River suffered minor damage from high water.  Many creeks and streams across the county were out of their banks.  Several roads remained under water as well, but no additional major flooding problems were reported.

The Union County Emergency Management Director reported that general flooding continued across the county following earlier flash flooding.  While some roads remained under water, no additional damage was reported.

The USGS stream gage on the Alcovy River near Lawrenceville reached its flood stage of 9.0 feet at 1205 pm EDT, crested at 9.70 feet at 145 pm EDT, and then fell below flood stage at 230 pm EDT.  Minor flooding was reported adjacent to the river.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Bibb County Emergency Management Director reported that flooding continued across much of the county following earlier flash flooding.  Several roads remained under water and closed.  Additional minor damage to roads an property was observed during this time frame.

The Bibb County Emergency Management Director reported that flooding continued across much of the county following earlier flash flooding.  Several roads remained under water and closed.  Additional minor damage to roads and property was observed during this time frame.

The USGS stream gage on the Alcovy River near Lawrenceville reached its flood stage of 9.0 feet at 1205 pm EDT, crested at 9.70 feet at 145 pm EDT, and then fell below flood stage at 230 pm EDT.  Minor flooding was reported adjacent to the river.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Morgan County Emergency Management Director reported that considerable flooding continued across the county much of the night following earlier flash flooding.  Several roads, especially in the southern part of the county, remained under water and closed, particularly U.S. Highway 441 and Georgia Highway 83.  Several creeks and streams in the central and southern part of the county were out of their banks.  Minor additional road damage was observed during this period.
