Paulding County Emergency Management personnel reported that at least ten lightning strike incidents were documented across the county during the late evening and early morning hours of thunderstorms and flash flooding.  At least two of the lightning strikes resulted in structural fires.  In addition, two Paulding county individuals were electrocuted by lightning in flood waters, but were not killed during the incidents.

Significant flash flooding continued and expanded from southern into western Cobb county during this time frame.  USGS stream gages showed that a number of creeks and streams across western and southern Cobb county were already in flood or rose to and exceeded flood stage during this time frame.  This included Powder Springs Creek, Noses Creek, and Sweetwater Creek.  Heavy rain and thunderstorms continued to track repeatedly from southwest to northeast across the same areas moving the area closer and closer to the record and historical flooding that unfolded during the early morning hours of the 21st.  During this time period, an increasing number of roads and culverts were damaged from the rising flood waters.  Damage during this time period across western Cobb county was estimated to exceed $200,000.

Paulding county Emergency Management personnel reported that flash flooding continued to expand and worsen across much of the county during this time frame.  Multiple road closures and a number of flash flood and high water rescues were conducted during this time frame.  However, no deaths were reported in Paulding county from the flash flooding.  Damage to roads and bridges continued to expand||As repeated thunderstorms with heavy rain tracked across the area from the southwest, numerous major roads were blocked by high water, including U.S. Highway 278 and Georgia Highway 92 near Hiram.  More than 69 roads were eventually closed across the county.  The county court house and at least two convenience stores on Georgia Highway 92 were closed because of flooding.  Schools were closed for several days because of flooded roads.||County emergency management personnel reported that 37 vehicles were rescued from flood waters and 46 residents of the county fell victim to rising flood waters and had to be rescued from peril.  Fifteen individuals were removed from their homes because of rising flood waters.  Two residents were electrocuted in flood waters by lightning strikes, but were not killed.  Three homes suffered wall collapses from flood waters.  At least eight gas leaks were caused by flood waters and eight power lines were either brought down or affected by trees downed in water logged soils.||During this time frame, flood damage was estimated to be $200,000.

The Catoosa County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding across the northern half of the county, especially in the Lakeview area.  Two people had to be rescued by boat from their homes as creeks rapidly rose out of their banks in the area.  Several apartments were flooded and sustained significant damage.  A number of cars were submerged in flood waters as well.  However, no injuries or deaths were reported from flash flooding in this county.  Monetary damage was mostly in the form of flooded apartments, homes, and vehicles.

Walker county emergency management personnel reported flash flooding across the northern half of the county.  The first floor of the Battlewood Apartments in Fort Oglethorpe were flooded, resulting in evacuations of several residents.  Several roads were flooded and closed as creeks rose several feet out of their banks.  Monetary damage in the county was primarily a result of damaged roads, bridges, and culverts.

Catoosa county emergency management personnel reported that extensive flooding was observed across much of the county as repeated thunderstorms with heavy rain tracked across the area for several hours.  Many roads became flooded and impassable and suffered considerable damage.  A number of home and apartments were flooded, especially in the Fort Oglethorpe and Midway areas.  Schools were closed for at least two days because of many impassable roads.  Monetary property damage during this time frame was estimated to be $340,000.

The Chattooga County Emergency Management Director reported significant flooding across the county.  Several roads in the county had water flowing across them as creeks exceeded flood stage in many locations.  Some roads had to be closed at creek crossings.  The most significant flooding was reported north of Cloudland.  Schools were closed in the county for at least two days because of impassable roads.  Monetary road damage was estimated to be at least $60,000, mostly a result of erosion.

Walker county emergency management personnel reported that significant flooding impacted parts of Walker county for the second time within a 12-hour period as repeated rounds of thunderstorms and heavy rain tracked across the area from southwest to northeast.  Many roads, homes, and apartments were flooded and sustained significant damage during this time frame.  The worst flooding occurred in the Chickamauga and Rossville area and from LaFayette to Mt. Carmel.  Many roads were closed and impassable.  Schools in much of the county were closed for at least two days.  Monetary damage to roads, homes, and apartments during this time frame was estimated to be in excess of $1 million.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported significant flash flooding in many parts of the county.  Several roads west of Rocky Face were flooded and closed as creeks exceeded flood stage in the area.  Dogwood Valley Road and Dunnigan Road were among some of the more significant roads closed in the area.  Many schools in the county were closed for at least two days because of impassable roads.  Monetary damage to roads, bridges, and culverts was estimated at $15,000.

The USGS stream gage on Noonday Creek at Woodstock reached its flood stage of 10 feet at 445 am EDT and remained above flood stage until 615 am EDT.  Minor flooding of several creeks and streams in the Woodstock area of southern Cherokee county was also observed.  Some roads in this portion of the county were flooded and became impassable during the early morning hours.  Damage, however, was confined to minor debris removal.

Several USGS stream gages showed significant flooding occurring across Cobb county as the record and catastrophic flash flooding continued to unfold across the county as repeated rounds of thunderstorms with heavy rain tracked from southwest to northwest across the area.  Rainfall amounts in excess of 10 inches were observed in much of the county during the nighttime and early morning hours.  Sope Creek near Marietta reached flood stage of 12 feet at 238 am EDT, Nickajack Creek near Mableton reached its flood stage of 10 feet at 504 am EDT, and the Chattahoochee River near Vinings and Cobb Parkway reached its flood stage of 14 feet at 346 am EDT.  Many roads adjacent these rivers and creeks suffered significant flooding, became impassable and were closed.  Many other smaller creeks and streams in these same general areas also went into flood.  Monetary damage to roads during this time frame was estimated at $10,000.

Several USGS stream gages showed significant flooding commencing during this time frame across DeKalb county as thunderstorms with heavy rain, which had been west of the area most of the night, began to edge east-northeast and develop across Fulton, DeKalb, and Gwinnett counties.  The South Fork of Peachtree Creek at Johnson Road reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 128 am EDT.  The North Fork of Peachtree Creek at Buford Highway reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 201 am EDT.  Many homes, apartments, and businesses began to experience significant flooding during this time frame, especially in the vicinity of the flooded creeks.  A number of roads also became flooded, impassable, and were closed.  Monetary damage to roads and property during this time frame was estimated to exceed $750,000.

Several USGS stream gages in Fulton county indicated that significant flooding was commencing across Fulton county, especially the central and northern portion of the county.  Peachtree Creek at Northside Drive reached its flood stage of 17 feet at 353 am EDT.  Nancy Creek at Rickenbacker Drive reached its flood stage of 11 feet at 444 am EDT.  The Chattahoochee River near Vingings and Paces Ferry Road reached its flood stage of 14 feet at 501 am EDT.  Many homes, apartments, businesses, and roads experienced at least moderate flooding by the end of this time period.  The heavy rain caused some trees to fall in water logged soil, causing minor power outages in the Sandy Springs area.  Monetary damage to roads and property during this time frame was near $4.5 million.

The USGS stream gage along the lower portion of Big Creek in the far southern portion of Forsyth county near the Fulton county line went into minor flood at 1245 am EDT on the 21st.  Damage at this time in this portion of the county was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the flooded portion of the creek.

Catastrophic flash flooding began to unfold across portions of Gwinnett county during the early morning hours of the 21st as a secondary area of very heavy rain and thunderstorms began to expand across the eastern Atlanta metropolitan counties.  Rainfall exceeded 12 inches in portions of the county during the night and early morning hours.  USGS stream gages verified that significant flooding was underway.  Crooked Creek at Norcross exceeded its flood stage of 11 feet at 306 am EDT.  Pew Creek near Lawrenceville reached its flood stage of 11 feet at 418 am EDT.  Many roads became flooded and impassable as they were submerged by several feet of water in some areas.  A 39-year old female lost her life as her vehicle was washed off Desiree Drive and she was carried away in the flood waters of a small tributary feeding into the Yellow River.  Many homes, apartments, businesses and roads from Norcross to Lawrenceville to Lilburn were flooded during this time frame.  Monetary damage to roads and property during this period was estimated to exceed $600,000.

The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that several roads were flooded in the Lawrenceville area from flooded creeks and streams as flooding from repeated thunderstorms with heavy rain began to expand into the southeastern portion of the county.  The USGS stream gage along the Alcovy River just southeast of Lawrenceville reached its flood stage of 9 feet at 823 am EDT.  Monetary damage to roads in this portion of the county was estimated to exceed $600,000 during this time frame.

The Hall County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding from Walnut Creek, just north of the Jackson county line in southeast Hall county.  Walnut Creek washed out portions of Cooper Bridge Road in this portion of the county.  Monetary damage during this time frame was confined to debris removal adjacent to the creek.  No homes or property were affected during this time period.

The USGS stream gage along the Alcovy River in extreme northern Walton county, near the Gwinett county line, showed that the river went into minor flood for a brief period during the morning.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal, with no damage to property or roads indicated during this time frame.

The Jackson County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding along Walnut Creek near the Hall county line in extreme northwest Jackson county.  The creek flooded and washed out the bridge on Cooper Bridge Road.  No damage to homes or businesses was observed during this time frame.  Monetary damage to the road was estimated to be $30,000.

The Oconee County Emergency Management Director reported minor flash flooding in some parts of the county as rainfall exceeded six inches in a 12-hour period.  One road in a Bogart subdivision was closed because of flooding.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The Madison County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding in some parts of the county.  One road was closed because of flooding.  An assisted living facility for senior citizens along the Broad River was threatened from flood waters as the Broad River rose to just below two feet of the base of the structure.  However, no evacuations were necessary and the facility did not suffer any flood damage.  A road in a historical park just south of Comer was also flooded and closed during the height of the flooding as a creek in the park exceeded bankfull.  Monetary damage was limited to minor debris removal.

The Greene County 911 Center reported flash flooding primarily in the northern and western portions of the county.  A portion of Macadonia Church Road was flooded and closed.  A commercial building in the same general area was also flooded.  Monetary damage to the road and property was estimated to be $10,000.

The Clarke County 911 Center reported flash flooding in parts of the county.  The most significant flash flooding was observed in the Winterville area where portions of Beaver Dam and Cherokee Roads were flooded and closed.  Over four inches of rain fell in a 6-hour period during the evening of the 21st.  Monetary damage to the roads was estimated to be $5000.

The Baldwin County 911 Center reported that heavy rain, on the order of two inches in a two hour period, resulted in flooding of Gum Cemetery Road, just northeast of Milledgeville.  No other significant flood events were reported from the county.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The USGS stream gage on the Little River near Eatonton reached its flood stage of 20 feet at 945 pm EDT.  It remained above flood stage for several hours thereafter.  Some areas near the river experienced minor flooding.  Monetary damage was limited to debris removal adjacent to the river.

The USGS stream gage on Kettle Creek just south of Washington reached its flood stage of 14 feet at 1145 pm EDT.  The creek remained above flood stage for several hours.  Monetary damage was confined to minor debris removal from areas adjacent to the creek.

The public observed flash flooding in the area one to two miles west-southwest of Warner Robins.  At least four feet of water was flowing over a road near Wright's Mill and a bridge on Nelson Road was submerged with large debris flowing over the bridge.  Several other roads in the area had up to one foot of water flowing over them.  Up to one foot of water was flowing through homes two miles north of Perry and at Filler's Convenience Store, one mile northeast of Perry.  Other stores in Perry had up to one foot of water lapping at store fronts.  Monetary damage to roads and property within this fairly heavily populated portion of the county was estimated to be $50,000.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported considerable flash flooding across the county as the final round of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rain tracked across the county from west to east.  The ground was totally saturated from previous rainfall earlier that day and during prior weeks.  At least 20 roads across the county were flooded and closed.  Coahulla Creek at Keith's Mill near Dalton reached its flood stage of 16 feet at 223 pm EDT and continued to rise during the afternoon, remaining above flood stage into the next day.  The flash flood event transitioned to an aerial flood event after 315 pm EDT.  Monetary damage was generally confined to debris removal and estimated at $10,000.

The public observed flash flooding in the far northwest part of the county, just northwest of Resaca.  Dry Creek along Cline Road was out of its banks flooding adjacent pastures.  A nearby house was threatened from by flood waters of the creek, but was not actually flooded.  Significant debris removal was required in the area placing the monetary damage estimate at $30,000.

The Dade County Emergency Management Director reported that flash flooding caused a mudslide when a 30 by 30 foot section of hillside washed onto White Oak Gap Road west of Trenton.  Removal of debris from the affected road was estimated to be $10,000.

The USGS stream gage on Nickajack Creek near Mableton reached its flood stage of 10 feet at 748 pm EDT as the final round of heavy showers and thunderstorms tracked from west to east across the area on totally saturated ground from several weeks of flooding rainfall.  This incident resulted in only minor debris removal with monetary damages estimated to be $2000.

The USGS stream gage along the North Fork of Peachtree Creek near Atlanta on Buford Highway reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 909 pm EDT.  The creek remained above flood stage for almost an hour.  Only minor debris removal was required as a result of this flood event.

The USGS stream gage along the upper portion of Peachtree Creek near the Fulton/DeKalb county reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 909 pm EDT.  The creek remained above flood stage for approximately an hour.  Only minor flooding was observed with this event.  Monetary damage was confined to minor debris removal.

Although flash flooding began to subside, extensive flooding was reported across the county and confirmed from several USGS stream gages.  Flooding expanded on areas earlier dexperiencing flash flooding.  Record flooding was observed along Sweetwater Creek near Powder Springs, Powder Springs Creek, Noses Creek, and numerous other small creeks and tributaries.  At least 100 roads across the county were closed, including portions of Interstate 20 and Interstate 285 near Six Flags.  Extensive rescue operations were conducted in many areas of the county as motorists found their vehicle submerged in flood waters.  At least a dozen people were evacuated in Powder Springs because of rising water from Sweetwater Creek near their homes.  Other neighborhoods in south Cobb county were also flooded.  Damage to home and businesses throughout much of the county was tremendous.  During this time period alone, it was estimated that roads and property in the county sustained damage nearing $6 million.

Earlier flash flooding evolved into record and catastrophic flooding as confirmed by emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages.  More than 40 roads across the county were completely washed out, including Post Road just south of Interstate-20.  A portion of Interstate-20 near Fairburn Road was closed for nearly 12-hours causing major traffic backups throughout the region.  The main line of the Norfolk-Southern railroad near Villa Rica was also washed out.  A seventh person in Douglas county fell victim to the raging flood waters.  A 29-year old female perished when she was swept away in her vehicle by flood waters from the Dog River at 451 am EDT.  Over 1200 residents in the county were left without power as several tress in water logged soils fell on adjacent power lines.  This primarily affected areas near and including Arbor Place Mall along Interstate-20 near Fairburn Road.  Schools throughout the county were closed because of many impassable and flooded roads.  Many homes, businesses, and roads across the county sustained tremendous damage.  Washed out bridges will result in some roads being closed for up to a year, including portions of Georgia Highway 166 near Campbellton.  Monetary damage to roads and property during this time frame was estimated to be close to $9 million.

Initial flash flooding evolved into a record and catastrophic flood event during this time frame.  Carroll county emergency management personnel reported that at least a dozen other people were rescued from flooded homes and cars around the county, including one woman who escaped to safety as her vehicle was washed as she was driving.  Substantial damage to homes, businesses, and roads were observed.  Monetary damage during this time period was estimated to be in excess of $16 million.

As was the case with the neighboring northwest Atlanta metropolitan counties of Carroll, Douglas, and Cobb, initial flash flooding evolved into a record and catastrophic flood event across the southeast part of Paulding county as well.  Extensive damage to roads and bridges were observed in this portion of the county.  Many creeks and streams rose well above flood stage and remained so for over a day.  Many homes and business sustained significant damage.  Several high water rescues had to be performed during the height of the flooding and subsequent hours, but fortunately no deaths occurred in Paulding county from the flooding.  Monetary damage to property and roads was estimated to be at least $2,000,000.||Numerous major roads were blocked by high water, including U.S. Highway 278 and Georgia Highway 92 near Hiram.  More than 69 roads were closed across the county.  The county court house and at least two convenience stores on Georgia Highway 92 were closed because of flooding.  Schools were closed for several days because of flooded roads.||County emergency management personnel reported that 37 vehicles were rescued from flood waters and 46 residents of the county fell victim to rising flood waters and had to be rescued from peril.  Fifteen individuals were removed from their homes because of rising flood waters.  Two residents were electrocuted in flood waters by lightning strikes, but were not killed.  Three homes suffered wall collapses from flood waters.  At least eight gas leaks were caused by flood waters and eight power lines were either brought down or affected by trees downed in water logged soils.||Damage from initial flash flooding and subsequent flooding was estimated to be close to $2.5 million.  Again, the majority of this damage occurred in the southeast part of the county near the Douglas and Cobb county borders.

Only minor flooding was observed across Heard county as compared with its neighboring counties to the east, Paulding, Douglas, and Carroll that were experiencing record to catastrophic flooding during this time period.  The Chattahoochee River at Franklin rose to its flood stage of 23 feet at 145 pm and remained above flood stage for several days thereafter.  Monetary damage within Heard county was confined to minor debris generally adjacent to creeks, streams, and rivers.

Catoosa county emergency management personnel confirmed that extensive flooding continued across much of the county, especially the northern areas.  The most significant flooding was observed in the northern portion of the county near Fort Oglethorpe.  Several roads were under water because of flooded creeks and streams.  Some property was damaged from flood waters.  Monetary damage during this time frame was estimated to be in excess of $150,000.

The Chattooga County Emergency Management Director reported that significant flooding continued across the county in the wake of earlier flash flooding.  The final flood victim of the September 20th and 21st record flood event was claimed in Chattooga county as a 14-year old boy attempted to rescue an individual from a vehicle caught in flood waters of the Chattooga River near Trion.  The boy drowned in the flood waters during this attempt.  The Chattooga River near Summerville rose above its flood stage of 14 feet at 904 am EDT and remained in flood for several hours throughout the day.  Several roads across the county were under water as a result of flooded streams and creeks.  Monetary damage to roads and property during this time period was estimated to be nearly $750,000.

Walker county emergency management personnel reported that several roads were under water across the county as a result of flooded creeks and streams.  The most significant flooding was observed in the Forth Oglethorpe and Rossville area, where several homes and businesses remained flooded from earlier flash flooding and continued flooding.  Monetary damage during this time period to roads and property was estimated to exceed $500,000.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported that considerable flooding continued in portions of the county, especially the northern areas.  Several roads remained under water as earlier flash flooding subsided, but aerial flooding continued for several hours.  Some homes and businesses continued to experience flooding during this time period.  Monetary damage during this time frame was estimated at $200,000.

Record and in some cases catastrophic, flooding continued to expand across the northern and western portions of the Atlanta metropolitan area as renewed rounds of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rain tracked repeatedly over the same areas throughout the day.  Portions of hundreds of roads in the county were closed from flooding and washed out bridges and/or culverts.  Even the Downtown Connector, Interstate-75/85, was closed for several hours because of flooding causing major traffic backups in the area.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, and businesses sustained significant flood damage.  Record flooding was occurring on Peachtree Creek and Nancy Creek in the north part of Atlanta.  A significant water treatment plant for the city of Atlanta was destroyed by flooding, with damage to this plant alone estimated to be $57,000,000.  Monetary damage during this time frame across Fulton county was estimated to be at least $48 million.

Record, and in some cases catastrophic, flooding continued to expand across the northern and western portions of the Atlanta metropolitan area as renewed rounds of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rain tracked repeatedly over the same areas throughout the day.  Portions of hundreds of roads in the county were closed from flooding and washed out bridges and/or culverts.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, and businesses sustained significant flood damage.  Record flooding was occurring on the Chattahoochee River at Vinings and on Sope Creek near Marietta.  Monetary damage during this time frame across Cobb county was estimated to be at least $10,000,000.  Total damages for Cobb county during this time frame were nearly $11.5 million.

Record, and in some cases catastrophic, flooding continued to expand across the northern and western portions of the Atlanta metropolitan area as renewed rounds of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rain tracked repeatedly over the same areas throughout the day.  Portions of hundreds of roads in the county were closed from flooding and washed out bridges and/or culverts.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, and businesses sustained significant flood damage.  Record flooding was occurring on Peachtree Creek, the North Fork of Peachtree Creek, and Nancy Creek in northeast Atlanta.  The interchange of Interstate-285 and Interstate-85 in northeast DeKalb county, known as Spaghetti Junction was completely shut down for nearly an hour early on the 21st because of flooding.  Major traffic backups occurred as a result.  A mud slide blocked two westbound lanes of U.S. Highway 78 at Hugh Howell Road.  Other mud slides were reported within the county.  These are just some of the more significant examples of flood damage in the county.  Monetary damage during this time frame across DeKalb county was estimated to exceed $6 million.

Significant to near record flooding continued to expand across the northern portions of the Atlanta metropolitan area as renewed rounds of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rain tracked repeatedly over the same areas throughout the day.  A number of roads, especially in the southern portion of the county, were closed from flooding and washed out bridges and/or culverts, including Georgia Highway 9 at Big Creek.  Many homes, apartments, and businesses sustained significant flood damage. Monetary damage to roads and property during this time frame across Forsyth county was estimated to exceed $2.5 million.

Record flooding continued to expand eastern the eastern suburbs of the Atlanta metropolitan area as renewed rounds of showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rain tracked repeatedly over the same areas throughout the day.  Portions of hundreds of roads in the county were closed from flooding and washed out bridges and/or culverts.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, and businesses sustained significant flood damage.  Record flooding was occurring on Suwanee Creek near Suwanee.  Some of the most significant flooding occurred in the Stone Mountain area on U.S. Highway 78 from the DeKalb county line to Ross Road.  Monetary damage to property and roads during this time frame across Gwinnett county was estimated to be near $12.5 million.

Moderate flooding was indicated by the USGS stream gage along the Alcovy River near the Gwinnett county line.  Portions of several roads were flooded from this and several other streams and creeks that were also in a minor to moderate flood state across the county.  Monetary damage to roads was estimated to be only $5,000 in this county, primarily in the form of debris removal.

Significant flooding continued across much of Gwinnett county during this period.  Several creeks and streams were in at least moderate flood from record rainfall.  The USGS stream gage on Shoal Creek near Lawrenceville exceeded its flood stage of 11 feet for several hours, beginning at 459 pm EDT, and the Apalachee River near Dacula exceeded its flood stage of 8 feet for several hours beginning at 604 pm EDT.  The Alcovy River, just southeast of Lawrenceville, went into moderate flood during this time period.  Additional monetary damage in excess of $600,000, primarily to roads, was estimated to have occurred during this time frame.

The Catoosa County Emergency Management Director reported that significant and widespread flooding continued across the county.  Many homes, apartments, and businesses remained or became flooded during this period.  The worst flooding was across the northern portion of the county, near Fort Oglethorpe.  A number of creeks and streams remained above flood stage.  Dozens of roads remained underwater, impassable, and closed.  Additional monetary damage during this time frame was at least $1 million.

The Chattooga County Emergency Management Director reported that significant and extensive flooding continued across much of the county.  The Chattooga River breached the levees and flooded parts of the city of Trion.  Dozens of homes and business were flooded and sustained significant damage, especially in the city of Trion.  A number of roads were also flooded, impassable, and closed.  Additional monetary damage nearing $7.5 million was incurred during this time frame.

Emergency Management personnel from Walker county reported that extensive flooding continued across the county and had expanded into southern portions as well.  Significant flooding was ongoing in the Rossville, Fort Oglethorpe, and LaFayette areas.  At least 20 roads were closed because of flooding.  Dozens of homes were flooded and suffered significant damage.  Additional monetary damage in the county from flooding during this time frame were estimated to be near $6 million.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported that significant flooding continued across much of the county during this time frame.  A number of roads remained flooded, impassable and closed.  Dozens of homes and businesses were flooded.  Coahulla Creek at Keith's Mill near Dalton exceeded flood stage of 16 feet at 1157 am EDT and remained above flood stage for several days.  Additional monetary damage during this time frame was estimated to be $500,000.

USGS stream gages on Settingdown Creek near Free Home and on Sharp Mountain Creek near Ballground both exceeded their flood stages of 13 and 18 feet, respectively.  The former occurred at 441 pm EDT and the later at 825 pm EDT.  Significant flooding was reported throughout the county, impacting roads, homes, apartments, and businesses.  Monetary damage was estimated to be near $9 million during this time frame.

The Pickens County 911 Center reported that Old Mill Road in Tate was closed because of flooding.  A number of residents were evacuated in the area as a precaution.  A portion of Georgia Highway 53 was also temporarily closed because of flooding.  However, no water rose into any homes.  Monetary damage was confined to minor debris removal in the area.

The USGS stream gage on the Etowah River near Cartersville exceeded its flood stage of 18 feet at 720 pm EDT and remained above flood stage throughout much of the night.  However, no significant damage to roads or property were reported in the county.  Monetary damage was confined to minor debris removal.
The USGS stream gage on the Etowah River near Cartersville remained in minor flood state for several hours.  Monetary damage in the area was confined to debris removal.

The Chattooga County Emergency Management Director reported that flooding continued across much of the county.  However, additional monetary damage during this time frame was estimated to be near $20,000.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported flooding across parts of Floyd county, especially in the Rome area.  A male was caught and injured in a storm drain when the raging high water attempted to carrying him downstream.  Minor flooding was observed on some roads in the county.  The monetary damage estimate was estimated to be $15,000, primarily in the form of debris removal.

The USGS stream gage on Euharlee Creek near Rockmart indicated that minor flooding was occuurring.  Some roads and adjacent property near the creek experienced flooding as a consequence for several hours.  Monetary damage, mainly in the form of debris removal, was estimated at $15,000.

The Union County 911 Center reported that two roads were closed near Blairsville because of flooding.  Creeks and streams across the county were near or slightly above bankful during this time frame.  Monetary damage was estimated to be $5000 in the form of debris removal along the flooded roads.

USGS stream gages indicated that minor flooding continued along the Etowah River and associated creeks and streams across the southern portion of the county.  Monetary damage was estimated to be $10,000 in the form of debris removal alongside the flooded creeks and streams.
The Barrow County 911 Center reported that numerous roads were flooded, impassable, and closed across the county.  Monetary damage to roads and bridges was estimated to be $100,000.

The Clayton County 911 Center reported that several roads were flooded throughout the county, especially the northern sections near the Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, Jonesboro, Riverdale, and Forest Park.  However, no roads were reported to have been closed during this time frame.  Some homes and apartments suffered minor flooding, especially in the Riverdale area.  Monetary damage was estimated to be $50,000.

The Gwinnett County 911 Center reported that significant flooding continued and was expanding into all parts of the county.  At least 30 roads were flooded, impassable, and closed throughout the county.  Dozens of homes were flooded as well.  Monetary damage of at least $5 million was incurred during this time frame.

The Hall County 911 Center reported that minor to moderate flooding continued across mainly the southern portion of the county.  At least three roads were closed in this portion of the county because of flooding.  Monetary damage to roads and property in the southern half of the county was estimated to be $50,000 during this time frame.

The Henry County 911 Center reported that significant flooding was occurring within the Pools Mobile Home Park in the northern portion of the county, five miles north of Stockbridge.  Several familes were trapped in their homes because of rising flood waters.  Minor flooding was reported on roads and many streams and creeks across the county were near or above bankfull.  Monetary damage to roads and property was estimated to be $250,000.

The Newton County Emergency Management Director reported that a mobile home community was completely flooded out.  Many creeks, streams, and rivers in the area were at or above bankfull.  Some roads were also flooded.  Monetary damage within the county, mostly within the flooded mobile home park, was estimated to be $700,000.

The Rockdale County Emergency Management Director reported that two subdivisions approximately five miles north of Conyers were evacuated as they were threatened from flood waters of adjacent creeks, streams, and rivers.  A third subdivision was put on alert for possible evacuation as well.  At least 18 roads across the county were closed.  The majority of the closed roads were in the northern portion of the county.  Monetary damage to roads and property was estimated to be nearly $1 million.

Cherokee county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major to record flooding continued across much of the county.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  A number of culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed, including portions of Interstate-575 near Woodstock.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained in major to record flood through 830 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding  continued to mount, with damages exceeding $44.5 million during this time frame, one of the highest flood damage amounts reported during this period of historical flooding.

Cobb county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that record to catastrophic flooding continued across much of the county.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  Many culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Some of the worst flooding during this event occurred in the Cobb and Douglas county area.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained in major to record flood through 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damage during this time frame exceeding $12.5 million.

DeKalb county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major to record flooding continued to expand into all parts of the county.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  A number of culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd, however, many areas remained in major to record flood through 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damage near $3.2 million during this time frame.

Douglas county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that record to catastrophic flooding continued across much of the county.  Some of the worst flooding during this event occurred in the Douglas and Cobb county areas.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  A number of culverts and/or bridges were washed out and many roads were closed.  Some will remain closed for months up to a year.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained in major to record flood until 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damage near $10.5 million, just during this time period.

Forsyth county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major flooding continued across much of the county, especially the southern sections.  Many homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  Several culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations, especially in the southern part of the county, remained in moderate to major flood until 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with an additional $330,000 during this time frame.

Fulton county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major to record flooding continued across much of the county.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  A number of culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd, however many locations, especially along the Chattahoochee River and the western border of the county, remained in moderate to major flood through 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damage nearing $22 million during this time period.

Gwinnett county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that record to catastrophic flooding continued across much of the county.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  A number of culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd.  However, many locations remained in major to record flood until 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damages exceeding $5.6 million during this time frame.

Rockdale county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major to record flooding continued across much of the county.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  Flood damages peaked across the county during this time frame as many culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Flood waters began to recede after 230 pm EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained flooded through 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage exceeded $2 million during this time frame.

Carroll county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that record to catastrophic flooding continued across much of the county, especially the eastern section.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  A number of culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd, but many areas remained in moderate to major flood until 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damages exceeding $5.5 million during this time frame.

Paulding county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that record to catastrophic flooding continued across much of the county, especially the southeast portion.  Hundreds of homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damages from flooding.  A number of culverts and/or bridges were washed out and several roads were closed.  Flood waters began to recede after 830 am EDT on the 22nd.  However, many locations remained in moderate to major flood until 715 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damages exceeding $1.25 million during this time frame.

USGS stream gages along the Chattahoochee River in the far western portion of the county near the Heard and Carroll county borders indicated that major to record flooding was occurring.  Property adjacent to the river was flooded for several days, but no significant damage to roads or property was suffered in Coweta county.  Major flooding continued through the early morning hours of the 23rd.  Monetary damage was confined to minor debris removal near the river.

USGS stream gages along the Chattahoochee River, which flows from northeast to southwest through Heard county and near Franklin, indicated that major to record flooding was occurring and continued for several days.  However, flooding was confined to areas adjacent to the river and no significant road or property damage was reported.  Monetary damage was limited to minor debris removal near the river.

Catoosa county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major to record flooding continued across much of the county.  Many homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damage from flooding.  Several roads were closed.  Monetary damages from flooding continued to mount, with an additional $340,000 incurred during this time frame, nearly all of which occurred prior to 845 am EDT on the 22nd.  Flood waters began to recede after 845 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained flooded through 845 am EDT on the 23rd.

Chattooga county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major to record flooding continued across much of the county.  Many homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damage from flooding.  Several roads were closed.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damages exceeding $3.7 million during this time frame, nearly all of which occurred prior to 845 am EDT on the 22nd.  Flood waters began to recede after 845 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained flooded through 845 am EDT on the 23rd.

Walker county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major to record flooding continued across much of the county.  Many homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damage from flooding.  Several roads were closed.  Monetary damage from flooding continued to mount, with damages exceeding $1 million during this time frame, nearly all of which occurred prior to 845 am EDT on the 22nd.  Flood waters began to recede after 845 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained flooded through 845 am EDT on the 23rd.

Whitfield county emergency management personnel and USGS stream gages confirmed that major flooding continued across much of the county.  Several homes, apartments, businesses, and roads sustained damage from flooding.  Several roads were closed.  Monetary damages from flooding continued to mount, with an additional $250,000 incurred during this time frame, nearly all of which occurred prior to 845 am EDT on the 22nd.  Flood waters began to recede after 845 am EDT on the 22nd, but many locations remained flooded through 845 am EDT on the 23rd.

The USGS stream gage along the Conasauga River at Eton reached its flood stage of 12 feet at 715 am EDT on the 22nd.  The river remained in flood for nearly 24 hours.  Minor flooding was reported to land adjacent to the river.  Monetary damage was limited to minor debris removal.

The USGS stream gage on the Turkey Creek at Byromville reached its flood stage of 10 feet at 1054 am EDT.  The creek remained above flood until 540 am EDT on the 23rd.  Monetary damage was confined to minor debris removal from areas adjacent to the creek.

The USGS stream gage on the Conasauga River near Eton reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 630 pm EDT.  The river runs along the Murray/Whitfield county line.  The river remained above flood stage through 915 pm EDT.  Monetary damage from this flooding was confined to minor debris removal to land adjacent to the river.  No siginficant property damage was reported.

The USGS stream gage on the Conasauga River near Eton reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 630 pm EDT.  The river runs along the Murray/Whitfield county line.  The river remained above flood stage through 915 pm EDT.  In addition, minor flooding continued along Coahulla Creek near Keith's Mill during this time period.  Monetary damage from this flooding was confined to minor debris removal to land adjacent to the river.  No siginficant property damage was reported.

The Chattooga County 911 Center reported that at least a dozen trees were blown down across the county, especially in the Summerville area.  Some power lines were also down as a result of the downed trees.
The Sumter County Sheriff observed quarter-sized hail in the Americus area.

The Sumter County Emergency Management Director confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down and tracked a little over two miles across the southern part of the county.  The tornado touched down approximately five miles south of Americus near U.S. Highway 19.  A grocery store on U.S. Highway 19, just south of McLittle Bridge Road, suffered a collapsed wall and roof damage.  A large tree also fell on a forestry building near the location.  A nearby home also suffered minor damage.  The tornado continued to a point approximately 5.5 miles southeast of Americus or near Georgia Highway 377.  Approximately 50 to 100 trees were uprooted along the path of the tornado.  Some power lines were also down along the path of the tornado.

The USGS stream gage on Noonday Creek near Woodstock rose to minor flood stage at 1230 pm EDT and remained in flood until 2:30 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creek.

USGS stream gages across Cobb county showed several locations going into flood.  On Sope Creek near Marietta, the flood stage of 12.0 feet was reached at 1037 am EDT.  At 1041 am EDT, Allatoona Creek near Mars Hill reached its flood stage of 13.0 feet.  At 1044 am EDT, Nickajack Creek near Mableton reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet.  Finally, at 1212 pm EDT, flood stage of 10.0 feet was reached on Noonday Creek near Woodstock.  The creeks and streams remained in flood through 230 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creeks and streams.

The USGS stream gage on the North Fork of Peachtree Creek near Atlanta reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet and remained in flood for nearly four hours.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creek.

The USGS stream gage on Dick Creek near Suwanee reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet at 1025 am EDT.  The creek remained in flood until 215 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creek.

USGS stream gages along Nancy Creek and Peachtree Creek in north Atlanta reached and exceeded their flood stages during an approximate three-hour period.  Nancy Creek reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet at 1148 am EDT while Peachtree Creek reached its flood stage of 17.0 feet at 150 pm EDT.  The creeks remained in flood through 230 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creeks.

Several USGS stream gages indicated flooding on creeks and streams across Gwinnett county.  At 914 am EDT, Pew Creek near Lawrenceville reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet.  At 1020 am EDT, Level Creek near Suwanee reached its flood stage of 9.0 feet.  At 1138 am EDT, the Alcovy River near Lawrenceville reached its flood stage of 9.0 feet.  At 1150 am EDT, Crooked Creek near Norcross reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet.  At 1259 pm EDT, Big Haynes Creek reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet.  Finally, the Yellow River near Lithonia reached its flood stage of 13.0 feet at 135 pm EDT.  Flooding continued along the creeks, streams, and rivers through 230 pm EDT.  However, damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creeks and streams.

The Banks County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding in certain areas across the county.  The most significant flooding occurred in the highly flash flood prone area of Banks Crossing near the intersection of Interstate-85 and U.S. Highway 441.  Portions of the roads experienced minor flooding.  Crooked Creek was out of its banks in the Commerce Factory Mall parking lot.  Damage was minor and confined to debris removal.

The Jackson County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding in the far northeast part of the county near the Banks county line in the Banks Crossing area, or near the intersection of Interstate-85 and U.S. Highway 441.  Flash flooding was observed in the Commerce Factory Mall parking lot, along the county line.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal.

The USGS stream gage on the Little River near Woodstock reached its flood stage of 11 feet at 333 pm EDT.  The Etowah River near East Canton reached its flood stage of 17 feet at 856 pm EDT.  Flooding subsided after 0130 am EDT on the 13th.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the rivers.

The USGS stream gage on Noses Creek near Powder Springs reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet at 742 pm EDT and remained in flood until 1130 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creek.

The USGS stream gage along the North Fork of Peachtree Creek in northeast Atlanta showed that minor flooding continued across the region following earlier flash flooding.  Minor flooding was also observed along the Yellow River in the eastern and southern part of the county.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creeks and rivers.

The USGS stream gage along Big Creek between Alpharetta and Cumming in the southwest part of the county showed that minor flooding continued across the area following earlier flash flooding.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creek.

The USGS stream gages along Nancy and Peachtree Creeks in north and northeast Atlanta, as well as along the Chattahoochee River, showed that minor flooding continued across areas adjacent to the creeks and rivers.  This followed earlier flash flooding along Peachtree Creek.  Additional damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creeks and rivers.

USGS stream gages indicated that minor flooding continued along Pew Creek, Level Creek, Crooked Creek, and Big Haynes Creek.  Minor flooding also continued along the Alcovy and Yellow Rivers.  This followed earlier flash flooding along many of these same creeks and rivers.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creeks, streams, and rivers.

The USGS stream gage along the Coosa River near Rome reached its flood stage of 24.0 feet at 307 am EDT and remained in flood until 745 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the river.
The Gordon County Emergency Management Director reported that around 30 roads were closed across the county because of high water.

The USGS stream gage on Lookout Creek at New England reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet.  This resulted in minor flooding adjacent to the creek.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal in these areas.

The Monroe County Emergency Management Director reported flooding in many areas of the county.  Several dirt roads were washed out in low-lying areas by swollen creeks and streams.  Some of the roads damaged and closed included Smith Road, Ebenezer Road, Marshall Road, Tredwell Road, and English Road.  A Forsyth resident had to be rescued from flood waters at the intersection of Marshall Road and Old Brent Road.  Swift flowing water was over one foot deep at the time of this event.  Some of the roads remained closed for several days.  Damage to culvert pipes and roads was estimated to be $15,000.

The Herald Gazette of Barnesville reported that Potato Creek on the west side of the county experienced minor flooding.  A 10-acre pond on U.S. Highway 41 in Redbone failed and flooded adjacent areas.  Only adjacent agricultural areas were affected.  Damages were mostly a result of the dam failure and associated debris removal.

Hurricane Ida moved inland near Mobile, Alabama early on the 10th and then tracked east-northeast across southern Alabama, southern Georgia, and the Florida Panhandle before emerging off the east coast as a strong low pressure system.  The remnants of the hurricane combined with a cold air wedge across north Georgia to bring abundant Atlantic and Gulf moisture into the region.  Twelve to 18-hour rainfall totals of 4-5 inches across north Georgia aggrevated totally saturated soils from an on of the wettest September and October periods on record to result in widespread creek, stream, and river flooding.  The generaly light to moderate intensity of the rainfall and its persistence over a long period of time resulted in limited flash flooding.  Damages from Hurricane Ida to Georgia were confined to minor flooding, mostly adjacent to rivers, creeks, and streams.  Some locations experienced flooding subsequently for several days.  Only 15 to 20 mph winds with some gusts to 25 mph were observed with the remnants of Ida as the tightly concentric wind field weakened rapidly with the inland movement.  In addition, no tornadoes were observed with the remnants of Ida as it tracked across the region.  Total damages from Ida within the Peachtree City, Georgia forecast area were well less than $100,000.

Only 15 to 20 mph winds with some gusts to 25 mph were observed with the remnants of Ida as the tightly concentric wind field weakened rapidly with the inland movement.  In addition, no tornadoes were observed with the remnants of Ida as it tracked across the region.  Total damages from Ida within the Peachtree City, Georgia forecast area were well less than $100,000.

The USGS stream gage on the Little Tallapoosa River near Tallapoosa reached its flood stage of 16.0 feet at 642 am EDT and remained in flood until 1130 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the river.

The Butts County Emergency Management Director reported that portions of Lucy Lane and Lunsford Road were covered with water much of the day and closed.  The flooding was a result of high water from the South River at Snapping Shoals.  The river crested at 12.9 feet with flood stage at 12.0 feet.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal from the affected roads.

The Banks County Emergency Management Director reported that four trees and two power lines were down as a result of gusty winds associated with the remnants of Hurricane Ida and totally saturated ground.

The USGS stream gage on Dick Creek near Suwanee reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet at 1025 am EDT and remained in minor flood through 215 pm EDT.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creek.

A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that damage across Monroe county was caused by 70 mph straight-line winds rather than a tornado.  Two homes suffered minor damage in the vicinity of Gosa Road and Callaway Road, approximately four miles southeast of Forsyth.  The damage was in the form of minor siding, roof, and gutter damage.  Television antennas were blown off two other nearby homes.  Two outbuildings in vicinity were also destroyed.  Approximately six mature pine trees were blown down from this area toward Lake Juliette in the northeast part of the county.

A storm survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down in the Piedmont National Wildlife Refuge, approximately 2.5 miles east-southeast of East Juliette or 3.0 miles east of Juliette in northwest Jones county and then traveled northeast a little less than two miles to a point near 3.5 miles east of East Juliette.  Maximum wind gusts were estimated to be 80 mph with the tornado path width estimated to be 100 yards.  The tornado traveled through a largely unpopulated, forested area.  Thus, damage was confined to from 50 to 100 mature pine trees that were snapped in half, mostly within the Piedmont Wildlife Refuge.  Some of the damaged trees were near a cemetery.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that yet another brief EF0 tornado touched down in central Georgia, this time in western Putnam county.  This tornado, as was the case with the earlier one in northern Jones county, touched down in a heavily forested area of the Oconee National Forest in western Putnam county.  The tornado touched down approximately 4.3 miles west of Eatonton and traveled approximately 1.5 miles on a northeastward path before lifting about 3.5 miles west-northwest of Eatonton.  Maximum winds with this tornado were estimated to be 85 mph with a maximum path width of 100 yards.  As was the case with the Jones county tornado, the damage was confined to trees.  In this case, nearly 500 trees were snapped off or uprooted along the damage path.  At least 50 of these trees were down across forestry roads.  Two hunters were trapped in the area by the downed trees, but were subsequently rescued unharmed when the forestry roads were cleared.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that yet a third tornado had touched down in central Georgia.  This tornado also touched down in Putnam county, but this time was rated an EF1 with maximum winds of 90 mph.  This tornado touched down near Little Road and Harmony Road, approximately 8.2 miles north-north of Eatonton, then moved north-northeast to a point near 9.0 miles north-northeast of Eatonton.  The maximum path width was determined to be 100 yards.  Hundreds of trees and several power lines were down along the path of the tornado.  One mobile home was rolled over on its side.  The occupant of the mobile home escaped uninjured, but was taken to the hospital anyway because of a coronary episode.  At least one outbuilding was destroyed, tin roofing was blown off a portion of one home's roof, and some fencing was also blown down along the path of the tornado.

The Jasper County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the southern part of the county along Georgia Highway 11, as well as Fullterton, Phillips, and Wenut Roads.  Most of the tree damage was within the Oconee National Forest area.  No structures or other property were reported to have been damaged.  Doppler radar data showed a clear mesocyclone detection within this area at the indicated time.

The Bibb County 911 Center reported that some power lines were down on Ayers Road two miles northwest of Macon.  While there were rain showers in the area at the time and severe thunderstorms in counties just to the northwest shortly thereafter, this damage was caused by strong gradient winds associated with strong upper dynamics.

The Baldwin County 911 Center reported that multiple trees and power lines were down in the northeast part of the county, northeast of Milledgeville.  That damage occurred as an area of moderate to heavy rain was moving by to the east and southeast of the area and thus was associated with strong gradient winds and strong upper-level atmospheric dynamics rather than from thunderstorm winds.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that strong straight-line winds up to 80 mph affected the northern parts of Lake Sinclair in southeastern Putnam county, near the Baldwin and Hancock county lines.  A mobile home on Twisting Hill Road suffered damage.  A loosely attached screen porch was thrown 20 yards from the mobile home and destroyed.  In addition, at least 20 trees were also down in the area from these strong winds.
The Greene County 911 Center reported that several trees were down near Greensboro.  Trees were down along Carry Station Road, Charles Road, and on Interstate-20.
The Oglethorpe County 911 Center reported that three trees were down between Philomath and Lexington.
The Wilkes County Emergency Management Director reported that a barn was blown across a field on Clark-Gresham Road, just northwest of Rayle near the Oglethorpe county line.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service hydrologist from Peachtree City, GA concluded that a flood had occurred in portions of Monroe county, generally southeast of Forsyth.  Small portions of Abernathy, Edwards, Treadwell, Smith, and Zellner Roads were covered with one to two feet of water from adjacent streams or creeks.  Minor erosion damage was observed to all of these roads.  In addition, portions of Joe Chambers Road also suffered erosion damage.  Drainpipes that had been replaced as recently as the previous April and May were observed to have severe erosion.  The road was closed to install larger drainpipes.  Estimated rainfall in the area was two to three inches in a 6-hour period.  The cost to repair these roads was estimated to be $30,000.

The Bartow County Emergency Management Director and the public reported that at least five trees were down in the Rydal area in the northern part of the county.  Three trees were down on East Valley Road and two were down on Givits Road.
A storm spotter measured a snowfall of 1.5 inches on exposed surfaces and grassy areas three miles south of Trenton.

The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director reported moderate snow and a temperature of 32 degrees.  A dusting of snow accumulated on grassy surfaces and elevated objects.  The roads in the area remained wet with no snow accumulation.
The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down across the county as a result of strong gradient winds.
The Floyd County 911 Center reported that up to five trees and a few power lines were down in the far northern part of the county near the Walker county line.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 40 trees were down across the county, most highly concentrated in the southern part of the county.  A few trees were down near Rocky Face and Dalton.  Several power lines were also down in the southern part of the county.

The Gordon County 911 Center reported that more than a dozen trees were blown down across the far northern portion of the county, generally west through north of Resaca.  Some fences were also damaged.
The Murray County 911 Center reported that at least eight trees were down across the southern portion of the county, especially near Ramhurst.

The Chattooga County 911 Center reported that considerable flash flooding was ongoing across the county, especially the northern portions.  Up to 18 roads in the countywere flooded and closed, including Dover Hill and Beavers Road.  One home, approximately eight miles southeast of Summerville, had two feet of water in its crawl space.  The Chattooga River at Summerville reached its flood stage of 14.0 feet and remained in flood for three hours.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that heavy rain during the morning hours caused several roads, especially in and around Rome, to become temporarily flooded and closed.  A home near Armuchee Creek in northern Floyd county suffered water damage when water rose nearly two feet deep in the crawl space causing damage to the heating system and well water pump.  A trailer home on Shorter Road, located within a flood prone area, also sustained water damage.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that 18 trees were down in around the Rome area.  At least one tree was down in the Lindale area.  Several power lines were also down between Rome and Lindale.
The Polk County 911 Center reported that at least seven trees were down between Cedartown, Fish Creek, and Rockmart.

The Gordon County Emergency Management Director reported that Snake Creek in the Sugar Valley area was out of banks, causing flooding of Baugh Mountain Road.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal from the road and adjacent areas.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding in several areas across the central and southern portion of the county.  Several roads were flooded and washed out when local creeks spilled out of their banks.  Drowning Bear Creek, Stover Creek, and Cohulla Creek were some of the more significant creeks flooded in the county.  At least 12 roads in the county were affected by flood waters.  Some of the roads flooded included Frazier Road, Vinewood Drive, Stover Creek Road, and Redwine Cove Road.  Three 6-foot diameter pipes were washed out on Stover Creek Road.  The USGS stream gage on Cohulla Creek near Keith's Mill below Dalton reached its flood stage of 16.0 feet during this time frame.  Monetary damage was estimated to be $50,000.
The Coweta County 911 Center and amateur radio operators reported that over a dozen trees and several power lines were down in the between Moreland, Newnan, Sharpsburg, and Thomas Crossroads.

The Fayette County 911 Center reported that several trees were down across the county, including within the cities of Peachtree City, Fayetteville, and Brooks.  Trees were down on the Georgia Highway 85 Connector just west of Brooks.  A foot bridge over a private pond near Brooks was crushed when a large tree fell on the structure.
The Rockdale County 911 Center reported that two trees and one power line were down in the far southern part of the county near Richardson Park.
The Spalding County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the far western part of the county, near the Fayette county line.
The Butts County 911 Center reported that a few trees were down north of Jackson.  One of the trees fell on a vehicle.  No injuries were reported.
The Clarke County 911 Center reported that two trees were down in the Athens area, one of which landed on a caused damage to a home.  Two power lines were also down near Athens.
The Jasper County 911 Center reported that a few trees and a few power lines were down in the western part of the county, approximately seven miles northwest of Monticello.

The Madison County 911 Center reported that at least five large trees and a few power lines were down in the southern part of the county.

The Oglethorpe County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the far northern part of the county, near the Madison county line.  Trees were down near Arnoldsville, Lake Hargrove, and on Chapel Road.  Damage was reported to a vehicle and a home from downed trees.  A roof was also blown off a barn.
The Warren County 911 Center reported that a few trees were down, scattered about the county.

The public reported that straight-line winds caused considerable damage to a Dacula neighborhood on Alcovy River Drive.  Nearly a dozen trees were down.  One home suffered minor damage when a tree fell on the structure.  In addition, a privacy fence was destroyed when a large pine tree crushed through the structure.
The public reported that a few trees were down on Glenn Road near the Troup county line.
The public reported that a few trees were down on Rock Mills Road in the far northwestern part of the county near the Heard county line.
The Dade County Emergency Managment Director reported that a few trees were down in the higher elevations of the county.  A couple of trees were down on Hail Gap Road, Brow Road, and New Home Road.
The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that two trees were down on a home on Lavton Drive in Rome causing damage to the structure.
A Walker County Sheriff's Deputy observed penny to nickel-sized hail on the south side of LaFayette.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding in the Cedar Creek Subdivision.  Water rose as high as the floor boards of six to seven homes, but did not actually enter the house.  However, the crawl spaces of the homes were flooded.  Several roads in the area were under water as well.  Pateville Road was closed because of flood waters from the northern branch of Swift Creek.  The Cedar Creek subdivision is located approximately one mile southwest of the intersection of Interstate-75 and the U.S. Highway 280.  Monetary damage to roads and property was estimated to be at least $50,000.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported that flash flooding evolved into several hours of general flooding in the Cedar Creek subdivision, just south of Cordele.  The flooding was a result of continued high water from Swift Creek and Cedar Creek in the area.  No additional monetary damage was incurred during this time period.

The USGS stream gage on Turkey Creek near Byromville reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet at 4 pm EST.  The river remained in flood for several hours.  In general, minor flooding was observed adjacent to the creek.  However, a portion of Robertson Road suffered erosion damage.  Monetary damage to the road and debris removal near the creek was estimated to be $2000.

The Sutmer County Sheriff reported that a large tree fell on a home on Oglethorpe Street in Americus causing damage to the home and trapping the three residents inside.  The occupants were rescued without injury.

The Sumter County Emergency Management Director relayed several reports of funnel clouds in the vicinity of Church Street in Americus.  No tornado touchdown was observed however.   A tornado warning was in effect for the area at the time and Doppler radar clearly indicated a mesocyclone in the vicinity at the time.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding in the Cedar Lake subdivision.  The flooding was a result of overflow from Cedar Lake.  Several homes in the subdivision were threatened by flood waters.  The water rose up into the crawl spaces of several homes in this neighborhood.  Several of the residential streets were flooded and impassable.  Monetary damage to roads and property was estimated to be $50,000.

The Sumter County Emergency Management Director reported that several ponds were over flowing their dams from heavy rain across the county.  Three dams in particular were affected, including McMath Mill Pond Dam, Murphy Mill Dam, and Lake Collins.  These ponds were 110 to 120 acres large.  These were as a result of excessive rain runoff from Wolf Creek, Mill Creek, and Parkers Mill Creek, respectively.  Fortunately, none of the dams actually failed.  Two people were rescued from their vehicle from flood waters from Mill Creek on Murphy Mill Road.  Several dirt roads across the county were washed out, but none of the paved roads suffered damage.  No injuries were reported.  Monetary damage was confined to debris removal in the area.

The Haralson County Emergency Management Director reported flooding from local creeks in the county.  Beech Creek was flooding portions of Old Ridgeway Road, five miles northwest of Bremen, and Brooks Creek was flooding portions of Frances-White Road, seven miles northeast of Buchanan.  Monetary damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the creeks.

The Whitfield County 911 Center reported 0.5 to 1.0 inch of snow and some sleet.  There were 247 accidents reported across the county.  Portions of Interstate-75 were closed during rush hour.  Roads remained icy for several days.
The Carroll County Emergency Management Director reported penny-sized hail near Roopeville.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported flash flooding, once again in the Cedar Creek Subdivision of Cordelle.  The flooding was largely the result of high water from adjacent Cedar Creek and overflow water from Cedar Creek Lake.  This was the same area that experienced flash flooding in December 2009.  Water approached the foundations of several homes in the subdivision.  The crawl spaces of several homes were flooded as a result causing minor damage to property.

A CoCoRaHS observer reported quarter-sized hail just south of Loganville near Between in the western part of Walton county.  The hail completely covered the ground and because of near freezing temperatures that followed subsequently as a cold front passed through the area, much of the hail remained on the ground overnight and into the next morning.  Ground accumulation of hail was observed across a near 7-mile long stretch of road in this area the next morning.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Lithonia.

The Troup County 911 Center reported that two trees were down in the county as a line of thunderstorms moved through the county.  One tree was down on a home on South Oak Drive, approximately five miles south of La Grange, and another tree was down on Whitaker Road three miles northeast of La Grange.  The strong winds also caused a porch of a home on Hamilton Street, approximately eight miles south of La Grange, to collapse.

The USGS stream gage on both the South and North Fork of Peachtree Creek indicated minor flooding was occurring.  The gage on the South Fork of the Peachtree Creek at Johnson Road near Atlanta reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 626 pm EST and remained above flood stage until 900 pm EST.  Along the North Fork of Peachtree Creek, the gage at Buford Highway reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet within the same time frame.  Minor flooding was observed at both locations.  Damage was confined to debris removal from areas adjacent to the creeks.

The USGS stream gage on the upper portion of Peachtree Creek near the merger of the North and South Fork of Peachtree Creek indicated that minor flooding was occurring.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal from areas adjacent to the creek.

USGS stream gages on Shoal Creek and Pew Creek indicated that minor flooding was occurring.  The gage on Shoal Creek at Paper Mill Road reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet at 623 pm EST and remained in flood until midnight EST.  Similarly, the gage on Pew Creek reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet and remained in flood during the same time frame.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal from areas adjacent to the creeks.

The Fayette County Emergency Management Director reported flooding of the Tinsley Mill Village Condominiums in Peachtree City as 2.0 to 3.0 inches of rain fell on totally saturated ground during the early afternoon from persistent rain and thunderstorms.  These structures are particularly susceptible to flooding because of poor engineering and have flooded many times in previous similar events.  Residents from 10 of the condominiums were rescued by boat.  One of the condominiums suffered minor damage when one to two inches of water flowed into the unit.  In addition, small branches of Flat Creek and Lake Peachtree in Peachtree City were overflowing and contributing to flooding in the Tinsley Mill Village area.

In addition, ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.50 inch were observed on Lookout Mountain causing several trees or tree limbs to fall on power lines.  Power outages were observed in the area.

Extensive icing was observed on trees and power lines in the area causing extended power outages to residents in this mountain community.  The area was largely inaccessible for the better part of three days except by emergency vehicles.  Many residents in the area were left without power for up to three days.  The icing extended into far northwest Dawson county as well.
