The Bartow County 911 Center reported that from 150 to 250 trees were blown down from the combination of strong winds and heavy rain during the early morning hours.  Much of the damage occurred in the East Valley Road and Maple Lane area.  More than 2400 residents of the county were left without power for 24 hours or more.

The Dade County 911 Center reported 1.5 to 2.0 inches of snow on Lookout Mountain and 1.5 inches of snow on Sand Mountain in the northern part of the county.  Elsewhere in the county, snowfall amounts were less than 1.0 inch.
The public reported penny-sized hail in the Thomaston area.
Two reports of penny-sized hail were received from the public, one in Warner Robins and the other in Kathleen.

The Times Herald of Newnan reported that lightning struck a home on Welcome-Sargent Road, west of Newnan, and blew out part of the kitchen wall, kitchen cabinets, and the some of the porch floorboards.  The crawl space was also set on fire by the lightning strike.
The Beacon Newspaper of Johns Creek reported that lightning struck a gas line adjacent to a home on Hillgate Crossing near Abbotts Bridge Road.  The home caught fire and sustained damage as a result.

The Georgia Forestry Commission reported that a human-caused wildfire in Whitfield county, labeled the Redwine Cove fire, burned 81 acres, took seven hours to contain, and resulted in $13,671 in damages.

The Georgia Forestry Commission reported that a human-caused wildfire fueled by strong northwest winds and low relative humidity burned 20 acres, took five hours to contain, and resulted in $4500 in damages.
The Banks County Emergency Management Director reported snowfall across the county ranging from 4.0 inches north to 0.0 inches in the south.
The Barrow county 911 Center reported an average of 1.5 inches of snow.
The Bartow County 911 Center reported an average of 1.0 inch of snow.
The Carroll County 911 Center reported an average of 1.0 inch of snow across the county, with up to 2.0 inches of snow in the Temple area.
The Catoosa County 911 Center reported an average of  2.0 inches of snow across the county, with up to 4.3 inches in the Ringgold area.
The Chattooga County 911 Center reported an average of 3.0 feet of snow, with amounts varying widely from 6.0 inches in the north to just 1.0 inch in the south.

The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director reported snowfall ranging from 3.0 inches in the west to 4.0 inches in the northeast part of the county.  However, there were reports of 7.0 inches of snow in Canton.
The Clarke County 911 Center reported 0.5 inch of less of snow across the county.
The FAA Observer at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport measured 1.1 inches of snow.  Elsewhere across the county, snowfall amounts were generally well less than 1.0 inch.
The Cobb County 911 Center reported an average of 3.0 inches of snow across the county, especially the northern sections.
The Dade County 911 Center reported an average of 2.0 to 3.0 inches of snow across the county, with 4.0 inches observed on Lookout and Sand Mountain.
The Dawson County 911 Center reported an average of 3.0 inches of snow across the county, with 5.0 inches observed in the northeast part of the county.
The DeKalb County 911 Center reported that on average the county observed 1.0 inches of snow, but the North Decatur area experienced 2.0 inches of snow.

The Haralson County 911 Center reported an average of 2.0 inches of snow across the county.

The Pickens County Emergency Management Director reported an average snowfall of 4.0 inches across the county, with amounts varying widely from 3.0 inches in the south to 8.0 inches in the Burnt Mountain area in the northeast part of the county.
The Polk County 911 Center reported an average of 3.5 inches of snow across the county, with up to 4.0 inches in the Cedartown area.
The Rockdale County 911 Center reported an average snowfall of only 0.25 inch across the county, with a maximum snowfall anywhere of 0.5 inch.
The Towns County 911 Center reported an average snowfall of 2.5 inches across the county, with amounts varying from 1.0 inch in the west to 4.0 inches in the east part of the county.

The Union County Emergency Management Director reported an average snowfall of 3.0 inches across the county with amounts varying from 1.5 inch in the west to 9.0 inches in the east in the Brasstown Bald and Suches areas.  This was the maximum snowfall reported from any north Georgia county during this event.
The Walker County 911 Center and CoCoRAHS observers reported an average snowfall of 3.0 inches across the county, with up to 7.0 inches in the higher elevations.
The White County Emergency Management Director reported an average snowfall of 3.5 inches across the county with amounts varying from 4.0 inches in the north to 2.0 inches in the south.

The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported an average of 2.5 inches of snow across the county, with amounts varying from less than 1.5 inch in the south to 4.0 inches in the north part of the county.
Employees at the Rising Fawn Post Office observed nickel to quarter-sized hail for up to 30 minutes.
The public observed penny to quarter-sized hail west of Ringgold.
The Chattooga County Emergency Management Director observed nickel-sized hail.  There were several other reports of hail received, but no size was given.
The public observed nickel to quarter-sized hail from between LaFayette and Cooper Heights northeast to near Chickamauga.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that extensive damage to trees and property southwest of Tunnel Hill was the result of a thunderstorm downburst with wind gusts estimated to be 70 mph.  The wind was also accompanied by 1/4 to 1/2 inch-diameter hail and very heavy rain.  The hail lasted up to five minutes at several spots along the path of the downburst and accumulated up to a depth of 12 to 18 inches at some locations.  Some of the hail was still on the ground up to 6 hours later.  The downburst affected a 3-mile long and 1-mile wide area, beginning near the intersection of Dogwood Valley Road and Houston Valley Road and ending near the intersection of Cottonwood Mill Road and Mount Vernon Road.  At least 100 trees were down along the path of the downburst.  Two mobile homes suffered extensive damage as a result of the downed trees.  Tin roofs were torn off a few barns.  Several homes sustained at least minor shingle damage.
The former Emergency Management Director for Oconee County observed penny to nickel-sized hail southwest of Bogart near the intersection of U.S. Highway 78 and Georgia Highway 53.
The public observed penny to nickel-sized hail across the north part of the county, especially in the Klondike Road area.
The public observed nickel-sized hail in Cordele and the Crisp County Emergency Management Director observed penny-sized hail near the intersection of U.S. Highway 41 and U.S. Highway 280.
A trained storm spotter observed penny-sized hail near Ellerslie.
Amateur radio operators relayed reports of nickel-sized hail, mostly south of Warner Robins.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a very weak and brief EF0 tornado caused minor damage just south of Unadilla.  The tornado touched down near the intersection of Taylor Street just west of Interstate-75 and continued approximately one mile east-northeast to a point on the east side of Interstate-75 near the intersection of 3rd District Road and Browns Chapel Road.  The maximum path width was determined to be 100 yards wide with maximum winds estimated to be 75 mph.  Near the touchdown point of the tornado, a tree fell causing minor damage to the corner of a home.  Another nearby home lost a few shingles.  As the tornado continued east, it crossed through a horse arena, where some tin roofing was torn from a portion of one row of horse stalls.  A large adjacent billboard was blown over on a car.  At the end point of the tornado, a tree top was broken out.

The Houston County Emergency Management Director reported that rainfall of 2.0 to 2.5 inches over a 2-hour period had resulted in six to seven inches of water on some roads, particularly in the Bonaire area.  Street flooding was observed at the intersection of Georgia Highway 96 and Georgia Highway 247.
The Bleckley County Emergency Management Director reported penny-sized hail just southwest of Cochran.
A National Weather Service Cooperative observed reported penny-sized hail from the Sautee area.  The hail lasted for up to five minutes.

The Lumpkin County 911 Center reported that at least six trees were down across the county, especially in the Dahlonega area.  Power was out from a downed power line in the Georgia Highway 52 area near Dahlonega.
WSB Television of Atlanta relayed a report of nickel-sized hail from the Dahlonega area.
The Forsyth County Emergency Management Director reported that four trees were blown down in the Cumming area.

Several reports of quarter-sized hail were received from the public across the central part of the county from Rocky Face to Dawnville.  An amateur radio operator reported a heavy accumulation of hail along U.S. Highway 76 on the north side of Dalton.
Amateur radio operators reported that several trees were down across the county, especially across the north part of Dalton.

The public observed golf ball-sized hail near Eton and quarter-sized hail west of Chatsworth.  Radar data suggests that at least quarter-sized hail continued east to northeast of Eton to near Conasauga Lake on the eastern border of the county.
The Murray County 911 Center reported that three trees were down in the Cisco area.
A storm spotter observed quarter-sized hail near Epworth.  Radar data suggests that hail of similar size likely continued northeast to near the Tennessee border and the city of McCaysville.

The Putnam County 911 Center reported golf ball-sized hail approximately six miles southeast of Eatonton.  The public observed quarter-sized hail on the Putnam county sided of Reynolds Plantation on Lake Oconee.
The public observed hail ranging in size from dimes to near quarters.
The Henry County Emergency Management Director relayed a report of penny to nickel-sized hail in the extreme southwest part of the county just north of Hampton.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in the Siloam area.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the far northern part of the county between Lyneville and Carters Grove.
An amateur radio operator observed penny-sized hail in the far southwest corner of the county near the Upson county line, south of Molena.

The Wilkes County Emergency Management Director relayed reports of golf ball-sized hail from the Rayle area.  Radar data suggests that quarter to golf ball-sized hail likely fell from just west-northwest of Tyrone along the Taliaferro county line, where golf ball-sized hail was also observed, to the northeast corner of the county, just north of Delhi.

The Upson County Emergency Management Director reported that dime to nickel-sized hail covered the ground at many locations across the county from southwest of Thomaston to The Rock.  The most significant reports of hail were received from the northeast part of the county between Thomaston and The Rock.
The public observed a considerable amount of penny to nickel-sized hail in the Barnesville area.  The ground was covered in some locations.

The public observed a funnel cloud in the Beall Springs area in far southwestern Warren county.  A tornado warning was in effect at the time and there was clear indication of a strong circulation on the Doppler radar.
A storm spotter observed golf ball-sized hail in the southeast part of the county, southeast of Warfield.

The Hancock County Emergency Management Director relayed a report of golf ball-sized hail from the western part of the county, northwest of Sparta.  The public observed golf ball-sized hail just north of Devereux, also in western Hancock county.
The Warren County 911 Center relayed a report of half dollar-sized hail from the far southern part of the county.
The Glascock County 911 Center relayed a report of half-dollar-sized hail from the far northern part of the county near the Warren county line.

Several reports of hail ranging in size from pennies to golf balls were received from the public and one trained storm spotter from the far north and northeast part of the county, near Lake Wildwood and Wesleyan.

The public observed penny-sized hail in the Gray area.  Radar data suggests that similar size hail likely fell from two separate storms, one that tracked across the far northern part of the county near Round Oak and another that tracked across the central part of the county later, just north of Gray.
The public observed penny-sized hail on Georgia Highway 140 near East Cherokee Street in the Canton area.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Temple.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported that a human-caused wildfire in the Anna Ruby Falls area of White county burned 17.3 acres during a 7-hour period and resulted in $10,000 in damages.

The Georgia Forestry Commission reported that a human-caused wildfire in the Union Hill area of the Oconee National Forest in Putnam county burned 4.3 acres during a 3-hour period and resulted in $900 in damages.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a brief EF1 tornado had touched down in northeast Morgan county, approximately two miles north-northeast of Bostwick.  The tornado first touched down on High Shoals Road, just south of the intersection with Rehoboth Road, then continued on an east-northeastward path across Rehoboth Road, Price Mill Road, and River Walk Road before lifting near the Appalachee River.  At the tornado touchdown point on High Shoals Road, the roof was blown off a chicken house.  As the tornado crossed Rehoboth Road, the roof of a home sustained significant damage and an adjacent barn was destroyed.  As the tornado continued across Price Mill Road, one home sustained major damage and was left uninhabitable.  Many trees were also either blown down or uprooted in the area.  As the tornado reached its final point along River Walk Road, a high voltage power line was destroyed and two additional homes sustained minor damage.  In total, five homes, one chicken house, and five out buildings were damaged.

The Macon County Sheriff's office reported that four trees were blown down near Georgia Highway 224 between Shiloh Church Road and Mennonite School Road, just east-northeast of Montezuma.  A funnel cloud was also observed by the public in this area at the time.
The public observed quarter-sized hail between Riverdale and Jonesboro.
The public observed quarter-sized hail on the east side of McDonough.
The Harris County Emergency Management Director relayed reports of penny-sized hail near Hamilton and Pine Mountain Valley.
The public observed quarter-sized hail from the west central part of the county near Yorkville to the central part of the county, just northwest of Dallas.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the west central part of the county, just northwest of Lost Mountain State Park.
The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that two trees and one power line were down between Lindale and Rome.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Offices in both Huntsville, Alabama and Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado, which initially touched down in eastern DeKalb county Alabama approximately three miles southeast of Valley Head, Alabama, continued into Chattooga county Georgia, crossing into Georgia approximately two miles northwest of Cloudland in northwest Chattooga county.  The tornado continued on a nearly 10 mile long path within Chattooga county ending approximately 2.5 miles northwest of Trion in north central Chattooga county.  The tornado was rated an EF1 with a maximum path width of 300 yards and maximum wind gusts estimated to be 105 mph.  Considerable damage was noted along the tornado path across far northwest and north central Chattooga county.  At the touchdown point, at least 15 large trees were down across a one-half mile wide area.  As the tornado continued eastward, it crossed Georgia Highway 157 at Gilreath Mill Road.  Hunderds of large mature trees were down near the intersection.  Just east of this location, the tornado strengthened to its maximum width and intensity.  This was determined to be the mid-point of the tornado path, between Georgia Highway 337 and Harrisburg Road.  Within this area, eight homes sustained significant damage.  Two garages, one carport, and several private storage buildings were destroyed.  At a small grass airport strip, one hanger was destroyed, another suffered extensive damage, and two airplanes were flipped over.  One of the airplanes was an 800 lb ultralight and the other was a 1500 lb Cessna.  Nearby, a home lost its roof, another suffered extensive shingle damage, and another storage building was destroyed.  At the location of this destroyed outbuilding, two lawn mowers were moved 90 feet.  From this point to the end of the tornado path, hundreds of large, mature oak, pecan, and pine trees were blown down or uprooted.  Center Post Road, near the end point of the tornado path, was blocked because of numerous downed trees.  Damage to homes, businesses, the airport, and timber land, along with cleanup, was estimated to be $1.2 million.

The Walker County 911 Center reported that more than seven trees were down along a path from near Center Post and the Chattooga county line toward Villanow.  This damage was caused by the same thunderstorm that spawned the tornado in Chattooga county.  No structural damage was observed in Walker county.
The Murray County Sheriff's Office reported that a few power lines were down in the Chatsworth area.
The Jasper County 911 Center reported penny-sized hail.
Amateur radio operators relayed reports of penny-sized hail near Kathleen.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that strong wind gusts associated with a line of showers and isolated thunderstorms blew down at least a dozen trees across the county.  An apartment building and adjacent garage were heavily damaged when a large oak tree fell on the structures. A vehicle was also damaged from a large downed tree limb.  Some power lines were also impacted by the downed trees.
The public observed penny-sized hail just east and southeast of Smyrna, especially near the intersection of Interstate-75 and Interstate-285.  Most of the hail was pea size.
The public observed penny-sized hail in downtown Atlanta and on the east side of Atlanta near Little Five Points.  Most of the hail was pea size.
The public observed penny-sized hail near East Lake in west central DeKalb county.  Most of the hail was pea size.

The Johnson County Emergency Management Director reported that at least seven trees were down between Wrightsville and Kite.  Two trees fell on and destroyed a batting cage on private property in Wrightsville.  A tree in Kite fell on an unoccupied vehicle.  Most of the downed trees were around Wrightsville.  Power was out in much of the county for about two hours.

The Georgia Forestry commission reported a wildfire in Gilmer county.  The human caused wildfire, labeled Brushy Head, burned 160 acres of forestry land and 240 acres of private land.  Losses sustained were estimated to be nearly $17,000.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a human-caused wildfire in the Narrows area of Chattooga county.  The fire burned 11 acres resulting in estimated damages of $8,300.

The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a human-caused wildfire in Fannin county.  This was one of two such events in Fannin county during April.  The fire, labeled Fruitkoff, burned 15.25 acres and resulted in $6,500 in damages.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a human-caused wildfire labeled County Line burned 3.0 acres and resulted in $5,000 in estimated damages.
The Georgia Forestry Commission reported a human-caused wildfire in the Haissiers Mill area (private land) burned six acres and resulted in roughly $2,000 in damages.

The Georgia Forestry Commission reported that the crash of a T9 military aircraft, performing in an air show near Blue Ridge, fueled a wildfire which burned 23 acres during a nearly 8-hour long period.  Damages sustained from this fire were estimated to be $26,000.
The Houston Home Journal of Perry reported that lightning struck and set a home on fire on Sandefur Road.  The home sustained major damage as the roof was almost completely destroyed.

The Times Herald of Newnan reported that strong winds from showers and isolated thunderstorms blew down a number of trees and several power lines across the county.  A home on Fifth Street near downtown sustained minor damage when a large tree fell on the structure.  The roof and guttering on the back of the home was damaged.  Power was out in the Newnan area for nearly an hour.
The Carroll county Emergency Management Director reported that lightning struck a gas main in the Grove Park subdivision igniting a fire.  No other damage or related incidents were reported.

Several creeks across DeKalb county reached and exceeded flood stage during this period.  This was verified by USGS stream gages.  On the South Fork of the Peachtree Creek at Johnson Road, the flood stage of 12.0 feet was reached at 640 am EDT.  The creek continued to rise and crested at 14.1 feet at 815 am EDT.  The North Fork of Peachtree Creek at Buford Highway reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 710 am EDT, then crested at 15.1 feet at 130 pm EDT.  On Snapfinger Creek in the southern part of the county, the flood stage of 12.0 feet was reached at 740 am EDT. The creek continued to rise to 12.7 feet at 915 pm EDT.  The DeKalb County Emergency Management Director reported that flood waters from the upper South Fork of Peachtree Creek flooded the crawl spaces of several apartments on Lansbury Village Drive.  Forty-five people had to be evacuated until the buildings were inspected and cleared of structural problems related to the flood waters.  Damages from the flash floods in DeKalb county were estimated to be $50,000.

Several creeks across Fulton county reached or exceeded flood stage during this period.  This information was verified by USGS stream gages on the creeks.  Proctor Creek at Jackson Parkway in Atlanta reached its flood stage of 13.0 feet at 655 am EDT.  The creek continued to rise and crested at 14.4 feet at 815 am EDT.  Flood stage on Peachtree Creek at Northside Drive of 18.0 feet was reached at 815 am EDT.  The creek continued to rise and crested at 19.2 feet at 1215 pm EDT.  On Nancy Creek at Rickenbacker Drive, major flood stage of 13.0 feet was reached at 1105 am EDT.  The creek eventually crested at 13.2 feet at 1200 pm EDT before finally beginning to fall.  The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that at least 50 homes were affected by the flood waters of Nancy and Peachtree Creeks.  A swift water rescue was required along Nancy Creek where a female had to be removed from the top of a home on Fairfield Road approximately four miles west of North Atlanta.  Flood waters covered portions of Cochran Mill Road, Cascade-Palmetto Highway, and Vandiver Road at Amen Road in central Fulton county, all a result of local creeks out of their banks.  Portions of Interstate-20 west of Atlanta were closed during the height of the flooding.  Damages to property and roads from the flooding were estimated to be $500,000.

Flash flooding was observed along several creeks in Gwinnett county as indicated by USGS stream gages.  Crooked Creek at Spalding Drive, three miles northwest of Norcross, reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet at 705 am EDT.  The creek crested at 13.1 feet at 915 am EDT.  Pew Creek at Paterson Road reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet at 805 am EDT and crested at 11.8 feet at 915 am EDT.  Sweetwater Creek at Club Drive reached its flood stage of 11.0 feet at 720 am EDT, then crested at 12.6 feet at noon EDT.  Several roads along the creeks were closed for several hours because of the flooding.  Water covered the grounds of the driving range at the Sugarloaf Golf Facility in Duluth.  Flood damage in Gwinnett county was primarily limited to debris removal and estimated to be $10,000.

The USGS stream gage on Nickajack Creek at the U.S. Highway 78 bridge reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet at 706 am EDT.  The creek crested at 13.4 feet at 1015 am EDT before beginning to fall.  Sweetwater Creek near Austell was nearly up to the bridge at Perkerson Mill Road.  Several roads in the area were closed.  Portions of Six Flag were submerged in standing water during the height of the heavy rain and flooding.  No damage was reported at the park, however.  Damage across the county was confined to minor debris removal from areas adjacent to the creek.

Flash flooding was indicated along the USGS stream gage on Sweetwater Creek at the Interstate-20 bridge where it reached its flood stage of 10.0 feet at 745 am EDT.  The creek continued to rise and crested at 11.0 feet at 930 am EDT.  The Douglas County Emergency Management Director indicated that a small dam near Post and Liberty roads was breached.  A pond on Rose Avenue also overtopped its dam and flooded parts of Rose Avenue with six inches of water.  Several roads in the county were closed because of slow drainage.  Several homes suffered flooded basements as well.  Damages to roads and property were estimated at $50,000.

The Carroll County Emergency Management Director reported that several road drainage culverts were washed out across the county.  Culverts were washed out on Hamp Chappell Road seven miles southeast of Carrollton, Horsley Mill Road near Little Snake Creek eight miles east of Carrollton, and at Dashboard Road 10 miles southwest of Carrollton.  At the height of the flooding, 18 roads across the county were closed.  Road repair cost the county $100,000.
The Carroll County Emergency Management Director reported that 10 roads across southern Carroll county were closed because of several inches of water on the roadways.

The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down in the vicinity of U.S. Highway 280 and Coney Road, west of Cordele.  At least two trees were down on a railroad track near Coney Road and U.S. Highway 280 blocking the tracks.

The Sumter County Emergency Management Director reported that up to eight trees were down across the county.  Radar data suggests that the majority of the incidents occurred between Maddox and Methvins where a line of strong thunderstorms passed.
The Pulaski County 911 Center reported that two to three trees were down in the Hawkinsville area.
The Telfair County 911 Center reported that two to three trees were down in the far northern part of the county near McRae.

Fox 5 Television of Atlanta reported that several trees and power lines were down in the Mountain Park area of far north Fulton county.  Laural Street in Roswell had to be closed for up to 24 hours to clear a large downed tree from the roadway.  The damage was the result of a thunderstorm downburst.

Information and evidence received from the Baldwin County Emergency Management Agency and Fox 24 Television of Macon, Georgia, along with a subsequent tornado survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, GA, confirmed that an EF0 tornado tracked across northern Baldwin county, from just northwest to just northeast of Milledgeville.  The tornado touched down near the intersection of Pettigrew Road and Willie J. Brown Jr. Road, or approximately 3/4 mile west-southwest of the intersection of Georgia Highway 22 and Pettigrew Road.  From here, the tornado traveled on a sporadic approximately eight mile-long path to the east-northeast, just north of Milledgeville, ending at the western edge of the Milledgeville Country Club, along North Jefferson Street just north of Log Cabin Road. The maximum path width was estimated to be 75 yards wide and maximum wind gusts were estimated to be 75 to 80 mph.  The majority of the damage occurred at the beginning and ending points of the tornado, with just sporadic tree damage in between.  At the beginning point along Pettigrew Road, several large hardwood trees were either snapped or uprooted.  A portion of a metal roof was ripped off one side of a home and tossed into the neighboring trees.  At the ending point of the tornado, along North Jefferson Street, a porch was ripped off the side of one home and scattered about the adjacent woods.  The adjacent home suffered minor to moderate roof damage.  Several trees in the area were either uprooted or snapped.  Portions of North Jefferson Street were blocked for several hours from downed trees.  Several large hardwood trees were downed just west of the Milledgeville Country Club's maintenance facility, where the tornado appeared to lift.
The public observed penny-sized hail in Dawsonville.

The public reported a thunderstorm downburst that resulted in minor damage to two recreational vehicles, a portion of a roof being blown off a building, five uprooted large pecan trees, and one downed power line.  Winds were estimated to be at least 75 mph.
A storm spotter observed half-dollar-sized hail in the far southeast corner of Dodge county between Jay Bird Springs and the Telfair county line.
A storm spotter observed half-dollar-sized hail from the far northeast corner of Telfair county, just northwest of Helena and McRae to just east of McRae.
The Telfair County 911 Center observed nickel-sized hail in the Lumber City area along the Telfair/Montgomery county line.  A couple of trees were also blown down in the area.
