The Treutlen County 911 Center and the public reported considerable wind damage in the Lothair community in the southwest part of the county.  Most of the damage was along Rosemont Church Road.  Here, two barns were destroyed, one of which was a 3-sided barn with a metal roof.  The other, a large barn, completely lost its metal roof.  Three homes had sustained moderate roof damage, and a mobile home sustained serious damage.  On Georgia Highway 46, one home sustained major roof damage and broken windows from large hail.  Many large trees were either blown down, splintered, or uprooted from Lothair to Soperton.  Some roadways were blocked from downed trees.

The Treutlen County 911 Center reported that quarter-sized hail fell across the county from Lothair in the southwest to near Gillis Springs in the northeast part of the county.  Damage was observed to roofs and windows of homes in the Lothair community from strong winds and hail combined.

Literally dozens of reports of large damaging hail were received from the public across southern Coweta county from Grantville, Moreland, eastward to Senoia.  Most of the hail was the size of golf balls, but hail the size of baseballs, tennis balls, and even isolated reports of grapefruit-sized hail were received from the Grantville area eastward to just south of Moreland.  Hail decreased in size to half-dollars by the time it reached areas just south of Senoia.  Significant accumulations of hail were noted on the ground in the area and much of the region was blanketed with a hail cover for an hour or more.  Extensive damage was observed to vehicles and roofs of homes in the area.
The public observed that several power lines were blown down around Moreland.

The public observed a funnel cloud near Grantville.  This was well supported by radar data and a tornado warning was in effect for the area at the time.  Doppler indicated rotational velocities were briefly near 50 knots at this time.
The Upson County Emergency Management Director reported quarter-sized hail near Roland in west central Upson county to nickel-sized hail in east central Upson county, just south of Logtown.
The Coweta County 911 Center reported two lightning-related house fires between Grantville and Moreland in southern Coweta county.  No further details or information were provided regarding damages.

The Spalding County Emergency Management Director and the public observed quarter to golf ball-sized hail along Georgia Highway 16 near Griffin.  Quarter to golf ball-sized hail was also observed in Coweta county near the Spalding county line.  Radar data suggested that similar-sized hail continued across much of central Spalding county along Georgia Highway 16.

The Douglas County Emergency Management Director reported that a middle-aged male was shocked indirectly by a nearby lightning strike while on a riding lawn mower just outside Douglasville.  Although fire and emergency medical personnel were dispatched to the scene, no medical treatment was provided.

Several reports of golf ball-sized hail were received from the western half of Bibb county from Lizella and Lake Tobesofkee to near Macon.  There was even one report of tennis-ball-sized hail near Lizella.  The hail decreased to quarter size as the storm moved into the western suburbs of Macon and to nickel size as it moved further into Macon.  However, there were several reports within the city of Macon of hail covering the ground like snow.  Nickel-sized hail was observed at the terminal station in downtown Macon.  There was also one report of a damaged camper at a campground near Macon caused by a downed tree.

A trained storm spotter and the public observed quarter-sized hail across the far southeastern part of Bibb county from Rutland to just northeast of the Macon airport.  Radar data suggests that similar-sized hail likely continued to near Franklinton.  This hail occurred from a separate thunderstorm that tracked across the southeast part of the county shortly after another thunderstorm had dumped damaging golf ball-sized hail across west central and north central Bibb county.

The public observed quarter-sized hail west of Senoia.  This was from a second a weaker storm that tracked across southern Coweta county in the wake of the large, damaging baseball to grapefruit-size hail storm that tracked across the southern part of Coweta county one hour prior.

The public observed quarter-sized hail across far southern Meriwether county near Warm Springs.  This was from a separate cell than the one which tracked across the northern part of the county an hour or so earlier.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in the Columbus area and half-dollar-sized hail in extreme northeast Muscogee county near Upatoi.
The public observed quarter to golf ball-sized hail near Georgia Veterans Memorial State Park in the far western part of the county, then quarter-sized hail further east toward Cordele.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia in conjunction with the Crisp County Emergency Management Office confirmed that straight-line thunderstorm outflow winds up to 75 mph caused considerable damage to a mobile home on Brock Road approximately five miles east of Arabi in the southeast part of the county.  A few trees were also down in the area, but no other damage of significance was noted.  The thunderstorm outflow winds were from a severe thunderstorm producing quarter to golf ball-sized hail across north central Crisp county near Cordele.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service and the Sumter and Crisp County Emergency Management Offices confirmed that a brief EF0 tornado touched down on the Sumter county side of Lake Blackshear, approximately two miles south-southwest of Georgia Veterans Memorial State Park and lifted on the Crisp county side of Lake Blackshear.  The tornado traveled a total length of 3/4 mile from Sumter into Crisp county, with approximately 0.4 mile of this tornado path length within Sumter county.  The maximum path width was estimated to be 200 yards with maximum wind gusts estimated to be 80 mph.  Within Sumter county, two homes on the west shore of Lake Blackshear were damaged from downed trees.  A few docks on the west side also suffered minor damage.  No damage was observed on the Crisp county side of the lake as the tornado lifted before reaching the east shore of the lake.  Note, this was the first tornado to touch down within the Peachtree City, Georgia county warning area during 2011.||[03/26-03/27/11:  Tornado #1, County #1-2, EF0, Sumter-Crisp, 2011:001].

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia in conjunction with the Sumter and Crisp County Emergency Management Offices confirmed that the brief EF0 tornado that touched down in extreme southeast Sumter county on the west shore of Lake Blackshear lifted 3/4 mile across the Crisp county side of Lake Blackshear, approximately two miles south-southwest of Georgia Veterans Memorial State Park.  No damage was observed from this tornado on the Crisp county side of the lake as the tornado lifted before reaching the eastern shore.  The total tornado path length was 3/4 mile with a maximum path width of 200 yards.  Maximum winds gusts in the tornado were estimated to be 80 mph.||[03/26-03/27/11: Tornado #1, County #2-2, EF0, Sumter-Crisp, 2011:001].
The public observed golf ball-sized hail across east central Johnson county near Kite.

The Johnson County Emergency Management Director reported that quarter-sized hail covered the ground north of Swainsboro.  The public and amateur radio operators provided several reports of penny-sized hail in this same area.  Golf ball-sized hail was observed near Kite along the Emanuel county line as the storm moved out of Johnson county.  WSR-88D suggests that two separate hail storms moved across the county during this time frame.  On the first storm produced hail as large as quarters and tracked from between Kite and Blundale to near Garfield.  The second storm produced only penny-sized hail and tracked from just east of Meeks to near Twin City.

The Stewart County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down along Canyon Road or Georgia Highway 39C between Lumpkin and Providence Canyon State Park.  The Emergency Manager thought the damage might have been from a tornado and strong rotation was indicated in the area at the time.  However, no tornado damage was confirmed from this event.

A storm spotter observed golf ball-sized hail just north of the Macon Regional Airport on Hartly Bridge Road.  An amateur radio operator relayed a report of half-dollar-sized hail from southern Bibb county and a trained spotter observed quarter-sized hail in southern Bibb county, just west of Rutland.
The Crawford County Emergency Management Director reported half dollar-sized hail across east central Crawford county between Sandy Point and Jack Brown Estates.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia in conjunction with the Peach County Emergency Management Director confirmed that straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts of 75 mph removed approximately 40 percent of a secondary roof of the Days Inn Motel in Byron.  This roof was a secondary structure installed over the original roof, which was not damaged.  A nearby billboard also sustained minor damage.

The public observed ping-pong ball-sized hail near Fort Oglethorpe and quarter-sized hail near Lakeview.  WSR-88D data suggests that similar-sized hail likely continued southeastward across the county toward Tunnel Hill.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of quarter to half-dollar-sized hail hail near Eton.  Radar data suggests that similar-sized hail was likely across much of the county from the west central to the southeast areas near Fort Mountain State Park.

The public observed quarter-sized hail across far northern Walker county near Rossville.  WSR-88D suggests that hail of similar size likely occurred across much of the northern one-third of the county.

A trained storm spotter observed half dollar-sized hail west of Calhoun in western Gordon county.  As the thunderstorm progressed eastward across Calhoun, the storm began to weaken and the public observed only quarter-sized hail across Calhoun.  The storm weakened further as it moved east-southeast toward Fairmount, producing nickel-sized hail in the far southeast part of the county.

The public observed quarter-sized hail across the Rome area.  WSR-88D suggests that similar-sized hail likely fell from northwest of Rome to east of Lindale.  The public also reported that wind gusts were on the order of 45 mph and were strong enough to blow over an outdoor cooking grill.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down in northeast Laurens county, approximately 1.8 miles west of Brewton, then traveled 3.5 miles to the east, lifting approximately 1.7 miles east of Brewton.  The tornado had a maximum path width of 500 yards with maximum winds estimated to be 90 mph.  Thirty structures were damaged along the path of the tornado, mostly residential homes.  The damage was mostly the result of large trees blown down onto the structures.  A few homes sustained minor roof and siding damage independent of the downed trees.  A front porch was also blown off one of the homes.  Several hundred trees were blown down, snapped, or uprooted along the path of the tornado.||[03/26-03/27/11: Tornado #2, County #1-1, EF1, Laurens, 2011:002].

The Sumter County Emergency Management Director reported that one home and a barn, approximately five miles east of Americus along Georgia Highway 27, sustained at least moderate damage from strong thunderstorm winds gusts.  Dozens of trees were also down in the vicinity.
The Sumter County Sheriff observed a funnel cloud approximately five miles east of Americus.  WSR-88D indicated weak rotation in the area at the time.
The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director observed quarter-sized hail approximately five miles northeast of Waleska.
The public observed quarter-sized hail across southern Bartow county.

The public observed golf ball-sized hail west of Kennesaw and near Due West, with quarter-sized hail southwest of Acworth and near Marietta.  WSR-88D suggests that at least quarter-sized hail continued southeast across the county toward Smyrna and Vinings.  Wind gusts of 45 mph were also noted at two separate locations in the county during this storm.
The public observed penny-sized hail southwest of Winston.  WSR-88D suggests that similar-sized hail continued across the southern half of the county.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in eastern Forsyth county from Cumming eastward to the Hall county line.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in far southern Forsyth county, in the Brookwood vicinity.

The public observed golf ball-sized hail in Flowery Branch.  Otherwise, mostly quarter-sized hail was observed elsewhere across the southern part of Hall county near Oakwood and Flowery Branch.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that quarter-sized hail likely continued eastward toward Chestnut Mountain.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in the Lawrenceville area.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that most of this occurred south and southeast of Lawrenceville.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Winder.
Amateur radio operators relayed reports of quarter-sized hail from Thomaston to just east of Thomaston.
The Bibb County Emergency Management Director observed penny-sized hail in downtown Macon.
The Greene County 911 Center reported that a structure on Fuller Road was struck by lightning and set on fire.  No further specific details were provided.
The public observed quarter-sized hail across the northern part of the county, just south of Maysville.

A storm spotter observed nickel-sized hail in western Upson county between Crest and Thomaston.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that penny to quarter-sized hail likely continued eastward to Redbones Crossroads.
The Greene County 911 Center relayed reports of quarter-sized hail in the far southeastern part of the county between Siloam and White Plains.

The Upson County 911 Center relayed reports of widespread quarter-sized hail across the southern part of the county.  The hail lasted from 10 to 15 minutes across the southern sections from Sprewell Bluff State Park, to south of Thomaston, to east of Logtown, near the Crawford county line.  This hail occurred with a separate thunderstorm cell from the one which produced, nickel-sized hail across the northern part of the county earlier.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of quarter-sized hail across northern Crawford county just south of Musella.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail likely fell from where it ended in Upson county just east of Logtown to the Bibb county line east of Sandy Point.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of quarter-sized hail across western Bibb county, approximately two miles south of Lizella.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail occurred from the Crawford county line west of Lizella to a point approximately four miles east-southeast of Lizella.

The Crawford County Emergency Management Director reported golf ball-sized hail just north of Roberta.  This hail fell from a separate thunderstorm cell from that which tracked across the northern part of the county producing quarter-sized hail near Musella, 40 to 45 minutes prior.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that quarter to golf ball-sized hail likely fell from just northwest to immediately east of Roberta.

A storm spotter observed quarter-sized hail across northern Laurens county just south of Tuckers Crossroads.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail fell from this area east-southeast to the Johnson county line near Scott, where nickel-sized hail was reported.

Amateur radio operators relayed reports that several trees were down across far northern and northeastern Laurens county from just southwest of Tuckers Crossroads to Brewton and Lovett.  Trees were down on Georgia Highway 319 near Lovett.  An amateur radio operator estimated that winds were sustained at 40 mph with gusts to 60 mph approximately four miles southeast of Tuckers Crossroads or about eight miles north of Dublin.

The Johnson County Emergency Management Director reported nickel-sized hail from the Scott area.  As the thunderstorm moved east-southeast it intensified.  The public and a trained spotter observed half-dollar-sized hail to golf ball-sized hail in Adrian along the Emanuel county line.
A trained spotter observed golf ball-sized hail from Adrian to Nunez.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that quarter-sized hail likely continued to Lexsy before the storm weakened below severe limits.

The public observed quarter-sized hail across northern Stewart county between Omaha and Louvale.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that quarter-sized hail likely fell across much of northern Stewart county, eastward toward Brooklyn.
The public and the Treutlen County 911 Center reported quarter-sized hail across the southern part of Treutlen county from Lothair, to Soperton, to Zaidee.
The public observed quarter-sized hail across northern Webster county near Preston.

Several reports of large damaging hail, ranging in size from golf balls to baseballs, were received from the public and the Sumter County 911 Center from across the county.  While the hail initially began as quarter-sized hail is it entered the northwestern part of the county north of Plains, it grew to golf ball and baseball size as it moved across Americus.

Several reports of quarter to golf ball-sized hail were received from the Dooly County 911 Center and the public across northern Dooly county, especially from the Pinehurst area.  Hail was observed from Byromville in the west to southeast of Unadilla in the east part of the county.

The Pulaski County Sheriff's Office observed golf ball-sized hail approximately five miles south of Hawkinsville.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that quarter to golf ball-sized hail likely fell across the county from west of Hawkinsville to southeast of Hawkinsville.
The public observed quarter-sized hail between Eastman and Plainfield.
The Montgomery County 911 Center reported quarter-sized hail near Mount Vernon.
The public observed quarter-sized to half-dollar-sized hail across the northern part of the county near Vidalia.
The Wheeler County 911 Center reported hail of unknown size across the county.  However, quarter-sized hail was supported by WSR-88D radar data in conjunction with reports from adjacent counties.
A storm spotter observed nickel-sized hail near Fort Valley.

Quarter-sized hail was observed by the Fort Benning military police at Lawson Army Air field and by the public in Fort Benning elsewhere within Fort Benning.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail likely continued eastward to just north of Cusseta before the thunderstorm dissipated.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in extreme western Coweta county, east of Powers Crossroads and well west of Newnan.
The public observed quarter-sized hail near Rome.

The public observed penny-sized hail near Dawnville.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail, possibly even larger, likely fell from west to east across the county from Tunnel Hill to Dawnville.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail east of Dublin near Brewton.  This is the same thunderstorm cell that spawned an EF1 tornado near Brewton.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of wind gusts to 50 mph at Midway school.  A few power lines were blown down in the area.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail around Fairplay.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail likely fell across much of far southern Douglas county from west of Fairplay to east of Hannah.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in the far southwest corner of Talbot county between Upatoi and Geneva near the Muscogee county line.

The Crawford County Emergency Management Director reported nickel-sized hail in extreme northeast Crawford county between Sandy Point and the Bibb county line.  This storm intensified as it moved into Bibb county and produced golf ball to tennis ball-sized hail near Lizella.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail and wind gusts of 50 mph, possibly greater, across northeast Polk county between Aragon and Taylorsville.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of quarter-sized hail from extreme northeast Harris county near the Meriwether county line and Georgia Highway Alternate 85.
Amatuer radio operators relayed reports of quarter-sized hail across northern Twiggs county, especially near Dry Branch.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of quarter-sized hail on the south side of Thomaston.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that hail of this size, possibly larger, likely fell from Sprewell Bluff State Park on the Talbot county border to just southeast of Thomaston.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail near Irwinton.

A storm spotter observed a funnel cloud just south of the Macon Regional Airport.  WSR-88D radar data detected a mesocyclone that traversed the area from Jack Brown Estates in extreme eastern Crawford county to near Elberta in Houston county during this time frame.
The public observed hail slightly less than quarter-size east of Alpharetta.

The public reported that a large pine tree was blown down across their privacy fence and also scraped the side of the house.  The tree tore off two screens and broke one window on the home.  Pea-sized hail was also observed at the time.
The public observed quarter-sized hail near Dahlonega.  Minor damage to vehicles was noted in the area.

The public reported that damaging straight-line thunderstorm winds caused considerable damage to trees and property around Dawsonville.  Dozens of trees were blown down and several homes sustained at least minor damage.  One individual reported that almost two-dozen shingles were blown off the roof of their home by the high winds.
A storm spotter observed penny-sized hail near Ringgold.

The Dade County 911 Center reported that approximately six trees were down across the northern part of the county.  At least one tree was down in the New Home Community and another was down in Murphy Hollow.

The Walker County 911 Center reported that nearly a dozen trees and almost as many power lines were down across the northern part of the county near the Tennessee line, but mainly in the Rossville area.  Power outages were noted in the Rossville area, where at least 200 people were without power during the peak of the event.
The Catoosa County 911 Center reported that four to five trees were down across the northern part of the county, but especially in the Fort Oglethorpe area.

The Walker County 911 Center reported that a second line of severe thunderstorms tracked across the southern part of the county producing wind damage once again.  This time, at least six trees and two power lines were down near LaFayette.
The Chattooga County 911 Center reported that at least three trees were down across the county, one of which was down on a power line in Trion on 11th Street.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported extensive and widespread damage to trees, power lines, and property across Floyd county as a line of severe thunderstorms tracked from northwest to southeast across the county.  Hundreds of trees were down across the county, many of which fell on power lines.  Dozens of homes and other structures were also damaged by the downed trees.  At least five house fires were the result of downed trees and power lines.  Many roads across the county were blocked throughout the night from numerous downed trees.

A survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia in conjunction with the Gilmer County Emergency Management Director confirmed that a brief EF1 tornado, sandwiched between two microbursts, had touched down in west central Gilmer county approximately 3.5 miles southeast of Tails Creek or just northeast of Carters Lake and traveled east-northeast 2.6 miles before lifting.  The maximum path width was determined to be 1/2 mile wide with maximum winds estimated to be 100 mph.  Hundreds of trees were either blown down, uprooted, or snapped along the path of the tornado as it traveled through the Rose Garden subdivision.  Approximately 100 homes in this area sustained at least minor damage as large trees fell on the structures.  Several sustained major damage.  There were reports from Atlanta television media that several people were trapped in their homes during this event, but this information was not confirmed.  No injuries or fatalities were reported from this event.||[04/04-04/05/11: Tornado #1, County #1-1, EF1, Gilmer, 2011:003].

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia in conjunction with the Gilmer County Emergency Management Director confirmed that a second EF0 tornado, again in combination with two brief microbursts, touched down approximately two miles north-northeast of Tails Creek almost simultaneously with the EF1 tornado that touched down southeast of Tails Creek.  This tornado also had a path width of 1/2 mile with maximum winds estimated to be 80 mph.  This EF0 tornado tracked 1.9 miles east-northeast before lifting.  Again, several hundred trees were either blown over, uprooted, or snapped along the path of the tornado.  The event likely consisted of two brief tornado segments either side of a longer lasting microburst.  Six chicken houses were either destroyed or heavily damaged.  A horse stable was also destroyed.  Three outbuildings were also heavily damaged.  No damage to homes was observed from this tornado.||[04/04-04/05/11: Tornado #2, County #1-1, EF0, Gilmer, 2011:004].
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of baseball-sized hail between Resaca and Nickelsville.  As the storm first intensified to the west near Resaca, it initially produced penny-sized hail.

The Gordon County 911 Center reported that a number of trees and several power lines were down from Nickelsville to just southeast of Calhoun.  The worst damage appeared to be around Nickelsville near the Murray county line where over a dozen trees were down and several power lines.  Further south, at least two power poles were down near the intersection of Interstate-75 and Georgia Highway 53 just east of Calhoun.  The public reported that awnings of a home were damaged from high winds in Calhoun.

The Murray County 911 Center reported that more than six trees were down across the southern end of the county, generally south of a line from the North Georgia Speedway to Ramhurst and toward Carters Lake.
The Whitfield County 911 Center reported that several, probably at least a dozen, trees and power lines were down across the northern end of the county between Cohutta and Beaverdale.
The Whitfield County 911 Center relayed several reports of penny to quarter-sized hail from the Dalton area.
The Pickens County 911 Center reported that over a dozen trees and a number of power lines were down across the county.  The most concentrated damage appeared to be in and around Jasper.
The Polk County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were down across the county, but especially around Cedartown.

The Fannin County 911 Center reported widespread damage to trees and power lines throughout the county from destructive thunderstorm wind gusts.  Over 40 trees were estimated to be down across the county with at least a dozen power lines down.  A chicken house approximately four miles east-southeast of Morganton suffered heavy damage.
The Bartow County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were down, mainly across the northern part of the county near Adairsville.

The Bartow County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were also down in the southern part of the county, especially around Euharlee as the southern part of the line of severe thunderstorms moved across that part of the county.
The public observed quarter-sized hail between Ivy Log and Blairsville.

The Union County Emergency Management Director reported that hundreds of trees and dozens of power lines were down throughout the county.  Four homes sustained minor to moderate damage from downed trees.  Fifty-four roads were closed, at least temporarily, from downed trees.  Much of the county was left without power for many hours.  The public reported that at least nine trees were down in the far western part of the county near the Fannin county line at a private residence.  Two of the trees fell on the home resulting in major damage to the structure.
The Towns County 911 Center reported that many trees and several power lines were down across the county.
The public observed quarter-sized hail in Young Harris.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that penny to quarter-size hail likely continued eastward across the county toward Titus.

The Paulding County 911 Center and amateur radio operators reported that dozens of trees and a number of power lines were down across the county.  Some of the worst damage was noted along Buchanan Highway west of Dallas and toward Burnt Hickory Ridge north of Dallas.  Amateur radio operators reported that the roof was blown off the Holy Cross Lutheran Church in Hiram.

The public observed golf ball-sized hail in the McClendon Creek subdivision.  The only area of the county where WSR-88D radar data suggested that hail of this size would have occurred was near Browning in the far southeast part of the county.
The Lumpkin County 911 Center reported that three to four trees were down across the county, including a couple which were down on roads in Dahlonega.
The White County 911 Center reported that at least a half-a-dozen trees were down across the county, mainly around Cleveland.
The Haralson County 911 Center reported that three trees were down, one in Buchanan, one tree just north of Buchanan, and one in Bremen.  Pea-sized hail was also observed near Bremen.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that extensive damage to trees and minor damage to structures along Georgia Highway 5 near Whitesburg in the southeast corner of Carroll county was the result of straight line thunderstorm winds and not a tornado.  Hundreds of trees were flattened along a five mile long path beginning near the intersection of Georgia Highway 5 and Reese Road traveling northeast to near the intersection of Georgia Highway 5 and Ringer Road.  Minor roof damage was noted to a few homes along the westernmost portion of the path.  Two trees were also down just north of Carrollton from a separate part of the line of thunderstorms.  The damage near Whitesburg appeared to be the result of a localized downburst along the line of severe thunderstorms or QLCS.
The Carroll County 911 Center reported penny-sized hail near Villa Rica.  WSR-88D suggested that similar-sized hail likely fell from the Haralson county line, just north of Abilene to Villa Rica.
The Cobb County 911 Center reported that several trees and power lines were down in the northwest part of the county near Kennesaw.

The Cobb County 911 Center reported that a second area of thunderstorm wind damage was observed in the southern part of the county.  Several trees and power lines were down from Austell to Mableton and eastward toward the Fulton county line.
Amateur radio operators relayed several reports of quarter-sized hail from Austell to Smyrna.

The Douglas County Emergency Management Director reported quarter-sized hail around Douglasville.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that quarter-sized hail likely fell across much of northern Douglas county from just northwest of Douglasville to Sweetwater Creek State Park.
The public reported that a tree was down on a houe and a vehicle in Chapel Hill.  The Douglas County 911 Center reported that another tree was down on a power line in Douglasville.
The public observed quarter-sized hail, possibly larger, in the far southeast corner of the county near Corinth.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees and power lines were down across the south end of the county from Palmetto to College Park, but a number of trees were down across the central and northern part of the county as well.  Trees were down on Old National Highway/Georgia Highway 279 and also Flat Shoals Road.  Several large trees also fell across the Georgia Tech campus, just north of downtown Atlanta.  One large downed tree caused significant damage to two dormitories and resulted in the displacement of 32 residents.  The public reported that trees and power lines were down in the central and northern part of the county in the Midtown area of Atlanta.  While not occurring during this actual event, a tree, weakened by the strong winds of these thunderstorms, fell on a 22-year old male in north Atlanta at 815 am EDT the next morning.  Widespread power outages were also reported throughout Atlanta and much of Fulton county following this event.
The Clayton County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees and power lines were down across the county, but mostly in the Jonesboro and northeast part of the county.

The Barrow County Emergency Management Director reported dozens of trees and power lines down throughout the county, with the worst damage in the Auburn and Winder areas.  Two homes in Winder sustained significant damage from downed trees.  The Barrow County Administrative Building suffered minor to moderate wind damage.  The County Health Building was closed because of this damage.  Georgia Highway 11 was closed between Pumpkin Junction and Watson Road as a result of numerous downed trees and power lines affecting the roadway.  Wind gusts of 58 mph were measured both by the public and an amateur radio operator in Auburn.

Numerous reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received from the Gwinnett County 911 Center, amateur radio operators, and the public across the entire county.  At least two reports of wind gusts near 58 mph were also received.  Wind damage was widespread with dozens of trees and power lines down throughout the county from Norcross to Lilburn, Lawrenceville, Dacula, and Grayson.  Less damage was noted in the northern part of the county.  The most significant damage appeared to be in the Lilburn area, where several homes suffered structural damage from downed trees.
The public observed quarter to possibly larger-sized hail.

The Banks County Emergency Management Director reported that more than a dozen trees were down across the county, including three on Interstate-85 near Banks Crossing.  Nearly the entire county was left without power following the damaging thunderstorm winds.
The Jackson County 911 Center reported that dozens of trees were down across the county.  The public reported that a sign at the Nicholson Baptist Church was destroyed by the strong winds.

The Fayette County 911 Center reported that over two dozen trees were down across the north end of the county, especially in the Sandy Creek, Kenwood, and west Fayetteville areas.  Trees were down on along Georgia Highway 92 near the Fulton County line, on Sandy Creek Road, Gingercake Lane, and Kenwood Road.  The Fayette County Emergency Management Director reported that a suspected microburst caused caused damage to the roof of Fire Station No. 3 in Tyrone.
The Coweta County 911 Center reported widespread tree and power line damage throughout the county.  Several dozen trees were down across the county, as well as many power lines.
The public observed golf ball-sized hail approximately five miles southwest of Palmetto near Cannongate near the intersection of Georgia Highway 54 and U.S. Highway 29.

The Harris County 911 Center reported that nearly two dozen trees were down across the county.  Most of the damage appeared to be concentrated in the West Point Lake and Cataula areas.  In Cataula, the public reported minor damage to their home when three trees came down in their yard.  One of the trees took out the electric line to the property.

The Merwiether County Emergency Management Director reported widespread thunderstorm wind damage across the county.  Dozens of trees and power lines were down across the county.  A total of four homes were damaged in the county.  Two mobile homes in Greenville were completely moved off their foundations.  One of the homes was destroyed, while the other was heavily damaged.  No evidence of a tornado was found.  The sun room of another home was damaged from a downed tree.  The two other homes sustained minor damage.  Ten roads across the county were closed from downed trees and power lines.

The Muscogee County 911 Center reported that more than six trees and at least one power line were down, mainly across the southern part of Columbus.  One home in the south part of Columbus sustained damage from a downed tree.

The public observed golf ball-sized hail near Hampton.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that golf ball-sized hail was more likely observed near Luella and Locust Grove, with quarter-sized hail near Hampton.

Reports from the public and the Newton County 911 Center indicated that between five and six dozen trees were down in the western part of the county near the Rockdale county line.  A number of power lines were also down in this area as well.  Many trees and power lines were down in other parts of the county as well.  One mobile home sustained damage from a downed tree.  Up to 15 roads were closed as a result of downed trees and power lines.
The Walton County 911 Center reported that nearly two dozen trees were down across the county.

The Butts County Emergency Management Director reported that over 100 trees were down across the entire county.  One large tree fell on a home on Seventh Street in Jackson killing a 34-year old man along with his 4-year old son.  In addition to the widespread tree damage, the side of an outbuilding near Stark suffered significant damage when one side was blown away.

The Monroe County Emergency Management Director reported that dozens of trees and several power lines were down throughout the county.  Considerable damage was noted in High Falls State Park in the northwest corner of the county and within the city of Forsyth.  A motorist was trapped in their vehicle in Forsyth at Georgia Highway 42 and Sharp Street when a large tree fell on the vehicle.  The roof was blown off a home three miles south of High Falls State Park.  Three other homes in the county suffered minor damage.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report that several large pine trees were down in the Concord area in the west central part of the county.

The Upson County Emergency Management Director reported that dozens of trees and power lines were down throughout the county.  Power outages were widespread.  Four structures in the county suffered minor damage from either downed trees and/or wind damage.  Georgia Highway 36 was blocked at the railroad track because of a large tree down across the track.
The Madison County 911 Center reported that more than a dozen trees and power lines were down across the county, but especially the northern half.
The Oconee County 911 Center reported that more than a dozen trees were down across the county.
The Oglethorpe County 911 Center reported that several dozen trees were down throughout the county.

The Marion County 911 Center reported extensive and widespread damage to trees and power lines across the county.  Several homes and business sustained minor to moderate damage from downed trees on the structures, especially within the city of Buena Vista.  Over 12 roads were closed as a result of downed trees and power lines.

The Stewart County Sheriff's Office reported that about a dozen trees were down across the county, including two at Florence Marina State Park, several near the county high school on Green Grove Road in Lumpkin, and at least one near Richland.  A cable line was also down in Richland as a result of downed trees and/or wind.
The Webster County 911 Center reported that over half-a-dozen trees were down across the county.
The Jasper County 911 Center reported that more than six trees were down across the county.  Some of the trees were blocking roadways.

The Morgan County Emergency Management Director reported that thunderstorm winds had caused extensive damage throughout the county.  A storm spotter reported that anywhere from 60 to 80 trees were down across the county.  At least five homes in the Madison area were damaged as a result of downed trees.  A family was trapped in one of these damaged homes, but was removed safely and without injury.  In addition, the roof was blown off a home in Buckhead.

The Crawford County Emergency Management Director reported that wind damage was widespread across the county.  Dozens of trees and power lines were down across the county.  Amateur radio operators reported that at least two dozen large trees were down just along U.S. Highway 80 east of Roberta.  Four homes sustained major damage from downed trees.  A fourth of the roof of the Crawford County Middle School sustained significant damage from wind.  Power outages were widespread across the county.
The Jasper County 911 Center relayed reports of penny-sized hail near Monticello.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar, possibly larger hail, fell near Turtle Cove and the Butts county line.

The Taylor County Emergency Management Director reported extensive and widespread damage across the county from hundreds of downed trees and dozens of downed power lines.  Up to 30 homes in the county sustained minor to moderate damage, with one home sustaining major damage.  In addition, five businesses were damaged.  Damage was particularly severe in the Reynolds area.  Parts of Taylor county, including the city of Reynolds, were declared in a local state of emergency as a result of the widespread damage.
The Dooly County 911 Center reported that more than a dozen trees were down across the county.  Scattered power outages were noted.
The Macon County 911 Center reported that at least 10 trees were down across the county.

The Schley County Sheriff's Office reported widespread downed trees and several power lines across the county.  At least a dozen trees were down across the county.  Three structures sustained damage from downed trees.

The Sumter County Emergency Management Director reported that approximately two dozen trees were down across the county.  At least 10 trees were down in Americus and nearly a dozen trees were down in the western end of the county near Plains.
The Putnam County 911 Center reported that at least half-a-dozen trees were down across the county, probably more.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that a brief EF1 tornado had touched down in southern Bibb county, approximately two miles southwest of Skipperton.  The tornado path length was approximately 1.1 miles long, maximum path width was 50 yards, and maximum wind speeds were estimated to be 105 mph.  The tornado touched down near the intersection of Sardis Church Road and Goodall Mill Road and tracked northeast 1.1 miles before lifting just east of the 6900 block of Andalusia Drive.  Around 100 trees were either blown over, uprooted, or snapped along the path of the tornado.  Nine homes suffered minor to moderate damage from downed trees and/or the tornadic winds.  One of the homes sustained significant damage when the wind blew out the garage and caused the entire home to shift off its foundation.  No fatalities or injuries were reported in conjunction with this tornado.||[04/04-04/05/11: Tornado #3, County #1-1, EF1, Bibb, 2011:005].

The Macon ASOS in southern Bibb County at the Middle Georgia Regional Airport recorded a wind gust of 65 mph at 137 am EDT.  The Bibb County Emergency Management Director reported that wind damage across the county was widespread.  Dozens of trees and power lines were down countywide, even outside the small area affected by the EF1 tornado, just southwest of Skipperton.  Seven roads across the county were closed as a result of downed trees and power lines.  Several homes sustained minor damage as a result of downed trees.  Heard Elementary school sustained significant roof damage, on the order of $12,000.

The Houston County Emergency Management Director reported that a number of trees and power lines were down across the northern part of the county from Centerville to Warner Robins.  Near Warner Robins, a number of trees were down on cars and homes causing minor to moderate damage.  Trees were also down around Centerville, with amateur radio operators reporting that Crestwood Drive at Crestwood Circle was blocked in Centerville by a large downed tree.

The Jones County Sheriff's Office reported that several trees and power lines were down across the county.  Five homes in the county sustained minor to moderate damage from downed trees.  Two roads were closed from downed trees and power lines.
The Peach County 911 Center reported that at least a half-a-dozen trees and power lines were down across the county.  Power lines and trees were down in Byron and Fort Valley.

The Twiggs County Emergency Management Director and the 911 Center reported that dozens of trees and power lines were down from Dry Branch to Jeffersonville, with a few other trees and power lines down in other parts of the county as well.  The hardest hit areas were in Dry Branch and Jeffersonville.  In Dry Branch, multiple trees were down on Georgia Kaoline Road.  One large tree was down on a home in Dry Branch with people trapped inside the structure.  In Jeffersonville, more than a dozen trees were down just within the city limits.
The Wilkinson County 911 Center reported widespread tree damage across the entire county.  Dozens of trees were down throughout the county.

The Hancock County Emergency Management Director reported that dozens of trees were down across the county, including several on homes.  Several people were trapped in homes from downed trees, but no injuries were reported.
The Warren County 911 Center reported that dozens of trees and power lines were down throughout the county.  Five homes in the county sustained minor damage from downed trees.
The Wilkes County Emergency Management Director reported that more than a dozen trees and several power lines were down across the county.  Two homes sustained minor to moderate damage.
The Crisp County Emergency Management Director reported that dozens of trees and power lines were down across the county.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF2 tornado tracked across northern Dodge county.  The tornado touched down approximately 10 miles northwest of Eastman near Friendship UMC Road, just outside the Gresston community, and traveled east-northeast to near the intersection of Friendship UMC Road and U.S. Highway 23.  The maximum path width was determined to be 50 yards wide with maximum winds of 130 mph.  At the initial touch down location of the tornado, a double-wide mobile home was completely destroyed.  A 45-year old male who resided in this mobile home, was killed.  Two other residents of the home suffered injuries.  Several trees nearby were also blown over or uprooted.  Further east near the end of the tornado's path, another mobile home had its roof and front porch destroyed.||[04/04-04/05/11: Tornado #4, County #1-1, EF2, Dodge, 2011:006].

The Dodge County 911 Center reported widespread damage to trees and power lines across the county.  Structural damage was reported to some homes near Chauncey in southeast Dodge county when trees fell on the structures.  This damage was in addition to the EF2 tornado that struck just outside the small community of Gresston, northwest of Eastman.

The Laurens County 911 Center reported that a few trees and a number of power lines were down, especially across the central portion of the county from Dexter to Rockledge.  An amateur radio operator reported that a tree was down on Interstate-16 near Rockledge blocking at least one of the eastbound lanes.
The Washington County 911 Center reported widespread damage to trees and power lines throughout the county.  Several dozen trees and power lines were down across the county.
A National Weather Service employee confirmed that a storage shed was blown over by straight-line winds, likely less than 50 knots.
The public observed nickel-sized hail southeast of Dexter.

The Greene County Emergency Management Director reported that dozens of trees were down throughout the county.  The Greshamville community in the western part of the county experienced the most damage.  Trees were down on Georgia Highway 15 near Greensboro as well.  Property damage across the county consistent of damage to a hanger at the Greene county airport, an EMS unit, and a high pressure natural gas main line.

The Johnson County Emergency Management Director reported that dozens of trees and a number of power lines were down throughout the county.  However, the majority of the damage was between Meeks and Kite in the southeast part of the county.  Georgia Highway 15 was blocked from downed trees in Wrightsville.  More than hundred residents of the county were left without power for several hours following the storms.
The Emanuel County 911 Center reported that dozens of trees were down across the county.
The Toombs County 911 Center reported that at least three trees were down around Lyons.
The Treutlen County 911 Center reported that at least three trees were down in the Orianna and Soperton areas.

The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported that a 22-year old male was killed when a large tree fell on his vehicle while driving along Tilden Street in the Howell Station neighborhood of Atlanta.  The tree was weakened by severe thunderstorms the evening before.  However, wind gusts of 30 to 35 mph were common in the area at the time and a wind advisory was in effect for the entire area when the fatal incident occurred.

The Gilmer County 911 Center reported that a number of trees and several power lines were down throughout the county, even outside the two areas in the west central part of the county affected by tornadoes.
The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that a home in Rome was struck by lightning.  Specific details regarding damages were not provided.

The Bleckley County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees and power lines were down across the county.  One road was closed as a major power transmission line was down across the road.

The Henry County Emergency Management Director reported significant and widespread damage across the county from downed trees.  Fourteen homes across the county were damaged from downed trees.  At one of the affected homes, a person was trapped and injured.  The person was later extricated and taken to a local medical facility.  Seventy-five roads across the county were impacted by downed trees and power lines, including Interstate-75 near mile marker 216.

The Pulaski County Emergency Management Director reported that up to 30 trees were down across the county.  A number of power lines were down as well.  Several roads were blocked at the height of the storm and Wood Street in Hawkinsville remained blocked from downed trees into the next day.  One mobile home was destroyed by a downed tree and two other homes sustained minor to moderate damage.
The Spalding County Emergency Management Director reported extensive damage to trees and power lines throughout the county.  Several homes were damaged from downed trees.

The Telfair County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees and power lines were down across the county.  However, much of the damage occurred in the Lumber City area in the far southeastern part of the county.  Here, one unit of the Village Square Apartments was destroyed and three other units sustained minor to moderate damage.
The Wilcox County Emergency Management Director reported that one home sustained minor damage from downed trees and thunderstorm wind, while another sustained minor damage.
The Henry County Emergency Management Director reported that two homes in the county sustained minor damage from lightning-related fires.
The Union County Emergency Management Director reported that there were two lightning-related structural fires in the county.  No specific details regarding damages were provided.
The Wilkinson County Emergency Management Director reported that a business was damaged in a lightning-related fire.
The Walton County Emergency Management Director reported that a single-family home was completely destroyed as a result of a lightning-related fire.

The public reported that several trees and power lines were down throughout the county.  However, damage was concentrated mainly in the southeast part of the county.  Several roads were blocked by downed trees, including Oak Grove Road, Smokey Road, Briley Road, Hamilton Road, and Stovall Road in the southeast part of the county as well as Mountville-Hogansville Road and Mooty Bridge Road in the northeast part of the county.

The Chattooga County 911 Center reported that at least a dozen trees were down across the county.  The public reported that a tree was down on a vehicle in Cloudland.  Power outages were noted in the Trion area.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the Trion area.

The Walker County 911 Center reported that at least a dozen trees were down.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that this was mainly across the southern half of the county, south of Cooper Heights and Rock Springs.
The Bartow County 911 Center reported that three trees were down near Adairsville.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that lightning struck a home about two miles west of Everett Springs.  The home was set on fire by the lightning strike, but no further details were provided regarding damages.
The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that a tree was blown down onto a home in Lindale causing at least minor damage to the structure.
The Douglas County 911 Center reported that a tree was blown down onto a home in Douglasville causing damage to the porch of the home.
The Haralson County 911 Center reported that at least a dozen trees were down, especially around Tallapoosa.
The Paulding County 911 Center reported that two homes were struck by lightning.  No details regarding specific damages were reported, but damage was assumed to be minimal to minor.

The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that at least six trees were down across the county.  WSR-88D radar data indicates that most of this occurred across the western half of the county before the storms weakened below severe limits.
The Harris County 911 Center reported that a tree was blown down onto a home in Waverly Hall.  An exterior wall of the home suffered significant damage as a result.
Amateur radio operators relayed reports of two trees down within the city of Thomaston.  Both trees fell on homes causing damage to the structures.
The public reported that a tree had fallen on a home on Spruce Street in Manchester, causing moderate damage to the roof of the home.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that extensive damage to trees in the south part of Rome toward Lindale was the result of strong straight-line thunderstorm winds, estimated to be on the order of 80 mph.  Up to 100 trees were uprooted or blown over in this area.  Two dozen homes sustained moderate to major damage.  One home was crushed by a very large tree which fell right across the middle of the structure.  In addition, at least five roads across the county were also closed as a result of downed trees.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director and the public observed quarter-sized hail on the southeast and east side of Rome.  The combination of the hail and strong winds of 70 to 80 mph resulted in significant damage to homes and vehicles throughout the area.  Although smaller pea-sized hail fell in Lindale, it completely covered the ground.

The Bartow County 911 Center reported that dozens of trees were blown down in the Adairsville area.  In addition, a large pole barn on Doris Road in Adairsville was flattened by the strong thunderstorm wind gusts.  An off duty National Weather Service meteorologist estimated wind gusts to be on the order of 60 mph along Interstate-75 east of Adairsville near mile marker 305.  One tree was down near mile marker 306 on Interstate-75 blocking one of the northbound lanes.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of ping-pong ball-sized hail near Adairsville.  The public observed penny-sized hail covering the ground east of Adairsville.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that penny to quarter-sized hail likely occurred across much of northwest and north central Bartow county from west of Adairsville to Folsom.
The public observed half-dollar-sized hail across the northwest part of Pickens county.

Several reports of hail, ranging in size from pennies to half-dollars, were received from the public across the southeast part of Gordon county from just south of Sonoraville along the Bartow county line to just east-northeast of Fairmount.

The Gordon County 911 Center reported widespread damage to trees and power lines across the southeast part of the county from Sonoraville to Fairmount and Ranger.  At least one home in the area suffered significant damage from several large trees blown down onto the structure.  Along U.S. Highway 41N, a portion of a roof of a commercial building was blown off into the adjacent parking lot.
The Gilmer County Emergency Management Director reported that up to 20 trees were blown down or uprooted across the southern part of the county.

The Union County Emergency Management Director reported that a few trees were down across the southern and southeastern part of the county.  Pea-sized hail also covered the ground in parts of Blairsville.
The Whitfield County 911 Center reported that several trees were down across the southern end of the county.
The Murray County 911 Center reported that several trees were down across the southern half of the county.

The Douglas County Emergency Management Director reported that a roof on a building in downtown Douglasville collapsed because of strong thunderstorm wind gusts.  Another building in Lithia Springs along Bankhead Highway also had a good portion of its roof torn off by strong thunderstorm wind gusts.  In addition, widespread damage to trees and power lines was observed throughout the county from just northwest of Fairplay to Lithia Springs.
The Carroll County Emergency Management Director reported penny-sized hail from the northeastern part of the county.

The public observed penny-sized hail around Douglasville.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that the intensifying thunderstorm across the county likely produced penny-sized hail from northwest of Fairplay in the southwest part of the county to Lithia Springs in the northeast part of the county.

The Harris County 911 Center reported widespread damage to trees and power lines across the county.  At least a 100 trees were down across the county.  The thunderstorm responsible for this damage tracked from just west-southwest of Mountain Hill to the northeast corner of the county, northeast of Pine Mountain Valley.  There was a brief EF0 tornado embedded within this that touched down approximately five miles southeast of Hamilton.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City confirmed that a brief EF0 tornado touched down approximately five miles southeast of Hamilton and tracked east-northeast just 0.43 mile before lifting.  The maximum path width was 50 yards with maximum wind speeds of 75 mph.  Ten trees along the path of the tornado were topped.  In addition, a gazebo and storage shed were destroyed by the tornado.  While there was widespread damage to trees and power lines across much of the county, other than the damage noted along this brief path, all of the other damage was the result of strong thunderstorm wind gusts and not a tornado.||[04/15-04/16/11: Tornado #1, County #1-1, EF0, Harris, 2011:007].

The public and amateur radio operators observed quarter, golf ball, and baseball-sized hail across the county from Mountain Hill to northeast of Pine Mountain Valley.  The largest hail, golf ball to baseball-sized was observed near and just east of Hamilton, decreasing to east of Pine-Mountain Valley.

The Cobb County 911 Center reported widespread tree and power line damage across the southeast half of the county.  Dozens of trees were down within this area.  The damage was most concentrated southeast of Marietta and near Smyrna.  Trees were down on cars near the intersection of Interstate-285 and Interstate-75 southeast of Marietta.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of quarter-sized hail just south of Smyrna.  Several reports of penny to quarter-sized hail were received from the public across eastern Cobb county near Marietta.  The public reported that hail, some as large as quarters, fell east of Marietta near the Fulton county line for up to 10 minutes.  The hail completely covered the ground at several locations.
The public observed quarter to golf ball-sized hail near and southwest of Sandy Springs in north Fulton county.  Hail as large as ping-pong balls was also observed around Roswell.

The Fulton County Emergency Management Director reported that more than 200 trees were down across the central and northern part of the county, but especially around Sandy Springs.  A large oak tree fell on a home in Sandy Springs on Riverview Road causing the house to collapse.  A couple inside the structure was trapped for several hours without injury until firefighters could remove the tree and rescue them.  The home was essentially destroyed.

The Meriwether County Emergency Management Director reported golf ball-sized hail along the southern border of the county near Manchester.  This hail was from the same supercell thunderstorm that spawned an EF0 tornado in northeast Harris county and also dumped baseball-sized hail across central and northeast Harris county near Hamilton and Pine Mountain Valley.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail from the far northern part of the county around Dunwoody.

The Lamar County 911 Center reported penny-sized hail near Barnesville.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail likely fell from the southwest corner of the county, south of Piedmont, to just southeast of Johnstonville in the east central part of the county.

Amateur radio operators and the public reported hail up to the size of half-dollars and ping-pong balls, possibly some as large as golf balls, across far northwest and north central Gwinnett county from Norcross, to Sugar Hill and Buford.  Several reports of penny to quarter-sized hail were also received from this same general area.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that the largest hail likely fell near Norcross.
The Gwinnett County 911 Center reported that at least two homes in the Norcross area were struck by lightning.  One of these, a two-story home, was set on fire and completely destroyed.
The public observed quarter-sized hail across the east central part of the county near Mount Bethel.

Amateur radio operators relayed reports that dozens of trees were down in the east central part of Cobb county near Mount Bethel.  Green Forest Parkway was closed at South Cobb Drive and South Atlanta Road.

An amateur radio operator relayed a report of penny-sized hail in the far western portion of Upson county, just north of Sprewell Bluff State Park.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that hail of similar size likely fell across much of the county from this point east-northeast to the Lamar county line northeast of The Rock.

The Monroe County Emergency Management Director reported quarter-sized hail near Forsyth.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that hail of quarter size likely began falling as the thunderstorm entered the western portion of the county near Collier then likely decreased to penny-size as the thunderstorm weakened and moved just north of Forsyth.
The Monroe County Emergency Management Director reported that lightning struck a barn near the Butts county line setting the structure on fire.  The barn was destroyed as a result.
The Gwinnett County 911 Center and the public reported that more than a half-a-dozen trees were either down or snapped half-way-up between Snellville and Lawrenceville.
The public reported that lightning struck a home on Georgia Highway 34 in Franklin setting the house on fire.  The house was completely destroyed by the fire.

The Fulton County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the Palmetto area.  A few shingles were also blown off a roof in North Fulton county in the Alpharetta area, but no other tree or structural damage was noted in that area at this time.

The Douglas County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down across the county from Fairplay to northeast of Douglasville.  The most significant damage appeared to be on the west and north side of Douglasville.  Several trees were down near the intersection of Georgia Highway 5 and Riley Road.  A large tree caused a roof to cave in on a structure located in the 6600 block of Bankhead Highway just southwest of Douglasville.

The Cobb County Emergency Management Director reported extensive and widespread thunderstorm wind damage across Cobb county from Austell, to Smyrna, to Vinings.  The most significant damage was near Austell.  In Austell, at least a dozen trees were down affecting five homes.  Four of the homes suffered minor to moderate damage, while another suffered minor damage to its roof.  The winds also ripped off a portion of the roof of a BJ's Warehouse building near Interstate-20.  Wind damage to trees was also observed in the Smyrna area where a spotter measured at least a 52 mph wind gust on personal weather equipment.  In Vinings, the public reported that a large sign was ripped off a store at a strip mall on Cobb Parkway with a tree down in the adjacent parking lot.  Several power lines were also down between Austell and Vinings, leaving over 1000 people without power.  In addition, several roads were blocked from downed trees.  Nearly two dozen trees affected roads in eastern Cobb county, including Paces Ferry, Powers Ferry, Kings Ferry, Paper Mill, Cumberland Parkway, Hurt Road, Stillhouse Road, Mabry Road, and Milford Church Road.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that straight-line thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to at least one tree and the roofs of three homes approximately two miles northeast of Fortson.  One tree has its top clipped off and three homes suffered minor shingle damage.

The Spalding County 911 Center reported that three to four trees were down from the Pike and Lamar county lines northward to the Griffin area.  A tree was down on Audubon Circle, Barnesville Road, and Ninth Street.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down within the Fort Benning Military Reservation approximately seven miles east-northeast of the Fort Benning Lawson Army Air Field or about 9.5 miles southeast of Columbus in far northern Chattahoochee county.  The tornado was determined to have a path length of 1/4 mile long with a path width of 50 yards.  The tornado removed one fourth of the roof and a portion of an exterior wall of a dormitory on the army base.  More than a dozen vehicles were tossed, turned, and flipped about by the tornado.  In addition, there were approximately 30 trees snapped, blown over, or uprooted along the path of the tornado.  There were no injuries and no fatalities from this tornado.||[04/15-04/16/11: Tornado #2, County #1-1, EF1, Chattahoochee, 2011:008].

A damage survey conducted by meteorologists from the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City, Georgia confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down approximately five miles northwest of Macon and tracked 2.5 to 3.5 miles lifting approximately five miles north-northwest of Macon.  The tornado tracked through the northern suburbs of Macon between Interstate-475 and Interstate-75, just south of the Monroe county line yet lifting just before reaching the Jones county line.  The maximum path width was determined to be 500 yards.  The maximum wind in the tornado was determined to be 110 mph.  Extensive damage was reported from a largely residential area of Bibb county.  From 20 to 25 homes sustained sustained damage.  Four of these homes were destroyed and another 10 of these suffered major damage.  A motel and an adjacent commercial building suffered roof damage.  Two storage buildings were destroyed or heavily damaged.  At least 200 trees were uprooted, snapped, or blown over by the tornado.  There were no fatalities or injuries reported from this tornado.||[04/15-04/16/11: Tornado #3, County #1-1, EF1, Bibb, 2011:009].

The USGS Stream Gage on Big Creek at Alpharetta (APHG1) reached its flood stage of 7.0 feet at 10:22 pm EDT on April 15, 2011.  The creek remained above flood stage at this location until 2:28 pm on April 17, 2011.  However, flash flooding was determined to have ended at 422 am on April 17, 2011.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal in the vicinity of the flooded creek.

The USGS Stream Gage on Sope Creek at Marietta (MARG1) reached its flood stage of 12.0 feet at 11:18 pm on April 15, 2011.  The creek remained above flood stage until 3:41 am EDT on April 16, 2011.  A vehicle was stranded in flood waters in the eastern part of the county and the basement of a home was flooded on Norman Road in Kennesaw.  Otherwise, damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the flooded creek.

The USGS stream gage on Big Creek at Cumming reached its flood stage of 6.0 feet at 1150 pm EDT on April 15, 2011.  The creek remained above flood stage until 115 pm EDT on April 16, 2011.  However, flash flooding was determined to have ended at 550 am EDT on April 16, 2011.  Damage was confined to minor debris removal adjacent to the flooded creek, especially along the Alpharetta Greenway.
The DeKalb County 911 Center reported that a large tree fell on a home in North Druid Hills causing significant damage to the structure.

A trained storm spotter reported that two large cedar trees were uprooted Round Pond Road a couple of blocks before the Lafayette High School.  The Walker County 911 Center reported that two trees were also down just east of Cedar Grove.

The Floyd County 911 Center reported that a number of trees and power lines were down across the county.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that most of this damage likely occurred between Cave Spring and Lindale, Silver Creek, and the south side of Rome.
The Cobb County 911 Center reported that a few trees were down around Marietta, especially on Pat Mell Road where one tree fell on an unoccupied vehicle.

The DeKalb County 911 Center reported that five trees and five power lines were down across the county.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that most of this likely occurred across the northern half of the county.
The public observed half-dollar-sized hail near Auraria and nickel-sized hail near Dahlonega.
A deputy with the Sandy Springs Police Department observed quarter-sized hail on the windshield of his patrol car.
The Forsyth County Emergency Management Director reported that three trees and a couple of power lines were down near Georgia Highway 369 and the town of Oscarville.

The Gwinnett County 911 Center reported that five trees and power lines were down across a couple of roads, mainly around Lawrenceville.  One of the trees fell on a van causing damage to the vehicle.  An amateur radio operator measured a wind gust of 55 mph on U.S. Highway 29 near Harbins Road.
The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director reported that lightning had struck and set a home on fire just east of Buffington.  The home suffered moderate fire and smoke damage.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report of nickel-sized hail on the east side of Duluth and south of Suwanee in northwest Gwinnett county.
The public observed nickel-sized hail on the north side of Murrayville.

The public observed penny-sized hail near Flowery Branch.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that penny-sized hail also likely fell between Flowery Branch and Lake Lanier Islands in the far southwest part of the county.  This hail was falling from a separate, yet simultaneously occurring thunderstorm north of Murrayville, which was producing nickel-sized hail.
A trained storm spotter observed nickel-sized hail for several minutes on the northwest side of Cleveland.

Several reports of quarter-sized hail were received from the public and the Cherokee County Emergency Management Director from Union Hill, in the southeast part of Cherokee county, north-northeastward to east of Buffington, near Lathemtown, northward to approximately 3 miles north-northwest of Lathemtown.

The Cherokee County Emergency Management Director reported that lightning struck and set on fire yet a second home in Cherokee county.  This time the incident was five miles east of Woodstock in the far southeast corner of the county.
The Peachtree City Police Department reported that five trees were down across the city.

The public observed nickel-sized hail near East Point.  WSR-88D radar data suggests that similar-sized hail likely fell from here northward to near Atlantic Station, just north of Atlanta.  One tree was also blown down along Cascade Road.

The Cobb County 911 Center reported that at least a dozen trees and over six power lines were down across the central and northern parts of the county, especially on the north side of Marietta and near Kennesaw.

Meteorologists with WRBL and WTVM Television in Columbus reported that a microburst or downburst had caused considerable damage in a small area on the northeast side of Columbus, or approximately one mile northeast of Kenwood.  The worst damage was near the intersection of Macon Road and Crystal Road where the Crystal Valley Mobile Home Park was located.  Other damage was noted from the Willow Bend residential area to Corporate Ridge Industrial Park.  Over 100 large mature trees, many oaks and pines, were either uprooted or split within a two to three square mile-wide area.   Several mobile homes were heavily damaged, including two of which were destroyed when large trees crushed them.  Several fences and metal gates were also destroyed when smashed by the large fallen trees.  WRBL Television reported that two injuries occurred at one of the mobile homes crushed by a large tree.  WTVM also noted wind damage just northeast of Bibb City as well, where a few more large trees were down, one of which crushed a fence.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Thomaston.
The public observed penny-sized hail near Dawsonville.
The public observed nickel-sized hail from near Red Top Mountain State Park northward about four miles, all remaining just west of the Cherokee county line.
The public observed penny-sized hail in the far southern central part of Jasper county, just south of Tate, along the Cherokee county line.

The Floyd County Emergency Management Director reported that strong thunderstorm winds, likely well in excess of 60 mph, caused widespread and extensive damage across the county.  Some of the worst damage was in the Cave Spring area.  All together, 157 homes and 13 commercial buildings sustained minor to moderate damage or were destroyed, many from downed trees.  Four injuries were reported during this event, three which occurred when a large tree fell on a vehicle and a fourth when a large tree fell on a home and injured an elderly lady.  Over 300 trees were down across the county causing 32 roads to be closed.  Over 15,000 homes and many businesses across the county were left without power for several hours.  Both Shorter University and Berry College were closed as neither institution had any power at the start of the business day.  The Emergency Manager estimated that monetary damages from this countywide thunderstorm wind event exceeded the damage that occurred later in the day with an EF2 tornado, during which the damage was more localized.

The Haralson County 911 Center reported that there were many downed trees across the county.  In addition, a tree had fallen on a home in Tallapoosa causing damage to the structure and an adjacent vehicle.
The Polk County 911 Center reported widespread damage to trees and power lines throughout the county.  No structural damage was reported.

The Catoosa County 911 Center reported that many trees were down in the northwest part of the county, especially around the city of Lakeview.  In addition, a tree was down on a home in Lakeview causing damage to the structure.

A damage survey conducted by the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Peachtree City confirmed that an EF1 tornado had touched down approximately two miles south-southwest of Trenton and tracked north-northeastward nearly nine miles, lifting just before reaching the Tennessee border.  This was the first of 15 tornadoes to touch down within the Peachtree City, Georgia forecast area during this historical tornado outbreak across the southern and eastern U.S.  The maximum tornado path width was determined to be 100 yards wide with maximum wind gusts estimated to be 100 mph.  Only very small portions of the tornado path were rated EF1, namely across Trenton and to the northeast near Lookout Mountain.  The rest of the tornado path was rated an EF0.  Several homes, mostly in the Trenton area, sustained minor damage as well as an elementary school and bank building on the south side of Trenton along Georgia Highway 136.  In addition, dozens of trees were damaged along the path of the tornado.||[04/27-04/28/11:  Tornado #1, County #1-1, EF1, Dade, 2011:010].

The Dade County Emergency Management Director reported that dozens of trees and power lines were down throughout the county, even outside the EF1 tornado path that tracked from just south-southwest of Trenton to near the Tennessee border near Wildwood.  The damage was the result of strong straight line winds of 60 mph or greater.

The Walker County 911 Center reported that several trees were down in the south central and southeast part of the county, especially around Suttles Mill.  The public reported that up to 50 treeswere down in the Flintstone area of northwest Walker county.  Another large tree was also down in the Beverly Hills subdivision in Rossville in the northeast part of the county destroying a large three-wall tin shed.
The Whitfield County Emergency Management Director reported that several trees were down across the southern half of the county.
